enrichment.interest_rationale: David's brief, civil response lacks dramatic or thematic weight.
enrichment.summary: David replies that he would have recognized her.

text:
‘Miss Murdstone has had the goodness,’ said Mr. Spenlow to me,
‘to accept the office—if I may so describe it—of my daughter
Dora’s confidential friend. My daughter Dora having, unhappily, no
mother, Miss Murdstone is obliging enough to become her companion and
protector.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Spenlow's exposition of Miss Murdstone's role is functional but unremarkable.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Spenlow explains that Miss Murdstone serves as his motherless daughter's companion and protector.

text:
A passing thought occurred to me that Miss Murdstone, like the pocket
instrument called a life-preserver, was not so much designed for purposes of
protection as of assault. But as I had none but passing thoughts for any
subject save Dora, I glanced at her, directly afterwards, and was thinking that
I saw, in her prettily pettish manner, that she was not very much inclined to
be particularly confidential to her companion and protector, when a bell rang,
which Mr. Spenlow said was the first dinner-bell, and so carried me off to
dress.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's witty reflection that Miss Murdstone is designed for assault rather than protection is sharp social commentary, even if briefly expressed before his absorption in Dora reasserts itself.
enrichment.best_quote: Miss Murdstone, like the pocket instrument called a life-preserver, was not so much designed for purposes of protection as of assault
enrichment.summary: David observes that Miss Murdstone, far from protecting Dora, is more likely a threat; he notes Dora's reluctance to be confidential with her, before he is called to dress for dinner.

text:
The idea of dressing one’s self, or doing anything in the way of action,
in that state of love, was a little too ridiculous. I could only sit down
before my fire, biting the key of my carpet-bag, and think of the captivating,
girlish, bright-eyed lovely Dora. What a form she had, what a face she had,
what a graceful, variable, enchanting manner!

not aware that it is any business of theirs, and that I repel that exhibition

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Micawber's confidence reveals Traddles as a moral comfort amid his financial embarrassments and hints at his desperate current situation (corn commission, financial strain); he also announces Mrs. Micawber's impending pregnancy and his family's disapproval, showing his pride and resilience.
enrichment.best_quote: I repel that exhibition of feeling with scorn, and with defiance!
enrichment.summary: Mr. Micawber confides that Traddles' presence is a comfort given his current difficulties; he is struggling financially from a low-paying corn commission job and has temporary embarrassments, though he expects something soon to turn up. He also reveals that Mrs. Micawber is pregnant again, and her family disapproves; he defiantly declares this is not their business.

text: Mr. Micawber then shook hands with me again, and left me.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief closing action with minimal content.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Micawber shakes hands with David again and departs.

text:
Whether I shall turn out to be the hero of my own life, or whether that station
will be held by anybody else, these pages must show. To begin my life with the
beginning of my life, I record that I was born (as I have been informed and
believe) on a Friday, at twelve o’clock at night. It was remarked that
the clock began to strike, and I began to cry, simultaneously.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The novel's opening declaration—one of literature's most famous narrative frames—establishes David's retrospective voice and the central question of identity and agency.
enrichment.best_quote: Whether I shall turn out to be the hero of my own life, or whether that station will be held by anybody else, these pages must show.
enrichment.summary: Adult David opens his narrative by asking whether he will be the hero of his own story, and recalls his birth on a Friday at midnight, when he cried as the clock struck twelve.

text:
In consideration of the day and hour of my birth, it was declared by the nurse,
and by some sage women in the neighbourhood who had taken a lively interest in
me several months before there was any possibility of our becoming personally
acquainted, first, that I was destined to be unlucky in life; and secondly,
that I was privileged to see ghosts and spirits; both these gifts inevitably
attaching, as they believed, to all unlucky infants of either gender, born
towards the small hours on a Friday night.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes folk superstitions about Friday births that colour the narrative's sense of destiny, though David ironically dismisses them.
enrichment.summary: The midwife and neighbourhood women declare that David, born on a Friday night, is destined to be unlucky and able to see ghosts—gifts supposedly given to all such infants.

text:
I need say nothing here, on the first head, because nothing can show better
than my history whether that prediction was verified or falsified by the
result. On the second branch of the question, I will only remark, that unless I
ran through that part of my inheritance while I was still a baby, I have not
come into it yet. But I do not at all complain of having been kept out of this
property; and if anybody else should be in the present enjoyment of it, he is
heartily welcome to keep it.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David humorously dismisses both superstitions, offering light comic relief while setting up the ironic framework for his narrative.
enrichment.summary: David wryly remarks that his history will show whether the luck prediction was true, and that he has never inherited the ability to see ghosts, though he bears no grudge.

text:
I was born with a caul, which was advertised for sale, in the newspapers, at
the low price of fifteen guineas. Whether sea-going people were short of money
about that time, or were short of faith and preferred cork jackets, I
don’t know; all I know is, that there was but one solitary bidding, and
that was from an attorney connected with the bill-broking business, who offered
two pounds in cash, and the balance in sherry, but declined to be guaranteed
from drowning on any higher bargain. Consequently the advertisement was
withdrawn at a dead loss—for as to sherry, my poor dear mother’s
own sherry was in the market then—and ten years afterwards, the caul was
put up in a raffle down in our part of the country, to fifty members at
half-a-crown a head, the winner to spend five shillings. I was present myself,
and I remember to have felt quite uncomfortable and confused, at a part of
myself being disposed of in that way. The caul was won, I recollect, by an old
lady with a hand-basket, who, very reluctantly, produced from it the stipulated
five shillings, all in halfpence, and twopence halfpenny short—as it took
an immense time and a great waste of arithmetic, to endeavour without any
effect to prove to her. It is a fact which will be long remembered as
remarkable down there, that she was never drowned, but died triumphantly in
bed, at ninety-two. I have understood that it was, to the last, her proudest
boast, that she never had been on the water in her life, except upon a bridge;
and that over her tea (to which she was extremely partial) she, to the last,
expressed her indignation at the impiety of mariners and others, who had the
presumption to go ‘meandering’ about the world. It was in vain to
represent to her that some conveniences, tea perhaps included, resulted from
this objectionable practice. She always returned, with greater emphasis and
with an instinctive knowledge of the strength of her objection, ‘Let us
have no meandering.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brilliant extended comic digression on the caul—mixing Dickensian satire of commercial enterprise and superstition with a richly detailed vignette of the old lady who owned it.
enrichment.best_quote: Let us have no meandering.
enrichment.summary: David describes how his birth caul was advertised for sale at fifteen guineas, then raffled for half-a-crown, eventually won by an old lady with a hand-basket who never drowned and lived to ninety-two, boasting she never went on the water except on a bridge.

text: Not to meander myself, at present, I will go back to my birth.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief transitional device signalling return to the main narrative after the caul digression.
enrichment.summary: David notes he will stop digressing and return to the subject of his birth.

text:
I was born at Blunderstone, in Suffolk, or ‘there by’, as they say
in Scotland. I was a posthumous child. My father’s eyes had closed upon
the light of this world six months, when mine opened on it. There is something
strange to me, even now, in the reflection that he never saw me; and something
stranger yet in the shadowy remembrance that I have of my first childish
associations with his white grave-stone in the churchyard, and of the
indefinable compassion I used to feel for it lying out alone there in the dark
night, when our little parlour was warm and bright with fire and candle, and
the doors of our house were—almost cruelly, it seemed to me
sometimes—bolted and locked against it.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces David's status as a posthumous child and establishes the emotional weight of his absent father—a recurring theme of loss and paternal absence.
enrichment.best_quote: There is something strange to me, even now, in the reflection that he never saw me; and something stranger yet in the shadowy remembrance that I have of my first childish associations with his white grave-stone in the churchyard.
enrichment.summary: David was born at Blunderstone in Suffolk, six months after his father's death, and recalls a melancholy childhood memory of his father's grave in the churchyard.

text:
An aunt of my father’s, and consequently a great-aunt of mine, of whom I
shall have more to relate by and by, was the principal magnate of our family.
Miss Trotwood, or Miss Betsey, as my poor mother always called her, when she
sufficiently overcame her dread of this formidable personage to mention her at
all (which was seldom), had been married to a husband younger than herself, who
was very handsome, except in the sense of the homely adage, ‘handsome is,
that handsome does’—for he was strongly suspected of having beaten
Miss Betsey, and even of having once, on a disputed question of supplies, made
some hasty but determined arrangements to throw her out of a two pair of
stairs’ window. These evidences of an incompatibility of temper induced
Miss Betsey to pay him off, and effect a separation by mutual consent. He went
to India with his capital, and there, according to a wild legend in our family,
he was once seen riding on an elephant, in company with a Baboon; but I think
it must have been a Baboo—or a Begum. Anyhow, from India tidings of his
death reached home, within ten years. How they affected my aunt, nobody knew;
for immediately upon the separation, she took her maiden name again, bought a
cottage in a hamlet on the sea-coast a long way off, established herself there
as a single woman with one servant, and was understood to live secluded, ever
afterwards, in an inflexible retirement.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduces Betsey Trotwood, one of the novel's most iconic characters, and her formidable personality through family history, including her abusive marriage and self-imposed retirement.
enrichment.best_quote: handsome is, that handsome does
enrichment.summary: David describes his great-aunt Betsey Trotwood, who was married to a younger, handsome but abusive husband, separated from him, and thereafter lived in solitary retirement in a seaside cottage.

text:
My father had once been a favourite of hers, I believe; but she was mortally
affronted by his marriage, on the ground that my mother was ‘a wax
doll’. She had never seen my mother, but she knew her to be not yet
twenty. My father and Miss Betsey never met again. He was double my
mother’s age when he married, and of but a delicate constitution. He died
a year afterwards, and, as I have said, six months before I came into the
world.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Explains the rift between Betsey and David's father, establishing the prior conflict that will drive Betsey's dramatic arrival during labour.
enrichment.best_quote: a wax doll
enrichment.summary: David reveals that Betsey took offence at his father's marriage to his mother (whom she dismissed as a 'wax doll'), and the two never met again; his father died a year after marrying.

text:
This was the state of matters, on the afternoon of, what I may be excused for
calling, that eventful and important Friday. I can make no claim therefore to
have known, at that time, how matters stood; or to have any remembrance,
founded on the evidence of my own senses, of what follows.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief scene-setting statement that marks the transition to the dramatic arrival of Betsey on the day of David's birth.
enrichment.summary: David notes that he has no personal memory of the events that follow, as they occurred during his birth.

text:
My mother was sitting by the fire, but poorly in health, and very low in
spirits, looking at it through her tears, and desponding heavily about herself
and the fatherless little stranger, who was already welcomed by some grosses of
prophetic pins, in a drawer upstairs, to a world not at all excited on the
subject of his arrival; my mother, I say, was sitting by the fire, that bright,
windy March afternoon, very timid and sad, and very doubtful of ever coming
alive out of the trial that was before her, when, lifting her eyes as she dried
them, to the window opposite, she saw a strange lady coming up the garden.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vivid portrayal of David's mother on the afternoon of his birth—her anxiety, vulnerability, and premonition of an impending visitor creates atmospheric tension.
enrichment.summary: David's pregnant mother sits by the fire on a March afternoon, distressed about her impending labour and the fatherless child she is about to bear, when she glimpses a strange lady approaching up the garden.

text:
My mother had a sure foreboding at the second glance, that it was Miss Betsey.
The setting sun was glowing on the strange lady, over the garden-fence, and she
came walking up to the door with a fell rigidity of figure and composure of
countenance that could have belonged to nobody else.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's arrival is announced with vivid physical description, building suspense as her identity becomes clear to David's anxious mother.
enrichment.summary: David's mother recognizes the strange lady as Miss Betsey Trotwood by her distinctive rigid figure and composure as she walks up the garden path.

text:
When she reached the house, she gave another proof of her identity. My father
had often hinted that she seldom conducted herself like any ordinary Christian;
and now, instead of ringing the bell, she came and looked in at that identical
window, pressing the end of her nose against the glass to that extent, that my
poor dear mother used to say it became perfectly flat and white in a moment.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's eccentric behaviour—pressing her nose against the window—is both comical and intensifies the dramatic tension of the scene.
enrichment.summary: Instead of ringing the bell, Betsey presses her nose against the window, flattening it against the glass—a gesture that shocks David's mother.

text:
She gave my mother such a turn, that I have always been convinced I am indebted
to Miss Betsey for having been born on a Friday.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief aside from adult David reflecting on the coincidence that Betsey's shock may have triggered his labour on a Friday night, connecting back to the superstitions introduced earlier.
enrichment.summary: David humorously suggests that Betsey's frightening appearance through the window may have caused his mother's labour to begin, thus fulfilling the Friday birth prophecy.

text:
My mother had left her chair in her agitation, and gone behind it in the
corner. Miss Betsey, looking round the room, slowly and inquiringly, began on
the other side, and carried her eyes on, like a Saracen’s Head in a Dutch
clock, until they reached my mother. Then she made a frown and a gesture to my
mother, like one who was accustomed to be obeyed, to come and open the door. My
mother went.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's commanding, imperious demeanour is established through vivid physical description and gesture, showing her absolute authority and unconventionality.
enrichment.best_quote: like a Saracen's Head in a Dutch clock
enrichment.summary: Betsey sweeps her eyes around the room methodically, then gestures imperiously to David's mother to come and open the door, which the frightened mother obeys.

text:
‘Mrs. David Copperfield, I think,’ said Miss Betsey; the emphasis
referring, perhaps, to my mother’s mourning weeds, and her condition.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief, conventional greeting that serves the dialogue function but lacks distinctive character voice or content.
enrichment.summary: Betsey greets David's mother, identifying her by her married name with emphasis on her mourning status.

text: ‘Yes,’ said my mother, faintly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A minimal, one-word response serving only functional dialogue continuity.
enrichment.summary: David's mother confirms her identity with a faint 'Yes'.

text:
‘Miss Trotwood,’ said the visitor. ‘You have heard of her, I
dare say?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey identifies herself as Miss Trotwood, maintaining her authoritative tone in introducing herself.
enrichment.summary: Betsey introduces herself as Miss Trotwood and asks whether David's mother has heard of her.

text:
My mother answered she had had that pleasure. And she had a disagreeable
consciousness of not appearing to imply that it had been an overpowering
pleasure.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's mother's response shows her discomfort and lack of genuine pleasure in meeting Betsey, adding subtle characterization.
enrichment.summary: David's mother faintly claims to have heard of Betsey, but with evident insincerity that betrays her discomfort.

text:
‘Now you see her,’ said Miss Betsey. My mother bent her head, and
begged her to walk in.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief transitional dialogue moving the scene forward as Betsey and David's mother enter the parlour.
enrichment.summary: Betsey observes that now David's mother sees her, and requests to enter the house.

text:
They went into the parlour my mother had come from, the fire in the best room
on the other side of the passage not being lighted—not having been
lighted, indeed, since my father’s funeral; and when they were both
seated, and Miss Betsey said nothing, my mother, after vainly trying to
restrain herself, began to cry. ‘Oh tut, tut, tut!’ said Miss
Betsey, in a hurry. ‘Don’t do that! Come, come!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's dismissive response to David's mother's tears—'Oh tut, tut, tut!'—establishes her unsympathetic, pragmatic character while David's mother's emotional breakdown shows her fragility.
enrichment.best_quote: Oh tut, tut, tut! Don't do that! Come, come!
enrichment.summary: In the parlour, David's mother begins to cry despite her efforts to restrain herself, and Betsey responds with brisk impatience.

text:
My mother couldn’t help it notwithstanding, so she cried until she had
had her cry out.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief account of David's mother continuing to cry despite Betsey's exhortations, showing the impossibility of controlling her emotions.
enrichment.summary: David's mother continues crying until she has exhausted her tears, unable to comply with Betsey's command.

text:
‘Take off your cap, child,’ said Miss Betsey, ‘and let me see
you.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's odd and commanding request to see David's mother's face signals her eccentric, intrusive authority while preparing for the moment she assesses the young widow.
enrichment.summary: Betsey orders David's mother to remove her cap so she can see her face clearly.

text:
My mother was too much afraid of her to refuse compliance with this odd
request, if she had any disposition to do so. Therefore she did as she was
told, and did it with such nervous hands that her hair (which was luxuriant and
beautiful) fell all about her face.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's mother's nervous obedience reveals her fear of Betsey; the detail that her luxuriant hair falls about her face foreshadows Betsey's next comment.
enrichment.summary: David's mother fearfully complies with Betsey's request, removing her cap; her beautiful hair tumbles about her face.

text:
‘Why, bless my heart!’ exclaimed Miss Betsey. ‘You are a very
Baby!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's exclamation—'You are a very Baby!'—crystallizes her critique of David's mother as childish and foolish, a dismissive judgment that will drive much of Betsey's subsequent behaviour.
enrichment.best_quote: You are a very Baby!
enrichment.summary: Betsey exclaims in surprise at David's mother's extreme youthfulness, apparently shocked by how young and childlike she appears.

text:
My mother was, no doubt, unusually youthful in appearance even for her years;
she hung her head, as if it were her fault, poor thing, and said, sobbing, that
indeed she was afraid she was but a childish widow, and would be but a childish
mother if she lived. In a short pause which ensued, she had a fancy that she
felt Miss Betsey touch her hair, and that with no ungentle hand; but, looking
at her, in her timid hope, she found that lady sitting with the skirt of her
dress tucked up, her hands folded on one knee, and her feet upon the fender,
frowning at the fire.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's mother's response reveals her insecurity and shame at her youth; the tender moment when she senses Betsey's gentle touch hints at a complex relationship developing.
enrichment.summary: David's mother acknowledges her youthful appearance and fears she will be an inadequate widow and mother; she senses Betsey touching her hair gently, though Betsey then turns away.

text:
‘In the name of Heaven,’ said Miss Betsey, suddenly, ‘why
Rookery?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's abrupt, seemingly random criticism of the house name introduces her tendency to seize on details and judge character by them.
enrichment.summary: Betsey suddenly asks why the house is called 'Rookery', with an edge of contempt in her tone.

text: ‘Do you mean the house, ma’am?’ asked my mother.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brief clarifying question that serves functional dialogue only.
enrichment.summary: David's mother asks whether Betsey means the house itself.

text:
‘Why Rookery?’ said Miss Betsey. ‘Cookery would have been
more to the purpose, if you had had any practical ideas of life, either of
you.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's sarcastic critique of the house name as lacking 'practical ideas of life' foreshadows her later judgment of David's father and reveals her utilitarian worldview.
enrichment.best_quote: Cookery would have been more to the purpose, if you had had any practical ideas of life, either of you.
enrichment.summary: Betsey sarcastically suggests that 'Cookery' would be a more practical name for the house, implying that both David and his mother lack practical sense.

text:
‘The name was Mr. Copperfield’s choice,’ returned my mother.
‘When he bought the house, he liked to think that there were rooks about
it.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's mother's explanation of the house name provides background information but lacks dramatic or emotional weight.
enrichment.summary: David's mother explains that her late husband named the house 'Rookery' because he liked to think there were rooks about it.

text:
The evening wind made such a disturbance just now, among some tall old
elm-trees at the bottom of the garden, that neither my mother nor Miss Betsey
could forbear glancing that way. As the elms bent to one another, like giants
who were whispering secrets, and after a few seconds of such repose, fell into
a violent flurry, tossing their wild arms about, as if their late confidences
were really too wicked for their peace of mind, some weatherbeaten ragged old
rooks’-nests, burdening their higher branches, swung like wrecks upon a
stormy sea.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A magnificent passage of atmospheric description in which the elms and rooks become metaphorical—the wind agitates them as Betsey's agitation over the house name builds, creating a vivid Dickensian Gothic mood.
enrichment.best_quote: As the elms bent to one another, like giants who were whispering secrets, and after a few seconds of such repose, fell into a violent flurry, tossing their wild arms about, as if their late confidences were really too wicked for their peace of mind.
enrichment.summary: A vivid description of the evening wind agitating tall elm trees at the bottom of the garden, causing their weathered rooks' nests to swing like wrecks on a stormy sea.

text: ‘Where are the birds?’ asked Miss Betsey.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's pointed question about the rooks sets up the revelation that there are none—another opportunity for her to criticise David's impractical romanticism.
enrichment.summary: Betsey asks where the rooks are, evidently expecting to see them given the house's name.

text: ‘The—?’ My mother had been thinking of something else.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A minimal response indicating David's mother's distraction, serving only to advance dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David's mother, lost in thought, begins a confused response about the rooks.

text: ‘The rooks—what has become of them?’ asked Miss Betsey.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey repeats her question with added emphasis, pushing David's mother to confront the discrepancy between the house's name and reality.
enrichment.summary: Betsey asks again what has become of the rooks, pressing for an answer.

text:
‘There have not been any since we have lived here,’ said my mother.
‘We thought—Mr. Copperfield thought—it was quite a large
rookery; but the nests were very old ones, and the birds have deserted them a
long while.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's mother's explanation that the nests were old and the birds had long since departed sets up Betsey's damning conclusion about David's lack of practical judgment.
enrichment.summary: David's mother explains that there have been no rooks since they lived there; the birds had deserted the old nests long ago.

text:
‘David Copperfield all over!’ cried Miss Betsey. ‘David
Copperfield from head to foot! Calls a house a rookery when there’s not a
rook near it, and takes the birds on trust, because he sees the nests!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's withering critique of David Copperfield's character—seeing himself in a romantic illusion rather than reality—is one of her most memorable speeches and reveals her keen judgment.
enrichment.best_quote: David Copperfield from head to foot! Calls a house a rookery when there's not a rook near it, and takes the birds on trust, because he sees the nests!
enrichment.summary: Betsey exclaims that the naming of the house is quintessentially David Copperfield—calling it a rookery based on illusion rather than reality, trusting in appearances.

text:
‘Mr. Copperfield,’ returned my mother, ‘is dead, and if you
dare to speak unkindly of him to me—’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's mother's passionate defence of her dead husband shows her love and loyalty, but also her weakness; her threat to assault Betsey is powerless and quickly abandoned.
enrichment.best_quote: Mr. Copperfield is dead, and if you dare to speak unkindly of him to me—
enrichment.summary: David's mother angrily defends her late husband against Betsey's criticism, threatening retaliation if Betsey continues to speak unkindly of him.

text:
My poor dear mother, I suppose, had some momentary intention of committing an
assault and battery upon my aunt, who could easily have settled her with one
hand, even if my mother had been in far better training for such an encounter
than she was that evening. But it passed with the action of rising from her
chair; and she sat down again very meekly, and fainted.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The moment David's mother collapses—her defiance immediately undermined by fainting—is both comic and tragic, showing her physical fragility in the midst of labour.
enrichment.summary: David's mother momentarily rises to strike Betsey, but the gesture fails; she immediately sits down meekly and then faints.

text:
When she came to herself, or when Miss Betsey had restored her, whichever it
was, she found the latter standing at the window. The twilight was by this time
shading down into darkness; and dimly as they saw each other, they could not
have done that without the aid of the fire.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The description of David's mother reviving and Betsey standing at the window establishes the atmospheric transition to evening and sets up the final stage of the labour narrative.
enrichment.summary: As David's mother revives, twilight is darkening into night; Betsey stands at the window, and the room is lit only by the fire.

text:
‘Well?’ said Miss Betsey, coming back to her chair, as if she had
only been taking a casual look at the prospect; ‘and when do you
expect—’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's casual question about when labour will begin serves as functional dialogue advancing the scene.
enrichment.summary: Betsey returns to her chair and asks David's mother when she expects the labour to begin.

text:
‘I am all in a tremble,’ faltered my mother. ‘I don’t
know what’s the matter. I shall die, I am sure!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's mother's panicked response reveals her terror and physical distress as labour approaches, showing the gravity of the impending birth.
enrichment.summary: David's mother expresses terror, saying she is trembling and fears she will not survive the labour.

text: ‘No, no, no,’ said Miss Betsey. ‘Have some tea.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's brisk, practical response—'Have some tea'—is in character but contributes little to the scene.
enrichment.summary: Betsey dismissively suggests that tea will help calm David's mother.

text:
‘Oh dear me, dear me, do you think it will do me any good?’ cried
my mother in a helpless manner.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's mother's anxious question about the tea's efficacy shows her desperation and reliance on Betsey, despite her earlier defiance.
enrichment.summary: David's mother asks anxiously whether tea will really help her.

text:
‘Of course it will,’ said Miss Betsey. ‘It’s nothing
but fancy. What do you call your girl?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's confident assertion and practical question about the servant's name show her assuming control of the household and taking charge.
enrichment.summary: Betsey says the tea will help, then asks for the name of the servant-girl.

text:
‘I don’t know that it will be a girl, yet, ma’am,’ said
my mother innocently.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's mother innocently clarifies that she doesn't yet know whether the baby will be a girl, misunderstanding Betsey's question.
enrichment.summary: David's mother misunderstands and says she doesn't yet know whether the unborn child will be a girl.

text:
‘Bless the Baby!’ exclaimed Miss Betsey, unconsciously quoting the

servant-girl.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's reaction—'Bless the Baby!'—ironically echoes the pincushion sentiment and shows her impatience with David's mother's misunderstanding.
enrichment.best_quote: Bless the Baby!
enrichment.summary: Betsey exclaims in exasperation, clarifying that she meant the servant-girl, not the unborn child.

text: ‘Peggotty,’ said my mother.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's mother answers simply with the servant's name, advancing the dialogue toward summoning Peggotty.
enrichment.summary: David's mother gives the servant's name as Peggotty.

text:
‘Peggotty!’ repeated Miss Betsey, with some indignation. ‘Do
you mean to say, child, that any human being has gone into a Christian church,
and got herself named Peggotty?’ ‘It’s her surname,’
said my mother, faintly. ‘Mr. Copperfield called her by it, because her

enrichment.best_quote: Do you mean to say, child, that any human being has gone into a Christian church, and got herself named Peggotty?
enrichment.summary: Betsey expresses indignation that anyone would be named Peggotty; David's mother explains it is the servant's surname, given by her late husband because her Christian name matched her own.

text:

‘Tea. Your mistress is a little unwell. Don’t dawdle.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's commanding summons to Peggotty shows her assuming complete authority in the house, speaking as if she has always lived there.
enrichment.summary: Betsey opens the parlour door and imperiously summons Peggotty, ordering her to bring tea and noting that her mistress is unwell.

text:
Having issued this mandate with as much potentiality as if she had been a
recognized authority in the house ever since it had been a house, and having

a sling, aimed a blow at Mr. Chillip’s head with it, put it on bent,
walked out, and never came back. She vanished like a discontented fairy; or
like one of those supernatural beings, whom it was popularly supposed I was
entitled to see; and never came back any more.

Until the day arrived on which I was to entertain my newly-found old friends, I
lived principally on Dora and coffee. In my love-lorn condition, my appetite
languished; and I was glad of it, for I felt as though it would have been an
act of perfidy towards Dora to have a natural relish for my dinner. The
quantity of walking exercise I took, was not in this respect attended with its
usual consequence, as the disappointment counteracted the fresh air. I have my
doubts, too, founded on the acute experience acquired at this period of my
life, whether a sound enjoyment of animal food can develop itself freely in any
human subject who is always in torment from tight boots. I think the
extremities require to be at peace before the stomach will conduct itself with
vigour.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes David's lovestruck state through humorous self-reflection about appetite and tight boots, introducing the chapter's tone.
enrichment.summary: David, lovesick over Dora, has lost his appetite and questions whether tight boots prevent proper digestion.

On the occasion of this domestic little party, I did not repeat my former
extensive preparations. I merely provided a pair of soles, a small leg of
mutton, and a pigeon-pie. Mrs. Crupp broke out into rebellion on my first
bashful hint in reference to the cooking of the fish and joint, and said, with
a dignified sense of injury, ‘No! No, sir! You will not ask me sich a
thing, for you are better acquainted with me than to suppose me capable of
doing what I cannot do with ampial satisfaction to my own feelings!’ But,
in the end, a compromise was effected; and Mrs. Crupp consented to achieve this
feat, on condition that I dined from home for a fortnight afterwards.

enrichment.summary: David arranges a simple dinner party and negotiates with Mrs. Crupp to cook, resulting in her demand for a fortnight's absence from cooking.

And here I may remark, that what I underwent from Mrs. Crupp, in consequence of
the tyranny she established over me, was dreadful. I never was so much afraid
of anyone. We made a compromise of everything. If I hesitated, she was taken
with that wonderful disorder which was always lying in ambush in her system,
ready, at the shortest notice, to prey upon her vitals. If I rang the bell
impatiently, after half-a-dozen unavailing modest pulls, and she appeared at
last—which was not by any means to be relied upon—she would appear
with a reproachful aspect, sink breathless on a chair near the door, lay her
hand upon her nankeen bosom, and become so ill, that I was glad, at any
sacrifice of brandy or anything else, to get rid of her. If I objected to
having my bed made at five o’clock in the afternoon—which I do
still think an uncomfortable arrangement—one motion of her hand towards
the same nankeen region of wounded sensibility was enough to make me falter an
apology. In short, I would have done anything in an honourable way rather than
give Mrs. Crupp offence; and she was the terror of my life.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vivid portrayal of Mrs. Crupp's tyranny through David's fearful memories, creating memorable comic characterization.
enrichment.best_quote: In short, I would have done anything in an honourable way rather than give Mrs. Crupp offence; and she was the terror of my life.
enrichment.summary: David reflects on Mrs. Crupp's power over him, describing her feigned illnesses and emotional manipulation as terrorizing.

I bought a second-hand dumb-waiter for this dinner-party, in preference to
re-engaging the handy young man; against whom I had conceived a prejudice, in
consequence of meeting him in the Strand, one Sunday morning, in a waistcoat

The ‘young gal’ was re-engaged; but on the stipulation that she
should only bring in the dishes, and then withdraw to the landing-place, beyond
the outer door; where a habit of sniffing she had contracted would be lost upon
the guests, and where her retiring on the plates would be a physical
impossibility.

To divert his thoughts from this melancholy subject, I informed Mr. Micawber
that I relied upon him for a bowl of punch, and led him to the lemons. His
recent despondency, not to say despair, was gone in a moment. I never saw a man
so thoroughly enjoy himself amid the fragrance of lemon-peel and sugar, the
odour of burning rum, and the steam of boiling water, as Mr. Micawber did that
afternoon. It was wonderful to see his face shining at us out of a thin cloud
of these delicate fumes, as he stirred, and mixed, and tasted, and looked as if
he were making, instead of punch, a fortune for his family down to the latest
posterity. As to Mrs. Micawber, I don’t know whether it was the effect of
the cap, or the lavender-water, or the pins, or the fire, or the wax-candles,
but she came out of my room, comparatively speaking, lovely. And the lark was
never gayer than that excellent woman.

I suppose—I never ventured to inquire, but I suppose—that Mrs.
Crupp, after frying the soles, was taken ill. Because we broke down at that
point. The leg of mutton came up very red within, and very pale without:
besides having a foreign substance of a gritty nature sprinkled over it, as if
if had had a fall into the ashes of that remarkable kitchen fireplace. But we
were not in condition to judge of this fact from the appearance of the gravy,
forasmuch as the ‘young gal’ had dropped it all upon the
stairs—where it remained, by the by, in a long train, until it was worn
out. The pigeon-pie was not bad, but it was a delusive pie: the crust being
like a disappointing head, phrenologically speaking: full of lumps and bumps,
with nothing particular underneath. In short, the banquet was such a failure
that I should have been quite unhappy—about the failure, I mean, for I
was always unhappy about Dora—if I had not been relieved by the great
good humour of my company, and by a bright suggestion from Mr. Micawber.

‘My dear friend Copperfield,’ said Mr. Micawber, ‘accidents
will occur in the best-regulated families; and in families not regulated by
that pervading influence which sanctifies while it enhances the—a—I
would say, in short, by the influence of Woman, in the lofty character of Wife,
they may be expected with confidence, and must be borne with philosophy. If you
will allow me to take the liberty of remarking that there are few comestibles
better, in their way, than a Devil, and that I believe, with a little division
of labour, we could accomplish a good one if the young person in attendance
could produce a gridiron, I would put it to you, that this little misfortune
may be easily repaired.’

There was a gridiron in the pantry, on which my morning rasher of bacon was
cooked. We had it in, in a twinkling, and immediately applied ourselves to
carrying Mr. Micawber’s idea into effect. The division of labour to which
he had referred was this:—Traddles cut the mutton into slices; Mr.
Micawber (who could do anything of this sort to perfection) covered them with
pepper, mustard, salt, and cayenne; I put them on the gridiron, turned them
with a fork, and took them off, under Mr. Micawber’s direction; and Mrs.
Micawber heated, and continually stirred, some mushroom ketchup in a little
saucepan. When we had slices enough done to begin upon, we fell-to, with our
sleeves still tucked up at the wrist, more slices sputtering and blazing on the
fire, and our attention divided between the mutton on our plates, and the
mutton then preparing.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lively description of collaborative cooking showing camaraderie and practical resourcefulness; shifts tone to action and cooperation.
enrichment.summary: The group divides labour to prepare spiced mutton slices on a gridiron, with Traddles cutting, Micawber seasoning, David cooking, and Mrs. Micawber preparing ketchup.

What with the novelty of this cookery, the excellence of it, the bustle of it,
the frequent starting up to look after it, the frequent sitting down to dispose
of it as the crisp slices came off the gridiron hot and hot, the being so busy,
so flushed with the fire, so amused, and in the midst of such a tempting noise
and savour, we reduced the leg of mutton to the bone. My own appetite came back
miraculously. I am ashamed to record it, but I really believe I forgot Dora for
a little while. I am satisfied that Mr. and Mrs. Micawber could not have
enjoyed the feast more, if they had sold a bed to provide it. Traddles laughed
as heartily, almost the whole time, as he ate and worked. Indeed we all did,
all at once; and I dare say there was never a greater success.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transformative moment where David's appetite returns and he forgets Dora; celebratory atmosphere shows genuine joy and fellowship overcoming initial anxiety.

We should not have been much discomposed, I dare say, by the appearance of
Steerforth himself, but we became in a moment the meekest of the meek before
his respectable serving-man. Mr. Micawber, humming a tune, to show that he was
quite at ease, subsided into his chair, with the handle of a hastily concealed
fork sticking out of the bosom of his coat, as if he had stabbed himself. Mrs.
Micawber put on her brown gloves, and assumed a genteel languor. Traddles ran
his greasy hands through his hair, and stood it bolt upright, and stared in
confusion on the table-cloth. As for me, I was a mere infant at the head of my
own table; and hardly ventured to glance at the respectable phenomenon, who had
come from Heaven knows where, to put my establishment to rights.

Meanwhile he took the mutton off the gridiron, and gravely handed it round. We

of eating it. As we severally pushed away our plates, he noiselessly removed

cleared the table; piled everything on the dumb-waiter; gave us our
wine-glasses; and, of his own accord, wheeled the dumb-waiter into the pantry.

teem with the expression of his fixed opinion that I was extremely young.

these words, and disappeared. My visitors seemed to breathe more freely when he

Our conversation, afterwards, took a more worldly turn; Mr. Micawber telling us
that he found Camden Town inconvenient, and that the first thing he
contemplated doing, when the advertisement should have been the cause of
something satisfactory turning up, was to move. He mentioned a terrace at the
western end of Oxford Street, fronting Hyde Park, on which he had always had
his eye, but which he did not expect to attain immediately, as it would require
a large establishment. There would probably be an interval, he explained, in
which he should content himself with the upper part of a house, over some
respectable place of business—say in Piccadilly,—which would be a
cheerful situation for Mrs. Micawber; and where, by throwing out a bow-window,
or carrying up the roof another story, or making some little alteration of that
sort, they might live, comfortably and reputably, for a few years. Whatever was
reserved for him, he expressly said, or wherever his abode might be, we might
rely on this—there would always be a room for Traddles, and a knife and
fork for me. We acknowledged his kindness; and he begged us to forgive his
having launched into these practical and business-like details, and to excuse
it as natural in one who was making entirely new arrangements in life.

that bound me to him were broken. In the keen distress of the discovery of his
unworthiness, I thought more of all that was brilliant in him, I softened more

might have made him a man of a noble nature and a great name, than ever I had
done in the height of my devotion to him. Deeply as I felt my own unconscious
part in his pollution of an honest home, I believed that if I had been brought
face to face with him, I could not have uttered one reproach. I should have
loved him so well still—though he fascinated me no longer—I should
have held in so much tenderness the memory of my affection for him, that I
think I should have been as weak as a spirit-wounded child, in all but the
entertainment of a thought that we could ever be re-united. That thought I

What a change in Mrs. Gummidge in a little time! She was another woman. She was
so devoted, she had such a quick perception of what it would be well to say,
and what it would be well to leave unsaid; she was so forgetful of herself, and
so regardful of the sorrow about her, that I held her in a sort of veneration.
The work she did that day! There were many things to be brought up from the
beach and stored in the outhouse—as oars, nets, sails, cordage, spars,
lobster-pots, bags of ballast, and the like; and though there was abundance of
assistance rendered, there being not a pair of working hands on all that shore
but would have laboured hard for Mr. Peggotty, and been well paid in being
asked to do it, yet she persisted, all day long, in toiling under weights that
she was quite unequal to, and fagging to and fro on all sorts of unnecessary
errands. As to deploring her misfortunes, she appeared to have entirely lost
the recollection of ever having had any. She preserved an equable cheerfulness
in the midst of her sympathy, which was not the least astonishing part of the
change that had come over her. Querulousness was out of the question. I did not
even observe her voice to falter, or a tear to escape from her eyes, the whole
day through, until twilight; when she and I and Mr. Peggotty being alone
together, and he having fallen asleep in perfect exhaustion, she broke into a
half-suppressed fit of sobbing and crying, and taking me to the door, said,
‘Ever bless you, Mas’r Davy, be a friend to him, poor dear!’
Then, she immediately ran out of the house to wash her face, in order that she
might sit quietly beside him, and be found at work there, when he should awake.

that I read in Mrs. Gummidge, and the new experience she unfolded to me.

sought for consolation in the image of Dora. The greater the accumulation of

Dora high above the world. I don’t think I had any definite idea where

above the rusty nails on the top, blowing kisses at the lights in the windows,

don’t exactly know what from, I suppose from fire. Perhaps from mice, to

Taking that part of the Commons which happened to be nearest to us—for
our man was unmarried by this time, and we were out of Court, and strolling
past the Prerogative Office—I submitted that I thought the Prerogative
Office rather a queerly managed institution. Mr. Spenlow inquired in what
respect? I replied, with all due deference to his experience (but with more
deference, I am afraid, to his being Dora’s father), that perhaps it was
a little nonsensical that the Registry of that Court, containing the original
wills of all persons leaving effects within the immense province of Canterbury,
for three whole centuries, should be an accidental building, never designed for
the purpose, leased by the registrars for their Own private emolument, unsafe,
not even ascertained to be fire-proof, choked with the important documents it
held, and positively, from the roof to the basement, a mercenary speculation of
the registrars, who took great fees from the public, and crammed the
public’s wills away anyhow and anywhere, having no other object than to
get rid of them cheaply. That, perhaps, it was a little unreasonable that these
registrars in the receipt of profits amounting to eight or nine thousand pounds
a year (to say nothing of the profits of the deputy registrars, and clerks of
seats), should not be obliged to spend a little of that money, in finding a
reasonably safe place for the important documents which all classes of people
were compelled to hand over to them, whether they would or no. That, perhaps,
it was a little unjust, that all the great offices in this great office should
be magnificent sinecures, while the unfortunate working-clerks in the cold dark
room upstairs were the worst rewarded, and the least considered men, doing
important services, in London. That perhaps it was a little indecent that the
principal registrar of all, whose duty it was to find the public, constantly
resorting to this place, all needful accommodation, should be an enormous
sinecurist in virtue of that post (and might be, besides, a clergyman, a
pluralist, the holder of a staff in a cathedral, and what not),—while the
public was put to the inconvenience of which we had a specimen every afternoon
when the office was busy, and which we knew to be quite monstrous. That,
perhaps, in short, this Prerogative Office of the diocese of Canterbury was
altogether such a pestilent job, and such a pernicious absurdity, that but for
its being squeezed away in a corner of St. Paul’s Churchyard, which few
people knew, it must have been turned completely inside out, and upside down,
long ago.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's passionate critique of the Prerogative Office is a brilliant satirical indictment of institutional corruption, mismanagement, and class exploitation—a tour-de-force of social commentary.
enrichment.best_quote: the Registry of that Court, containing the original wills of all persons leaving effects within the immense province of Canterbury, for three whole centuries, should be an accidental building, never designed for the purpose, leased by the registrars for their Own private emolument, unsafe, not even ascertained to be fire-proof
enrichment.summary: David delivers a comprehensive critique of the Prerogative Office as a mercenary sinecure, with inadequate facilities, corrupt registrars, and unjust fees—a pestilent absurdity.

Mr. Spenlow smiled as I became modestly warm on the subject, and then argued
this question with me as he had argued the other. He said, what was it after
all? It was a question of feeling. If the public felt that their wills were in
safe keeping, and took it for granted that the office was not to be made
better, who was the worse for it? Nobody. Who was the better for it? All the
Sinecurists. Very well. Then the good predominated. It might not be a perfect
system; nothing was perfect; but what he objected to, was, the insertion of the
wedge. Under the Prerogative Office, the country had been glorious. Insert the
wedge into the Prerogative Office, and the country would cease to be glorious.
He considered it the principle of a gentleman to take things as he found them;
and he had no doubt the Prerogative Office would last our time. I deferred to
his opinion, though I had great doubts of it myself. I find he was right,
however; for it has not only lasted to the present moment, but has done so in
the teeth of a great parliamentary report made (not too willingly) eighteen
years ago, when all these objections of mine were set forth in detail, and when
the existing stowage for wills was described as equal to the accumulation of
only two years and a half more. What they have done with them since; whether
they have lost many, or whether they sell any, now and then, to the butter
shops; I don’t know. I am glad mine is not there, and I hope it may not
go there, yet awhile.

enrichment.summary: Mr. Spenlow argues that reform is unwise and that the office will survive, embodying the gentleman's principle of accepting established institutions.

On a table by the window in Buckingham Street, we set out the work Traddles
procured for him—which was to make, I forget how many copies of a legal
document about some right of way—and on another table we spread the last
unfinished original of the great Memorial. Our instructions to Mr. Dick were
that he should copy exactly what he had before him, without the least departure
from the original; and that when he felt it necessary to make the slightest
allusion to King Charles the First, he should fly to the Memorial. We exhorted
him to be resolute in this, and left my aunt to observe him. My aunt reported
to us, afterwards, that, at first, he was like a man playing the kettle-drums,
and constantly divided his attentions between the two; but that, finding this
confuse and fatigue him, and having his copy there, plainly before his eyes, he
soon sat at it in an orderly business-like manner, and postponed the Memorial
to a more convenient time. In a word, although we took great care that he
should have no more to do than was good for him, and although he did not begin
with the beginning of a week, he earned by the following Saturday night ten
shillings and nine-pence; and never, while I live, shall I forget his going
about to all the shops in the neighbourhood to change this treasure into
sixpences, or his bringing them to my aunt arranged in the form of a heart upon
a waiter, with tears of joy and pride in his eyes. He was like one under the
propitious influence of a charm, from the moment of his being usefully
employed; and if there were a happy man in the world, that Saturday night, it
was the grateful creature who thought my aunt the most wonderful woman in
existence, and me the most wonderful young man.

With this introduction (which greatly affected him), Mr. Micawber placed his
I.O.U. in the hands of Traddles, and said he wished him well in every relation
of life. I am persuaded, not only that this was quite the same to Mr. Micawber
as paying the money, but that Traddles himself hardly knew the difference until
he had had time to think about it. Mr. Micawber walked so erect before his
fellow man, on the strength of this virtuous action, that his chest looked half
as broad again when he lighted us downstairs. We parted with great heartiness
on both sides; and when I had seen Traddles to his own door, and was going home
alone, I thought, among the other odd and contradictory things I mused upon,
that, slippery as Mr. Micawber was, I was probably indebted to some
compassionate recollection he retained of me as his boy-lodger, for never
having been asked by him for money. I certainly should not have had the moral
courage to refuse it; and I have no doubt he knew that (to his credit be it
written), quite as well as I did.

By this time, we were quite settled down in Buckingham Street, where Mr. Dick

signal victory over Mrs. Crupp, by paying her off, throwing the first pitcher
she planted on the stairs out of window, and protecting in person, up and down
the staircase, a supernumerary whom she engaged from the outer world. These
vigorous measures struck such terror to the breast of Mrs. Crupp, that she
subsided into her own kitchen, under the impression that my aunt was mad. My
aunt being supremely indifferent to Mrs. Crupp’s opinion and everybody
else’s, and rather favouring than discouraging the idea, Mrs. Crupp, of
late the bold, became within a few days so faint-hearted, that rather than
encounter my aunt upon the staircase, she would endeavour to hide her portly
form behind doors—leaving visible, however, a wide margin of flannel
petticoat—or would shrink into dark corners. This gave my aunt such
unspeakable satisfaction, that I believe she took a delight in prowling up and
down, with her bonnet insanely perched on the top of her head, at times when
Mrs. Crupp was likely to be in the way.

text:
At last, after an agony of supplication and protestation, I got Dora to look at
me, with a horrified expression of face, which I gradually soothed until it was
only loving, and her soft, pretty cheek was lying against mine. Then I told
her, with my arms clasped round her, how I loved her, so dearly, and so dearly;
how I felt it right to offer to release her from her engagement, because now I
was poor; how I never could bear it, or recover it, if I lost her; how I had no
fears of poverty, if she had none, my arm being nerved and my heart inspired by
her; how I was already working with a courage such as none but lovers knew; how
I had begun to be practical, and look into the future; how a crust well earned
was sweeter far than a feast inherited; and much more to the same purpose,
which I delivered in a burst of passionate eloquence quite surprising to
myself, though I had been thinking about it, day and night, ever since my aunt
had astonished me.

up. I ravaged Miss Mills’s work-box for a smelling-bottle, and in my
agony of mind applied an ivory needle-case instead, and dropped all the needles
over Dora. I shook my fists at Jip, who was as frantic as myself. I did every
wild extravagance that could be done, and was a long way beyond the end of my
wits when Miss Mills came into the room.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A brilliantly comic and touching passage showing David in complete emotional chaos; his absurd gestures of despair (plucking at hair, searching Miss Mills's work-box, dropping needles, shaking his fists) are both hilarious and poignant.
enrichment.best_quote: I ravaged Miss Mills's work-box for a smelling-bottle, and in my agony of mind applied an ivory needle-case instead, and dropped all the needles over Dora.
enrichment.summary: David descends into frantic despair, convinced he has killed Dora; he sprinkles water, falls on his knees, plucks at his hair, denounces himself, rummages through work-boxes, and generally behaves with wild extravagance until Miss Mills arrives.

I replied, ‘I, Miss Mills! I have done it! Behold the

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's melodramatic self-denunciation and hiding in sofa cushions is comic and shows his overwrought emotional state in response to Miss Mills's question.
enrichment.best_quote: I, Miss Mills! I have done it! Behold the destroyer!
enrichment.summary: David dramatically declares himself the destroyer and hides his face in the sofa cushion, taking full responsibility for Dora's distress.

text:
At first Miss Mills thought it was a quarrel, and that we were verging on the

affectionate little Dora, embracing her, began exclaiming that I was ‘a
poor labourer’; and then cried for me, and embraced me, and asked me

Mills’s neck, sobbing as if her tender heart were broken.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Mills's misunderstanding followed by the revelation that Dora believes David is a poor labourer (or possibly a navigator) shows the gap between David's anxious self-disclosure and Dora's comprehension.

text:
Miss Mills must have been born to be a blessing to us. She ascertained from me
in a few words what it was all about, comforted Dora, and gradually convinced
her that I was not a labourer—from my manner of stating the case I
believe Dora concluded that I was a navigator, and went balancing myself up and
down a plank all day with a wheelbarrow—and so brought us together in
peace. When we were quite composed, and Dora had gone up-stairs to put some

told Miss Mills that she was evermore my friend, and that my heart must cease
to vibrate ere I could forget her sympathy.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Mills emerges as a sympathetic mediator and confidante; her practical wisdom and emotional intelligence resolve the crisis and establish her as David's ally in understanding both his ideals and Dora's nature.
enrichment.best_quote: Miss Mills must have been born to be a blessing to us.
enrichment.summary: Miss Mills ascertains what has happened, comforts Dora, gently corrects her misunderstanding about David being a labourer, and brings them together in peace; David declares her his eternal friend.

text:
I then expounded to Miss Mills what I had endeavoured, so very unsuccessfully,
to expound to Dora. Miss Mills replied, on general principles, that the Cottage
of content was better than the Palace of cold splendour, and that where love
was, all was.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's exposition of his plans to Miss Mills is met with her philosophical but ultimately evasive response about contentment; shows the mutual understanding between them.
enrichment.summary: David explains his practical plans to Miss Mills, who responds philosophically that the Cottage of content is better than the Palace of cold splendour, and where love is, all is.

text:
I said to Miss Mills that this was very true, and who should know it better
than I, who loved Dora with a love that never mortal had experienced yet? But
on Miss Mills observing, with despondency, that it were well indeed for some
hearts if this were so, I explained that I begged leave to restrict the
observation to mortals of the masculine gender.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's response is a playful romantic assertion about his unique love; affectionate but largely connective dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David claims to love Dora with a love no mortal has ever experienced, then gallantly restricts this observation to masculine hearts.

text:
I then put it to Miss Mills, to say whether she considered that there was or
was not any practical merit in the suggestion I had been anxious to make,
concerning the accounts, the housekeeping, and the Cookery Book?

enrichment.interest_rationale: David solicits Miss Mills's opinion about the practical value of his suggestions; brief, transactional dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David asks Miss Mills whether she thinks there is practical merit in his suggestions about accounts, housekeeping, and a Cookery Book.

text: Miss Mills, after some consideration, thus replied:

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transitional tag indicating Miss Mills's response; contains no substantive content.
enrichment.summary: Miss Mills prepares to deliver her considered response.

text:
‘Mr. Copperfield, I will be plain with you. Mental suffering and trial
supply, in some natures, the place of years, and I will be as plain with you as
if I were a Lady Abbess. No. The suggestion is not appropriate to our Dora. Our
dearest Dora is a favourite child of nature. She is a thing of light, and
airiness, and joy. I am free to confess that if it could be done, it might be
well, but—’ And Miss Mills shook her head.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Mills's response is a touching and wise assessment of Dora's nature; she acknowledges both David's idealistic hopes and the fundamental reality of Dora being 'a favourite child of nature' unsuited to practical training.

enrichment.summary: Miss Mills candidly tells David that while his suggestions about practical training might theoretically be beneficial, Dora is by nature unsuited to such concerns—she is a creature of light, airiness, and joy.

text:
I was encouraged by this closing admission on the part of Miss Mills to ask
her, whether, for Dora’s sake, if she had any opportunity of luring her
attention to such preparations for an earnest life, she would avail herself of
it? Miss Mills replied in the affirmative so readily, that I further asked her
if she would take charge of the Cookery Book; and, if she ever could insinuate
it upon Dora’s acceptance, without frightening her, undertake to do me
that crowning service. Miss Mills accepted this trust, too; but was not
sanguine.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David enlists Miss Mills's help in subtly introducing practical knowledge to Dora, securing her agreement though she remains skeptical of success.
enrichment.summary: David asks Miss Mills if she would take charge of introducing a Cookery Book to Dora when possible, and she agrees though without optimism about success.

text:
And Dora returned, looking such a lovely little creature, that I really doubted
whether she ought to be troubled with anything so ordinary. And she loved me so
much, and was so captivating (particularly when she made Jip stand on his hind
legs for toast, and when she pretended to hold that nose of his against the hot
teapot for punishment because he wouldn’t), that I felt like a sort of
Monster who had got into a Fairy’s bower, when I thought of having
frightened her, and made her cry.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A tender and revealing moment where David's self-awareness peaks; he sees the fundamental incongruence between Dora's ethereal beauty and his concerns about practical life, recognizing himself as a monster intruding on a fairy's world.
enrichment.best_quote: And she loved me so much, and was so captivating (particularly when she made Jip stand on his hind legs for toast, and when she pretended to hold that nose of his against the hot teapot for punishment because he wouldn't), that I felt like a sort of Monster who had got into a Fairy's bower, when I thought of having frightened her, and made her cry.
enrichment.summary: Dora's loveliness and playful charm with Jip make David feel he is a monster in a fairy's bower when he recalls having frightened her; her innocence and joy stand in stark contrast to his practical concerns.

text:
After tea we had the guitar; and Dora sang those same dear old French songs
about the impossibility of ever on any account leaving off dancing, La ra la,
La ra la, until I felt a much greater Monster than before.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A charming scene of Dora singing French songs about dancing, which increases David's sense of being monstrous; the repetitive refrain emphasizes her escapism.
enrichment.summary: After tea, Dora plays guitar and sings old French songs about the impossibility of stopping dancing, making David feel even more monstrous for having frightened her.

text:
We had only one check to our pleasure, and that happened a little while before
I took my leave, when, Miss Mills chancing to make some allusion to tomorrow
morning, I unluckily let out that, being obliged to exert myself now, I got up
at five o’clock. Whether Dora had any idea that I was a Private Watchman,
I am unable to say; but it made a great impression on her, and she neither
played nor sang any more.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A subtle but revealing moment where David's mention of rising at five o'clock disturbs Dora; she may have misinterpreted his role, showing both her confusion and her anxiety about his circumstances.
enrichment.summary: When David accidentally mentions that he rises at five o'clock due to work, Dora becomes troubled; David wonders if she imagines him to be a Private Watchman.

text:
It was still on her mind when I bade her adieu; and she said to me, in her
pretty coaxing way—as if I were a doll, I used to think:

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief dialogue as Dora addresses David's early rising; minor conversation without new depth.
enrichment.summary: The narrator notes that Dora's concern about David's early rising lingers as he says goodbye, expressed in a coaxing tone as if to a doll.

text:
‘Now don’t get up at five o’clock, you naughty boy.
It’s so nonsensical!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's brief plea is affectionate but offers no new information; routine dialogue about his schedule.
enrichment.best_quote: Now don't get up at five o'clock, you naughty boy. It's so nonsensical!
enrichment.summary: Dora playfully scolds David for rising at five o'clock, calling it nonsensical.

text: ‘My love,’ said I, ‘I have work to do.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's practical response is brief and direct; routine explanation without drama.
enrichment.summary: David calmly explains that he has work to do, offering a straightforward answer.

text:
‘But don’t do it!’ returned Dora. ‘Why should
you?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's simple rejection of necessity is characteristic but repetitive; light dialogue without substance.
enrichment.summary: Dora questions why David must work, showing her fundamental refusal to accept economic necessity.

text:
It was impossible to say to that sweet little surprised face, otherwise than
lightly and playfully, that we must work to live.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrative commentary noting David's inability to answer directly; brief and transitional.
enrichment.summary: David finds it impossible to answer Dora's question seriously because her innocent face is too charming.

text: ‘Oh! How ridiculous!’ cried Dora.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's brief dismissal of the necessity of work is characteristic; minimal dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Dora finds the idea that they must work to live ridiculous.

text: ‘How shall we live without, Dora?’ said I.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's simple restatement of economic necessity is routine dialogue without new depth.
enrichment.summary: David asks how they shall live without work, restating the basic economic argument.

text: ‘How? Any how!’ said Dora.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's dismissive response is characteristic but offers nothing new; connective dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Dora vaguely answers that they can live "any how," refusing to engage with practical reality.

text:
She seemed to think she had quite settled the question, and gave me such a
triumphant little kiss, direct from her innocent heart, that I would hardly
have put her out of conceit with her answer, for a fortune.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A touching moment where Dora's innocent, victorious kiss and her refusal to entertain practical concerns reveal David's complete emotional capitulation to her charm.
enrichment.best_quote: She seemed to think she had quite settled the question, and gave me such a triumphant little kiss, direct from her innocent heart, that I would hardly have put her out of conceit with her answer, for a fortune.
enrichment.summary: Dora's triumphant kiss and innocent conviction that she has resolved the question make David unwilling to disabuse her of her belief, even for a fortune.

text:
Well! I loved her, and I went on loving her, most absorbingly, entirely, and
completely. But going on, too, working pretty hard, and busily keeping red-hot
all the irons I now had in the fire, I would sit sometimes of a night, opposite
