make my way with a guitar-case through the forest of difficulty, until I used
to fancy that my head was turning quite grey.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A powerful and reflective conclusion showing David's recognition of the tension between his love for Dora and his practical ambitions; the image of him sitting opposite his aunt, head turning grey with worry, captures the emotional cost of navigating his 'undisciplined heart.'
enrichment.best_quote: I would sit sometimes of a night, opposite my aunt, thinking how I had frightened Dora that time, and how I could best make my way with a guitar-case through the forest of difficulty, until I used to fancy that my head was turning quite grey.
enrichment.summary: David concludes by describing his continued absorption in loving Dora while working hard and keeping multiple irons in the fire; he sits with his aunt at night, worried about having frightened Dora and uncertain about navigating life's difficulties.

text:
The first objects that assume a distinct presence before me, as I look far
back, into the blank of my infancy, are my mother with her pretty hair and
youthful shape, and Peggotty with no shape at all, and eyes so dark that they
seemed to darken their whole neighbourhood in her face, and cheeks and arms so
hard and red that I wondered the birds didn’t peck her in preference to
apples.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Opening meditation on memory and childhood introduces the novel's central first-person perspective and David's two most formative early relationships with vivid, affectionate characterization.
enrichment.best_quote: my mother with her pretty hair and youthful shape, and Peggotty with no shape at all, and eyes so dark that they seemed to darken their whole neighbourhood in her face
enrichment.summary: Adult David recalls his earliest memories: his mother's beauty and Peggotty's unusual physical appearance and devotion.

text:
I believe I can remember these two at a little distance apart, dwarfed to my
sight by stooping down or kneeling on the floor, and I going unsteadily from
the one to the other. I have an impression on my mind which I cannot
distinguish from actual remembrance, of the touch of Peggotty’s
forefinger as she used to hold it out to me, and of its being roughened by
needlework, like a pocket nutmeg-grater.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Sensory detail of childhood memory—Peggotty's finger roughened by needlework—demonstrates David's observational faculty and reinforces the intimacy of his bond with her.
enrichment.best_quote: the touch of Peggotty's forefinger as she used to hold it out to me, and of its being roughened by needlework, like a pocket nutmeg-grater
enrichment.summary: David recalls physical memories of Peggotty holding out her work-roughened finger for him as an infant.

text:
This may be fancy, though I think the memory of most of us can go farther back
into such times than many of us suppose; just as I believe the power of
observation in numbers of very young children to be quite wonderful for its
closeness and accuracy. Indeed, I think that most grown men who are remarkable
in this respect, may with greater propriety be said not to have lost the
faculty, than to have acquired it; the rather, as I generally observe such men
to retain a certain freshness, and gentleness, and capacity of being pleased,
which are also an inheritance they have preserved from their childhood.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Philosophical digression on childhood memory and observation that is thematic but somewhat digressive from narrative action.
enrichment.summary: David reflects on the reliability of early memory and the remarkable powers of observation in young children, which often persist into adulthood.

text:
I might have a misgiving that I am ‘meandering’ in stopping to say
this, but that it brings me to remark that I build these conclusions, in part
upon my own experience of myself; and if it should appear from anything I may
set down in this narrative that I was a child of close observation, or that as
a man I have a strong memory of my childhood, I undoubtedly lay claim to both
of these characteristics.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Self-aware authorial note defending against charges of digression; establishes David as narrator claiming the characteristics he has just described.
enrichment.summary: David acknowledges his digression and claims for himself both close observation skills and strong childhood memory.

text:
Looking back, as I was saying, into the blank of my infancy, the first objects
I can remember as standing out by themselves from a confusion of things, are my
mother and Peggotty. What else do I remember? Let me see.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transition back to main narrative thread; routine connective prose returning to childhood memory.
enrichment.summary: David signals return to his narrative, asking what else he can remember from infancy.

text:
There comes out of the cloud, our house—not new to me, but quite
familiar, in its earliest remembrance. On the ground-floor is Peggotty’s
kitchen, opening into a back yard; with a pigeon-house on a pole, in the
centre, without any pigeons in it; a great dog-kennel in a corner, without any
dog; and a quantity of fowls that look terribly tall to me, walking about, in a
menacing and ferocious manner. There is one cock who gets upon a post to crow,
and seems to take particular notice of me as I look at him through the kitchen
window, who makes me shiver, he is so fierce. Of the geese outside the
side-gate who come waddling after me with their long necks stretched out when I
go that way, I dream at night: as a man environed by wild beasts might dream of
lions.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vivid sensory description of the childhood home and its menacing animals reveals David's anxious perspective; the imagery is distinctly Dickensian and establishes atmosphere effectively.
enrichment.best_quote: Of the geese outside the side-gate who come waddling after me with their long necks stretched out when I go that way, I dream at night: as a man environed by wild beasts might dream of lions.
enrichment.summary: David describes his family home—Peggotty's kitchen, the back yard with its animals, particularly the fierce cock and menacing geese that terrify him.

text:
Here is a long passage—what an enormous perspective I make of
it!—leading from Peggotty’s kitchen to the front door. A dark
store-room opens out of it, and that is a place to be run past at night; for I
don’t know what may be among those tubs and jars and old tea-chests, when
there is nobody in there with a dimly-burning light, letting a mouldy air come
out of the door, in which there is the smell of soap, pickles, pepper, candles,
and coffee, all at one whiff. Then there are the two parlours: the parlour in
which we sit of an evening, my mother and I and Peggotty—for Peggotty is
quite our companion, when her work is done and we are alone—and the best
parlour where we sit on a Sunday; grandly, but not so comfortably. There is
something of a doleful air about that room to me, for Peggotty has told
me—I don’t know when, but apparently ages ago—about my
father’s funeral, and the company having their black cloaks put on. One
Sunday night my mother reads to Peggotty and me in there, how Lazarus was
raised up from the dead. And I am so frightened that they are afterwards
obliged to take me out of bed, and show me the quiet churchyard out of the
bedroom window, with the dead all lying in their graves at rest, below the
solemn moon.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended Gothic passage through the house and church episode is atmospherically rich, combines childhood fear (store-room, funeral memories) with vivid domestic detail; demonstrates David's mature voice capturing youthful anxiety.
enrichment.best_quote: a dark store-room opens out of it, and that is a place to be run past at night; for I don't know what may be among those tubs and jars and old tea-chests, when there is nobody in there with a dimly-burning light, letting a mouldy air come out of the door
enrichment.summary: David describes the layout of the house's interior, the frightening store-room, the two parlours, and a traumatic childhood memory of hearing the story of Lazarus and fearing the dead from the churchyard.

text:
There is nothing half so green that I know anywhere, as the grass of that
churchyard; nothing half so shady as its trees; nothing half so quiet as its
tombstones. The sheep are feeding there, when I kneel up, early in the morning,
in my little bed in a closet within my mother’s room, to look out at it;
and I see the red light shining on the sun-dial, and think within myself,
‘Is the sun-dial glad, I wonder, that it can tell the time again?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Beautiful pastoral meditation on the churchyard and childhood wonder transforms Gothic terror into serenity and philosophical observation; displays mature David reflecting on youthful consciousness.
enrichment.best_quote: Is the sun-dial glad, I wonder, that it can tell the time again?
enrichment.summary: David describes the beautiful, peaceful churchyard where he watches sheep graze from his bedroom window and muses on the sun-dial.

text:
Here is our pew in the church. What a high-backed pew! With a window near it,
out of which our house can be seen, and IS seen many times during the
morning’s service, by Peggotty, who likes to make herself as sure as she
can that it’s not being robbed, or is not in flames. But though
Peggotty’s eye wanders, she is much offended if mine does, and frowns to
me, as I stand upon the seat, that I am to look at the clergyman. But I
can’t always look at him—I know him without that white thing on,
and I am afraid of his wondering why I stare so, and perhaps stopping the
service to inquire—and what am I to do? It’s a dreadful thing to
gape, but I must do something. I look at my mother, but she pretends not to see
me. I look at a boy in the aisle, and he makes faces at me. I look at the
sunlight coming in at the open door through the porch, and there I see a stray
sheep—I don’t mean a sinner, but mutton—half making up his
mind to come into the church. I feel that if I looked at him any longer, I
might be tempted to say something out loud; and what would become of me then! I
look up at the monumental tablets on the wall, and try to think of Mr. Bodgers
late of this parish, and what the feelings of Mrs. Bodgers must have been, when
affliction sore, long time Mr. Bodgers bore, and physicians were in vain. I
wonder whether they called in Mr. Chillip, and he was in vain; and if so, how
he likes to be reminded of it once a week. I look from Mr. Chillip, in his
Sunday neckcloth, to the pulpit; and think what a good place it would be to
play in, and what a castle it would make, with another boy coming up the stairs
to attack it, and having the velvet cushion with the tassels thrown down on his
head. In time my eyes gradually shut up; and, from seeming to hear the
clergyman singing a drowsy song in the heat, I hear nothing, until I fall off
the seat with a crash, and am taken out, more dead than alive, by Peggotty.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended comic set-piece of David's church boredom brilliantly captures childhood consciousness with humor and whimsy; demonstrates Dickens's comic mastery and David's observational talent. Highly entertaining.
enrichment.best_quote: I feel that if I looked at him any longer, I might be tempted to say something out loud; and what would become of me then!
enrichment.summary: David recounts his struggles to stay awake and attentive during Sunday church service, describing his wandering observations of the clergyman, a stray sheep, monumental tablets, and finally falling asleep and crashing off the pew.

text:
And now I see the outside of our house, with the latticed bedroom-windows
standing open to let in the sweet-smelling air, and the ragged old
rooks’-nests still dangling in the elm-trees at the bottom of the front
garden. Now I am in the garden at the back, beyond the yard where the empty
pigeon-house and dog-kennel are—a very preserve of butterflies, as I
remember it, with a high fence, and a gate and padlock; where the fruit
clusters on the trees, riper and richer than fruit has ever been since, in any
other garden, and where my mother gathers some in a basket, while I stand by,
bolting furtive gooseberries, and trying to look unmoved. A great wind rises,
and the summer is gone in a moment. We are playing in the winter twilight,
dancing about the parlour. When my mother is out of breath and rests herself in
an elbow-chair, I watch her winding her bright curls round her fingers, and
straitening her waist, and nobody knows better than I do that she likes to look
so well, and is proud of being so pretty.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lyrical pastoral passage capturing idyllic childhood moments in garden and parlour, emphasizing maternal beauty and family bonds before tragedy; important for establishing emotional baseline of happiness.
enrichment.best_quote: where the fruit clusters on the trees, riper and richer than fruit has ever been since, in any other garden
enrichment.summary: David recalls summer in the garden and winter dancing with his mother, describing her prettiness, his enjoyment of the gooseberries, and her vanity about her appearance.

text:
That is among my very earliest impressions. That, and a sense that we were both
a little afraid of Peggotty, and submitted ourselves in most things to her
direction, were among the first opinions—if they may be so
called—that I ever derived from what I saw.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief reflection on early impressions of Peggotty's dominance and the mutual fear between mother and Peggotty, sketching out the family dynamic.
enrichment.summary: David notes that his earliest impressions include a sense that both he and his mother were somewhat afraid of Peggotty and deferred to her direction.

text:
Peggotty and I were sitting one night by the parlour fire, alone. I had been
reading to Peggotty about crocodiles. I must have read very perspicuously, or
the poor soul must have been deeply interested, for I remember she had a cloudy
impression, after I had done, that they were a sort of vegetable. I was tired
of reading, and dead sleepy; but having leave, as a high treat, to sit up until
my mother came home from spending the evening at a neighbour’s, I would
rather have died upon my post (of course) than have gone to bed. I had reached
that stage of sleepiness when Peggotty seemed to swell and grow immensely
large. I propped my eyelids open with my two forefingers, and looked
perseveringly at her as she sat at work; at the little bit of wax-candle she
kept for her thread—how old it looked, being so wrinkled in all
directions!—at the little house with a thatched roof, where the
yard-measure lived; at her work-box with a sliding lid, with a view of St.
Paul’s Cathedral (with a pink dome) painted on the top; at the brass
thimble on her finger; at herself, whom I thought lovely. I felt so sleepy,
that I knew if I lost sight of anything for a moment, I was gone.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Charming scene of childhood intimacy between David and Peggotty, full of sensory detail and affection; establishes their deep bond and David's youthful curiosity. Humor and tenderness combined.
enrichment.best_quote: I had reached that stage of sleepiness when Peggotty seemed to swell and grow immensely large. I propped my eyelids open with my two forefingers, and looked perseveringly at her

text:
‘Lord, Master Davy,’ replied Peggotty. ‘What’s put
marriage in your head?’

enrichment.summary: Peggotty responds with surprise, asking what put marriage in David's head.

text:
She answered with such a start, that it quite awoke me. And then she stopped in
her work, and looked at me, with her needle drawn out to its thread’s
length.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Narrative transition indicating Peggotty's emotional reaction; routine descriptive prose.
enrichment.summary: David notes that Peggotty starts and stops her work, looking at him intently with her needle drawn out.

text:
‘But WERE you ever married, Peggotty?’ says I. ‘You are a
very handsome woman, an’t you?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Charming moment where David, half-asleep, compliments Peggotty on her appearance, showing his youthful affection and innocent perception of beauty.

depth in it to be looked into—which, when it is abstracted, seems from

awe, and wondered what he was thinking about so closely. His hair and whiskers
were blacker and thicker, looked at so near, than even I had given them credit
for being. A squareness about the lower part of his face, and the dotted
indication of the strong black beard he shaved close every day, reminded me of
the wax-work that had travelled into our neighbourhood some half-a-year before.

I should like to see such a Parliament anywhere else! My aunt and Mr. Dick
represented the Government or the Opposition (as the case might be), and
Traddles, with the assistance of Enfield’s Speakers, or a volume of
parliamentary orations, thundered astonishing invectives against them. Standing
by the table, with his finger in the page to keep the place, and his right arm
flourishing above his head, Traddles, as Mr. Pitt, Mr. Fox, Mr. Sheridan, Mr.
Burke, Lord Castlereagh, Viscount Sidmouth, or Mr. Canning, would work himself
into the most violent heats, and deliver the most withering denunciations of
the profligacy and corruption of my aunt and Mr. Dick; while I used to sit, at
a little distance, with my notebook on my knee, fagging after him with all my
might and main. The inconsistency and recklessness of Traddles were not to be
exceeded by any real politician. He was for any description of policy, in the
compass of a week; and nailed all sorts of colours to every denomination of
mast. My aunt, looking very like an immovable Chancellor of the Exchequer,
would occasionally throw in an interruption or two, as ‘Hear!’ or
‘No!’ or ‘Oh!’ when the text seemed to require it:
which was always a signal to Mr. Dick (a perfect country gentleman) to follow
lustily with the same cry. But Mr. Dick got taxed with such things in the
course of his Parliamentary career, and was made responsible for such awful
consequences, that he became uncomfortable in his mind sometimes. I believe he
actually began to be afraid he really had been doing something, tending to the
annihilation of the British constitution, and the ruin of the country.

in the office, and the insatiable relish with which our people talked about it,
and other people came in and out all day, and gorged themselves with the
subject—this is easily intelligible to anyone. What I cannot describe is,
how, in the innermost recesses of my own heart, I had a lurking jealousy even
of Death. How I felt as if its might would push me from my ground in
Dora’s thoughts. How I was, in a grudging way I have no words for,
envious of her grief. How it made me restless to think of her weeping to

unseasonable time of all times.

Dickens captures the unsightly aspects of young love with unflinching honesty.
enrichment.best_quote: What I cannot describe is, how, in the innermost recesses of my own heart, I had a lurking jealousy even of Death. How I felt as if its might would push me from my ground in Dora's thoughts. How I was, in a grudging way I have no words for, envious of her grief.
enrichment.summary: David reflects on the disturbing selfishness beneath his grief: his unacknowledged jealousy of Death itself, his envy of the consolation Dora receives from others, and his grasping wish to be everything to her.

text:
In the trouble of this state of mind—not exclusively my own, I hope, but
known to others—I went down to Norwood that night; and finding from one
of the servants, when I made my inquiries at the door, that Miss Mills was
there, got my aunt to direct a letter to her, which I wrote. I deplored the
untimely death of Mr. Spenlow, most sincerely, and shed tears in doing so. I
entreated her to tell Dora, if Dora were in a state to hear it, that he had
spoken to me with the utmost kindness and consideration; and had coupled
nothing but tenderness, not a single or reproachful word, with her name. I know
I did this selfishly, to have my name brought before her; but I tried to
believe it was an act of justice to his memory. Perhaps I did believe it.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's letter to Miss Mills is sincere but self-serving; he deplores Spenlow's death (which he does feel) while strategically ensuring his name is brought before Dora (which he consciously desires).
enrichment.summary: David travels to Norwood, learns Miss Mills is there, and sends a letter through his aunt expressing sincere sorrow for Mr. Spenlow's death while asking Miss Mills to tell Dora of his kind final words.

text:
My aunt received a few lines next day in reply; addressed, outside, to her;
within, to me. Dora was overcome by grief; and when her friend had asked her
should she send her love to me, had only cried, as she was always crying,
‘Oh, dear papa! oh, poor papa!’ But she had not said No, and that I
made the most of.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Mills' report shows Dora's overwhelming grief and her refusal (through silence) to forbid David's affections; this gives David false hope that his devotion is still welcome.
enrichment.summary: David receives a brief reply showing that Dora is inconsolable, weeping for her father; when asked about David, she says nothing, which David interprets as a sign of hope.

Mr. Jorkins, who had been at Norwood since the occurrence, came to the office a
few days afterwards. He and Tiffey were closeted together for some few moments,
and then Tiffey looked out at the door and beckoned me in.

‘Oh!’ said Mr. Jorkins. ‘Mr. Tiffey and myself, Mr.
Copperfield, are about to examine the desks, the drawers, and other such
repositories of the deceased, with the view of sealing up his private papers,
and searching for a Will. There is no trace of any, elsewhere. It may be as
well for you to assist us, if you please.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Jorkins explains the task matter-of-factly; the objective is to search for a will and secure private papers.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Jorkins formally explains that he and Tiffey are searching Mr. Spenlow's desk and papers to find any will, with David's assistance.

I had been in agony to obtain some knowledge of the circumstances in which my
Dora would be placed—as, in whose guardianship, and so forth—and
this was something towards it. We began the search at once; Mr. Jorkins
unlocking the drawers and desks, and we all taking out the papers. The
office-papers we placed on one side, and the private papers (which were not
numerous) on the other. We were very grave; and when we came to a stray seal,
or pencil-case, or ring, or any little article of that kind which we associated
personally with him, we spoke very low.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's personal interest in Dora's situation—who will be her guardian, where will she live—underlies his participation; the solemn, reverent handling of Mr. Spenlow's effects shows respect for the deceased.
enrichment.summary: The search begins; David is eager to discover Dora's future circumstances while maintaining respectful quiet about Mr. Spenlow's personal effects.

We had sealed up several packets; and were still going on dustily and quietly,
when Mr. Jorkins said to us, applying exactly the same words to his late
partner as his late partner had applied to him:

‘Mr. Spenlow was very difficult to move from the beaten track. You know

enrichment.summary: Mr. Jorkins suggests that Mr. Spenlow, reluctant to change his routines, likely never made a will.

They both stopped and looked at me. ‘On the very day when I last saw
him,’ said I, ‘he told me that he had, and that his affairs were
long since settled.’

‘My good Mr. Copperfield!’ said Tiffey, laying his hand upon my
arm, and shutting up both his eyes as he shook his head: ‘if you had been
in the Commons as long as I have, you would know that there is no subject on
which men are so inconsistent, and so little to be trusted.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tiffey's world-weary wisdom about testamentary inconsistency is illuminating; he lectures David on men's unreliability regarding wills, a subtle satirical commentary on human nature and legal practice.

enrichment.summary: Tiffey responds with experienced cynicism, asserting that testamentary intentions are the most unreliable of human commitments.

text:
‘Why, bless my soul, he made that very remark!’ I replied
persistently.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David insists on the exactness of Mr. Spenlow's remark; the disagreement is substantive but brief.
enrichment.summary: David reiterates that Mr. Spenlow made the exact remark that Tiffey just quoted, suggesting his words applied to himself.

‘I should call that almost final,’ observed Tiffey. ‘My
opinion is—no will.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tiffey's observation is brief and dismissive; he concludes no will exists based on the rarity of follow-through.
enrichment.summary: Tiffey concludes that Spenlow's remark about testamentary inconsistency almost certainly means he never made a will himself.

text:
It appeared a wonderful thing to me, but it turned out that there was no will.
He had never so much as thought of making one, so far as his papers afforded
any evidence; for there was no kind of hint, sketch, or memorandum, of any
testamentary intention whatever. What was scarcely less astonishing to me, was,
that his affairs were in a most disordered state. It was extremely difficult, I
heard, to make out what he owed, or what he had paid, or of what he died
possessed. It was considered likely that for years he could have had no clear
opinion on these subjects himself. By little and little it came out, that, in
the competition on all points of appearance and gentility then running high in
the Commons, he had spent more than his professional income, which was not a
very large one, and had reduced his private means, if they ever had been great
(which was exceedingly doubtful), to a very low ebb indeed. There was a sale of
the furniture and lease, at Norwood; and Tiffey told me, little thinking how
interested I was in the story, that, paying all the just debts of the deceased,
and deducting his share of outstanding bad and doubtful debts due to the firm,
he wouldn’t give a thousand pounds for all the assets remaining.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The revelation that Mr. Spenlow had no will and his financial affairs are in chaos is stunning; Dickens satirizes his obsession with appearance and gentility at the expense of sound financial practice, reducing his estate to nearly worthless.
enrichment.best_quote: in the competition on all points of appearance and gentility then running high in the Commons, he had spent more than his professional income...and had reduced his private means...to a very low ebb indeed
enrichment.summary: The search confirms no will exists; moreover, Mr. Spenlow's affairs are hopelessly disordered due to his habit of living beyond his professional income to maintain appearances, leaving barely a thousand pounds in assets after debts.

text:
This was at the expiration of about six weeks. I had suffered tortures all the
time; and thought I really must have laid violent hands upon myself, when Miss
Mills still reported to me, that my broken-hearted little Dora would say
nothing, when I was mentioned, but ‘Oh, poor papa! Oh, dear papa!’
Also, that she had no other relations than two aunts, maiden sisters of Mr.
Spenlow, who lived at Putney, and who had not held any other than chance
communication with their brother for many years. Not that they had ever
quarrelled (Miss Mills informed me); but that having been, on the occasion of
Dora’s christening, invited to tea, when they considered themselves
privileged to be invited to dinner, they had expressed their opinion in
writing, that it was ‘better for the happiness of all parties’ that
they should stay away. Since which they had gone their road, and their brother
had gone his.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Over six weeks, David has been in emotional torment while Dora grieves silently; the revelation that her only relations are two maiden aunts at Putney who had quarreled with her father changes her entire situation.
enrichment.summary: Six weeks pass in David's agony while Dora remains inconsolable; Miss Mills reports that Dora has no relations but two estranged aunts at Putney who quarreled with her father over a slight.

text:
These two ladies now emerged from their retirement, and proposed to take Dora
to live at Putney. Dora, clinging to them both, and weeping, exclaimed,
‘O yes, aunts! Please take Julia Mills and me and Jip to Putney!’
So they went, very soon after the funeral.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The aunts emerge and propose taking Dora to Putney; Dora's emotional plea to bring Julia Mills and Jip shows her devastation and need for her support network.
enrichment.best_quote: 'O yes, aunts! Please take Julia Mills and me and Jip to Putney!'
enrichment.summary: Dora's aunts come to take her to Putney; Dora, clinging to them and weeping, insists that Julia Mills and Jip accompany her.

text:
How I found time to haunt Putney, I am sure I don’t know; but I
contrived, by some means or other, to prowl about the neighbourhood pretty
often. Miss Mills, for the more exact discharge of the duties of friendship,
kept a journal; and she used to meet me sometimes, on the Common, and read it,
or (if she had not time to do that) lend it to me. How I treasured up the
entries, of which I subjoin a sample—!

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's devoted haunting of Putney and his treasure of Miss Mills' journal entries, though self-mockingly presented, show his romantic persistence and the absurdity of his situation.
enrichment.summary: David contrives to visit Putney frequently; Miss Mills keeps a journal and occasionally shares entries or lends it to him, which he treasures for any news of Dora.

text:
‘Monday. My sweet D. still much depressed. Headache. Called attention to
J. as being beautifully sleek. D. fondled J. Associations thus awakened, opened
floodgates of sorrow. Rush of grief admitted. (Are tears the dewdrops of the
heart? J. M.)

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Mills' journal entry about Dora's depression, the mention of Jip awakening 'floodgates of sorrow,' and her self-conscious musing on tears is a brilliant parody of sentimental diary-keeping and affected consolation.
enrichment.best_quote: 'Are tears the dewdrops of the heart? J. M.'
enrichment.summary: Miss Mills' Monday entry shows Dora still depressed with headache; mentioning Jip's sleek appearance triggers memories and sorrow, prompting Miss Mills' sentimental philosophical musing.

text:
‘Tuesday. D. weak and nervous. Beautiful in pallor. (Do we not remark
this in moon likewise? J. M.) D., J. M. and J. took airing in carriage. J.
looking out of window, and barking violently at dustman, occasioned smile to
overspread features of D. (Of such slight links is chain of life composed! J.
M.)

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Tuesday entry parodies sentimentality further: Dora's 'beautiful in pallor,' the moon comparison, Jip's barking at the dustman causing Dora to smile, and Miss Mills' philosophical reflection on life's 'slight links' is masterfully absurd.
enrichment.best_quote: 'Of such slight links is chain of life composed! J. M.'
enrichment.summary: Miss Mills' Tuesday entry notes Dora's pallor as beautiful, draws an analogy to the moon, and records how Jip's antics caused Dora to smile briefly.

text:
‘Wednesday. D. comparatively cheerful. Sang to her, as congenial melody,
“Evening Bells”. Effect not soothing, but reverse. D. inexpressibly
affected. Found sobbing afterwards, in own room. Quoted verses respecting self
and young Gazelle. Ineffectually. Also referred to Patience on Monument. (Qy.
Why on monument? J. M.)

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Wednesday entry is superb satire: Miss Mills sings 'Evening Bells' to cheer Dora, but it has the opposite effect; she quotes poetry about patience and gazelles, all ineffectual. Miss Mills' final question ('Qy. Why on monument?') adds absurdist humor.
enrichment.best_quote: 'Qy. Why on monument? J. M.'
enrichment.summary: Miss Mills attempts to comfort Dora with music and poetry, but Dora breaks down again; Miss Mills reflects on her own referential techniques and questions metaphorical conventions.

text:
‘Thursday. D. certainly improved. Better night. Slight tinge of damask
revisiting cheek. Resolved to mention name of D. C. Introduced same,
cautiously, in course of airing. D. immediately overcome. “Oh, dear, dear
Julia! Oh, I have been a naughty and undutiful child!” Soothed and
caressed. Drew ideal picture of D. C. on verge of tomb. D. again overcome.
“Oh, what shall I do, what shall I do? Oh, take me somewhere!” Much
alarmed. Fainting of D. and glass of water from public-house. (Poetical
affinity. Chequered sign on door-post; chequered human life. Alas! J. M.)

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Thursday entry is pivotal: Miss Mills mentions David's name, Dora breaks down, admits her 'naughty' behavior, and faints; Miss Mills' reference to David as 'verge of tomb' and Dora's anguished plea combines pathos with satire.
enrichment.best_quote: 'Oh, what shall I do, what shall I do? Oh, take me somewhere!'
enrichment.summary: Miss Mills cautiously mentions David's name on Thursday; Dora is overcome with guilt and sorrow, fainting at the thought of what she has done to him.

text:
‘Friday. Day of incident. Man appears in kitchen, with blue bag,
“for lady’s boots left out to heel”. Cook replies, “No
such orders.” Man argues point. Cook withdraws to inquire, leaving man
alone with J. On Cook’s return, man still argues point, but ultimately
goes. J. missing. D. distracted. Information sent to police. Man to be
identified by broad nose, and legs like balustrades of bridge. Search made in
every direction. No J. D. weeping bitterly, and inconsolable. Renewed reference
to young Gazelle. Appropriate, but unavailing. Towards evening, strange boy
calls. Brought into parlour. Broad nose, but no balustrades. Says he wants a
pound, and knows a dog. Declines to explain further, though much pressed. Pound
being produced by D. takes Cook to little house, where J. alone tied up to leg
of table. Joy of D. who dances round J. while he eats his supper. Emboldened by
this happy change, mention D. C. upstairs. D. weeps afresh, cries piteously,
“Oh, don’t, don’t, don’t! It is so wicked to think of
anything but poor papa!”—embraces J. and sobs herself to sleep.
(Must not D. C. confine himself to the broad pinions of Time? J. M.)’

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Friday entry is masterpieces of Dickensian satire and narrative complexity: the man with the blue bag and stolen Jip, the bumbling investigation, the strange boy with balustrades-like legs, the pound paid for recovery, and David's name triggering Dora's guilt anew. The cascading absurdities and final quote create both comedy and tragic irony.
enrichment.best_quote: 'Oh, don't, don't, don't! It is so wicked to think of anything but poor papa!'—embraces J. and sobs herself to sleep
enrichment.summary: Miss Mills' Friday entry details an elaborate incident: a suspicious man attempts to steal Jip, who is mysteriously recovered by a strange boy for a pound; when Miss Mills mentions David, Dora weeps afresh, declaring it wicked to think of anything but her father.

text:
Miss Mills and her journal were my sole consolation at this period. To see her,
who had seen Dora but a little while before—to trace the initial letter
of Dora’s name through her sympathetic pages—to be made more and
more miserable by her—were my only comforts. I felt as if I had been
living in a palace of cards, which had tumbled down, leaving only Miss Mills
and me among the ruins; I felt as if some grim enchanter had drawn a magic
circle round the innocent goddess of my heart, which nothing indeed but those
same strong pinions, capable of carrying so many people over so much, would
enable me to enter!

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's final reflection on Miss Mills and her journal as his sole consolation is both touching and darkly comic; his image of a 'palace of cards' tumbling and Miss Mills as the only companion in ruins reveals his emotional isolation and dependence on her affected sympathy.
enrichment.best_quote: I felt as if I had been living in a palace of cards, which had tumbled down, leaving only Miss Mills and me among the ruins
enrichment.summary: David concludes that Miss Mills' journal entries—tracing the initial letter of Dora's name through her pages—and Miss Mills' presence are his only comforts as he contemplates the collapse of his romantic dreams.

text:
I did not allow my resolution, with respect to the Parliamentary Debates, to
cool. It was one of the irons I began to heat immediately, and one of the irons
I kept hot, and hammered at, with a perseverance I may honestly admire. I
bought an approved scheme of the noble art and mystery of stenography (which
cost me ten and sixpence); and plunged into a sea of perplexity that brought
me, in a few weeks, to the confines of distraction. The changes that were rung
upon dots, which in such a position meant such a thing, and in such another
position something else, entirely different; the wonderful vagaries that were
played by circles; the unaccountable consequences that resulted from marks like
flies’ legs; the tremendous effects of a curve in a wrong place; not only
troubled my waking hours, but reappeared before me in my sleep. When I had
groped my way, blindly, through these difficulties, and had mastered the
alphabet, which was an Egyptian Temple in itself, there then appeared a
procession of new horrors, called arbitrary characters; the most despotic
characters I have ever known; who insisted, for instance, that a thing like the
beginning of a cobweb, meant expectation, and that a pen-and-ink sky-rocket,
stood for disadvantageous. When I had fixed these wretches in my mind, I found
that they had driven everything else out of it; then, beginning again, I forgot
them; while I was picking them up, I dropped the other fragments of the system;
in short, it was almost heart-breaking.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's passionate, comic struggle with stenography shows his determination and self-improvement while providing insight into his character through vivid, self-aware narration.
enrichment.best_quote: the wonderful vagaries that were played by circles; the unaccountable consequences that resulted from marks like flies' legs
enrichment.summary: David describes his ardent but frustrating efforts to master stenography for reporting Parliamentary debates, comparing the symbols to cryptic hieroglyphics and Egyptian temples.

text:
My aunt, beginning, I imagine, to be made seriously uncomfortable by my
prolonged dejection, made a pretence of being anxious that I should go to
Dover, to see that all was working well at the cottage, which was let; and to
conclude an agreement, with the same tenant, for a longer term of occupation.
Janet was drafted into the service of Mrs. Strong, where I saw her every day.
She had been undecided, on leaving Dover, whether or no to give the finishing
touch to that renunciation of mankind in which she had been educated, by
marrying a pilot; but she decided against that venture. Not so much for the
sake of principle, I believe, as because she happened not to like him.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine exposition explaining Betsey Trotwood's motivation for sending David to Dover and noting Janet's domestic arrangements.
enrichment.summary: Betsey Trotwood sends David to Dover to inspect her cottage and settle the tenant's lease, while Janet moves into service with Mrs. Strong.

text:
Although it required an effort to leave Miss Mills, I fell rather willingly
into my aunt’s pretence, as a means of enabling me to pass a few tranquil
hours with Agnes. I consulted the good Doctor relative to an absence of three
days; and the Doctor wishing me to take that relaxation,—he wished me to
take more; but my energy could not bear that,—I made up my mind to go.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief transitional passage noting David's willingness to leave London to visit Agnes, with minimal dramatic content.
enrichment.summary: David agrees to travel to Dover for three days, consulting Dr. Strong about his absence and looking forward to spending time with Agnes.

text:
As to the Commons, I had no great occasion to be particular about my duties in
that quarter. To say the truth, we were getting in no very good odour among the
tip-top proctors, and were rapidly sliding down to but a doubtful position. The
business had been indifferent under Mr. Jorkins, before Mr. Spenlow’s
time; and although it had been quickened by the infusion of new blood, and by
the display which Mr. Spenlow made, still it was not established on a
sufficiently strong basis to bear, without being shaken, such a blow as the
sudden loss of its active manager. It fell off very much. Mr. Jorkins,
notwithstanding his reputation in the firm, was an easy-going, incapable sort
of man, whose reputation out of doors was not calculated to back it up. I was
turned over to him now, and when I saw him take his snuff and let the business
go, I regretted my aunt’s thousand pounds more than ever.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes David's professional struggles at Doctors' Commons, foreshadowing future career difficulties and providing context for his anxiety.
enrichment.best_quote: I regretted my aunt's thousand pounds more than ever.
enrichment.summary: The law practice at Doctors' Commons has declined since Mr. Spenlow's death, with Mr. Jorkins proving incapable of managing it, and David expresses regret about his aunt's investment.

text:
But this was not the worst of it. There were a number of hangers-on and
outsiders about the Commons, who, without being proctors themselves, dabbled in
common-form business, and got it done by real proctors, who lent their names in
consideration of a share in the spoil;—and there were a good many of
these too. As our house now wanted business on any terms, we joined this noble
band; and threw out lures to the hangers-on and outsiders, to bring their
business to us. Marriage licences and small probates were what we all looked
for, and what paid us best; and the competition for these ran very high indeed.
Kidnappers and inveiglers were planted in all the avenues of entrance to the
Commons, with instructions to do their utmost to cut off all persons in
mourning, and all gentlemen with anything bashful in their appearance, and
entice them to the offices in which their respective employers were interested;
which instructions were so well observed, that I myself, before I was known by
sight, was twice hustled into the premises of our principal opponent. The
conflicting interests of these touting gentlemen being of a nature to irritate
their feelings, personal collisions took place; and the Commons was even
scandalized by our principal inveigler (who had formerly been in the wine
trade, and afterwards in the sworn brokery line) walking about for some days
with a black eye. Any one of these scouts used to think nothing of politely
assisting an old lady in black out of a vehicle, killing any proctor whom she
inquired for, representing his employer as the lawful successor and
representative of that proctor, and bearing the old lady off (sometimes greatly
affected) to his employer’s office. Many captives were brought to me in
this way. As to marriage licences, the competition rose to such a pitch, that a
shy gentleman in want of one, had nothing to do but submit himself to the first
inveigler, or be fought for, and become the prey of the strongest. One of our
clerks, who was an outsider, used, in the height of this contest, to sit with
his hat on, that he might be ready to rush out and swear before a surrogate any
victim who was brought in. The system of inveigling continues, I believe, to
this day. The last time I was in the Commons, a civil able-bodied person in a
white apron pounced out upon me from a doorway, and whispering the word
‘Marriage-licence’ in my ear, was with great difficulty prevented
from taking me up in his arms and lifting me into a proctor’s. From this
digression, let me proceed to Dover.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended satirical digression on the corrupt touting system at Doctors' Commons, with vivid comic characters and sharp social critique that entertains while condemning institutional practices.
enrichment.best_quote: Kidnappers and inveiglers were planted in all the avenues of entrance to the Commons, with instructions to do their utmost to cut off all persons in mourning, and all gentlemen with anything bashful in their appearance, and entice them to the offices in which their respective employers were interested
enrichment.summary: David digresses at length about the corrupt touting and inveigling practices of clerks and outsiders at Doctors' Commons who prey on clients seeking marriage licences and probates.

I found everything in a satisfactory state at the cottage; and was enabled to
gratify my aunt exceedingly by reporting that the tenant inherited her feud,
and waged incessant war against donkeys. Having settled the little business I
had to transact there, and slept there one night, I walked on to Canterbury
early in the morning. It was now winter again; and the fresh, cold windy day,
and the sweeping downland, brightened up my hopes a little.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Simple account of David's visit to Dover and his walk to Canterbury; mostly transitional description without significant incident.
enrichment.summary: David completes his business at the cottage, where the tenant amuses Betsey by continuing her feud with donkeys, then sets out for Canterbury.

text:
Coming into Canterbury, I loitered through the old streets with a sober
pleasure that calmed my spirits, and eased my heart. There were the old signs,
the old names over the shops, the old people serving in them. It appeared so
long, since I had been a schoolboy there, that I wondered the place was so
little changed, until I reflected how little I was changed myself. Strange to
say, that quiet influence which was inseparable in my mind from Agnes, seemed
to pervade even the city where she dwelt. The venerable cathedral towers, and
the old jackdaws and rooks whose airy voices made them more retired than
perfect silence would have done; the battered gateways, one stuck full with
statues, long thrown down, and crumbled away, like the reverential pilgrims who
had gazed upon them; the still nooks, where the ivied growth of centuries crept
over gabled ends and ruined walls; the ancient houses, the pastoral landscape
of field, orchard, and garden; everywhere—on everything—I felt the
same serener air, the same calm, thoughtful, softening spirit.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lyrical and atmospheric passage evoking Canterbury's changelessness, the nostalgia of David's return, and the spiritual association between Agnes and the city itself.

‘I am not fond of professions of humility,’ I returned, ‘or
professions of anything else.’ ‘There now!’ said Uriah,
looking flabby and lead-coloured in the moonlight. ‘Didn’t I know
it! But how little you think of the rightful umbleness of a person in my
station, Master Copperfield! Father and me was both brought up at a foundation
school for boys; and mother, she was likewise brought up at a public, sort of
charitable, establishment. They taught us all a deal of umbleness—not
much else that I know of, from morning to night. We was to be umble to this
person, and umble to that; and to pull off our caps here, and to make bows
there; and always to know our place, and abase ourselves before our betters.
And we had such a lot of betters! Father got the monitor-medal by being umble.
So did I. Father got made a sexton by being umble. He had the character, among
the gentlefolks, of being such a well-behaved man, that they were determined to
bring him in. “Be umble, Uriah,” says father to me, “and
you’ll get on. It was what was always being dinned into you and me at
school; it’s what goes down best. Be umble,” says father,
“and you’ll do!” And really it ain’t done bad!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uriah's extensive account of his upbringing in humility, his father's teaching that humility brings advancement, and his deliberate practice of it; a crucial revelation of his origins and psychology.
enrichment.best_quote: Be umble, Uriah, says father to me, and you'll get on. It was what was always being dinned into you and me at school; it's what goes down best. Be umble, says father, and you'll do!
enrichment.summary: Uriah recounts how he and his father were taught humility at a charity school and how his father advised him to practice humility as the path to advancement, which has indeed proved successful.

text:
It was the first time it had ever occurred to me, that this detestable cant of
false humility might have originated out of the Heep family. I had seen the
harvest, but had never thought of the seed.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's reflection on the origins of the 'cant of false humility' in the Heep family; he has seen the harvest but not the seed, suggesting deeper understanding.
enrichment.best_quote: I had seen the harvest, but had never thought of the seed.
enrichment.summary: David reflects that this false humility originates in the Heep family's upbringing, and he has only now understood its roots.

text:
‘When I was quite a young boy,’ said Uriah, ‘I got to know
what umbleness did, and I took to it. I ate umble pie with an appetite. I
stopped at the umble point of my learning, and says I, “Hold hard!”
When you offered to teach me Latin, I knew better. “People like to be
above you,” says father, “keep yourself down.” I am very
umble to the present moment, Master Copperfield, but I’ve got a little
power!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uriah's account of how he learned and mastered humility as a young boy, and how he deliberately limited his learning to keep himself 'umble' and maintain his power; extraordinary revelation of deliberate self-corruption.
enrichment.best_quote: I got to know what umbleness did, and I took to it. I ate umble pie with an appetite. I stopped at the umble point of my learning, and says I, Hold hard! When you offered to teach me Latin, I knew better. People like to be above you, says father, keep yourself down. I am very umble to the present moment, Master Copperfield, but I've got a little power!
enrichment.summary: Uriah describes his deliberate adoption of humility as a strategy, his willingness to limit his own education to maintain his humble appearance, and his claim that humility has paradoxically given him power.

text:
And he said all this—I knew, as I saw his face in the
moonlight—that I might understand he was resolved to recompense himself
by using his power. I had never doubted his meanness, his craft and malice; but
I fully comprehended now, for the first time, what a base, unrelenting, and
revengeful spirit, must have been engendered by this early, and this long,
suppression.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's analysis of Uriah's malice and the psychological consequences of suppression; understands for the first time the true nature of Uriah's 'base, unrelenting, and revengeful spirit.'
enrichment.best_quote: I fully comprehended now, for the first time, what a base, unrelenting, and revengeful spirit, must have been engendered by this early, and this long, suppression.
enrichment.summary: David reflects that Uriah's confession has finally revealed to him the truly malevolent and revengeful nature that Uriah's long suppression and humiliation must have created.

text:
His account of himself was so far attended with an agreeable result, that it
led to his withdrawing his hand in order that he might have another hug of
himself under the chin. Once apart from him, I was determined to keep apart;
and we walked back, side by side, saying very little more by the way. Whether
his spirits were elevated by the communication I had made to him, or by his
having indulged in this retrospect, I don’t know; but they were raised by
some influence. He talked more at dinner than was usual with him; asked his
mother (off duty, from the moment of our re-entering the house) whether he was
not growing too old for a bachelor; and once looked at Agnes so, that I would
have given all I had, for leave to knock him down.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uriah's mood lifts after his confession, he withdraws his hand and expresses heightened spirits; shows his satisfaction at having manipulated David.
enrichment.best_quote: Once apart from him, I was determined to keep apart
enrichment.summary: Uriah's mood improves after his confession, and he releases David's hand; he talks more at dinner and at one point looks at Agnes so aggressively that David wants to strike him.

text:
When we three males were left alone after dinner, he got into a more
adventurous state. He had taken little or no wine; and I presume it was the
mere insolence of triumph that was upon him, flushed perhaps by the temptation
my presence furnished to its exhibition.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David notes Uriah's increasingly insolent behavior after dinner when alone with the men, emboldened by David's revelation of his engagement.
enrichment.summary: David observes that Uriah becomes more adventurous and insolent after dinner, emboldened by the knowledge of David's engagement.

text:
I had observed yesterday, that he tried to entice Mr. Wickfield to drink; and,
interpreting the look which Agnes had given me as she went out, had limited
myself to one glass, and then proposed that we should follow her. I would have
done so again today; but Uriah was too quick for me.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David recalls his observation from yesterday and his precaution about wine; functional exposition.
enrichment.summary: David recalls that Uriah tried to make Mr. Wickfield drink yesterday, and David limited himself to avoid a similar trap.

text:
‘We seldom see our present visitor, sir,’ he said, addressing Mr.
Wickfield, sitting, such a contrast to him, at the end of the table, ‘and
I should propose to give him welcome in another glass or two of wine, if you
have no objections. Mr. Copperfield, your elth and appiness!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uriah's toast to David, addressed to Mr. Wickfield; conversational opening to the drinking scene.
enrichment.summary: Uriah proposes a toast to David's health and happiness in the presence of Mr. Wickfield.

text:
I was obliged to make a show of taking the hand he stretched across to me; and
then, with very different emotions, I took the hand of the broken gentleman,
his partner.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David shakes hands with Uriah and then with Mr. Wickfield; functional action describing different emotional responses.
enrichment.summary: David obligingly shakes hands with Uriah and then with Mr. Wickfield with very different emotions.

text:
‘Come, fellow-partner,’ said Uriah, ‘if I may take the
liberty,—now, suppose you give us something or another appropriate to
Copperfield!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uriah's toast proposal to Mr. Wickfield on David's behalf; functional dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Uriah asks Mr. Wickfield to propose a second toast to David.

text:
I pass over Mr. Wickfield’s proposing my aunt, his proposing Mr. Dick,
his proposing Doctors’ Commons, his proposing Uriah, his drinking
everything twice; his consciousness of his own weakness, the ineffectual effort
that he made against it; the struggle between his shame in Uriah’s
deportment, and his desire to conciliate him; the manifest exultation with
which Uriah twisted and turned, and held him up before me. It made me sick at
heart to see, and my hand recoils from writing it.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's refusal to detail the painful spectacle of Mr. Wickfield's drunken degradation and vulnerability to Uriah's dominance; expresses the emotional toll of witnessing this abuse.
enrichment.best_quote: I pass over Mr. Wickfield's proposing my aunt, his proposing Mr. Dick, his proposing Doctors' Commons, his proposing Uriah, his drinking everything twice; his consciousness of his own weakness, the ineffectual effort that he made against it; the struggle between his shame in Uriah's deportment, and his desire to conciliate him; the manifest exultation with which Uriah twisted and turned, and held him up before me. It made me sick at heart to see, and my hand recoils from writing it.
enrichment.summary: David refuses to detail the sordid spectacle of Mr. Wickfield's drunken weakness, his shame, and Uriah's exultant manipulation, saying he cannot bear to write it.

text:
‘Come, fellow-partner!’ said Uriah, at last, ‘I’ll give
you another one, and I umbly ask for bumpers, seeing I intend to make it the
divinest of her sex.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uriah's second toast for 'bumpers,' declaring his intention to propose a toast to someone unspecified; builds tension toward the climax.
enrichment.best_quote: Come, fellow-partner, I'll give you another one, and I umbly ask for bumpers, seeing I intend to make it the divinest of her sex.
enrichment.summary: Uriah proposes another toast, requesting bumpers and hinting that he intends to toast someone he considers divine.

text:
Her father had his empty glass in his hand. I saw him set it down, look at the
picture she was so like, put his hand to his forehead, and shrink back in his
elbow-chair.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Wickfield's anguished response to Uriah's impending toast to Agnes, setting down his glass and looking at her portrait; foreshadows his emotional collapse.
enrichment.best_quote: I saw him set it down, look at the picture she was so like, put his hand to his forehead, and shrink back in his elbow-chair.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Wickfield immediately senses Uriah's intention and emotionally responds, looking at Agnes's portrait before withdrawing in his chair.

text:
‘I’m an umble individual to give you her elth,’ proceeded
Uriah, ‘but I admire—adore her.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uriah's explicit declaration that he admires and adores Agnes, claiming the humble position of offering her a toast.
enrichment.best_quote: I'm an umble individual to give you her elth, but I admire—adore her.
enrichment.summary: Uriah humbly states that he admires and adores Agnes, though he is an humble individual to propose her health.

text:
No physical pain that her father’s grey head could have borne, I think,
could have been more terrible to me, than the mental endurance I saw compressed
now within both his hands.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's observation of Mr. Wickfield's internal suffering, compressed in his hands; a powerful image of parental anguish.
enrichment.best_quote: No physical pain that her father's grey head could have borne, I think, could have been more terrible to me, than the mental endurance I saw compressed now within both his hands.
enrichment.summary: David observes the profound mental anguish compressed within Mr. Wickfield's clasped hands at the prospect of Uriah's ambition.

text:
‘Agnes,’ said Uriah, either not regarding him, or not knowing what
the nature of his action was, ‘Agnes Wickfield is, I am safe to say, the
divinest of her sex. May I speak out, among friends? To be her father is a
proud distinction, but to be her usband—’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uriah's declaration of ambition to marry Agnes, appearing oblivious or indifferent to Mr. Wickfield's reaction; the trigger for the father's emotional breakdown.
enrichment.best_quote: To be her father is a proud distinction, but to be her usband—
enrichment.summary: Uriah states that while being Agnes's father is a distinction, his ambition is to be her husband.

text:
Spare me from ever again hearing such a cry, as that with which her father rose
up from the table! ‘What’s the matter?’ said Uriah, turning
of a deadly colour. ‘You are not gone mad, after all, Mr. Wickfield, I
hope? If I say I’ve an ambition to make your Agnes my Agnes, I have as
good a right to it as another man. I have a better right to it than any other
man!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: The climactic moment when Mr. Wickfield rises from the table with a terrible cry, his emotional breakdown triggered by Uriah's declaration about marrying Agnes; extraordinarily dramatic and emotionally intense.
enrichment.best_quote: Spare me from ever again hearing such a cry, as that with which her father rose up from the table!
enrichment.summary: Mr. Wickfield rises from the table with a terrible cry of anguish, and Uriah callously asks if he has gone mad, asserting his right to aspire to Agnes.

text:
I had my arms round Mr. Wickfield, imploring him by everything that I could
think of, oftenest of all by his love for Agnes, to calm himself a little. He
was mad for the moment; tearing out his hair, beating his head, trying to force
me from him, and to force himself from me, not answering a word, not looking at
or seeing anyone; blindly striving for he knew not what, his face all staring
and distorted—a frightful spectacle.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended and vivid description of Mr. Wickfield's mad frenzy—tearing his hair, beating his head, trying to break free from David's arms; an extraordinary depiction of psychological and emotional breakdown.
enrichment.best_quote: He was mad for the moment; tearing out his hair, beating his head, trying to force me from him, and to force himself from me, not answering a word, not looking at or seeing anyone; blindly striving for he knew not what, his face all staring and distorted—a frightful spectacle.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Wickfield becomes temporarily mad with anguish, tearing his hair and beating his head while David tries to restrain him.

text:
I conjured him, incoherently, but in the most impassioned manner, not to
abandon himself to this wildness, but to hear me. I besought him to think of
Agnes, to connect me with Agnes, to recollect how Agnes and I had grown up
together, how I honoured her and loved her, how she was his pride and joy. I
tried to bring her idea before him in any form; I even reproached him with not
having firmness to spare her the knowledge of such a scene as this. I may have
effected something, or his wildness may have spent itself; but by degrees he
struggled less, and began to look at me—strangely at first, then with
recognition in his eyes. At length he said, ‘I know, Trotwood! My darling
child and you—I know! But look at him!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's impassioned efforts to calm Mr. Wickfield by invoking Agnes, and the father's gradual return to consciousness and recognition; deeply moving resolution of the frenzy.
enrichment.best_quote: At length he said, 'I know, Trotwood! My darling child and you—I know! But look at him!'
enrichment.summary: David implores Mr. Wickfield to think of Agnes and remember his love for her and David, eventually calming him enough that he recognizes David and realizes the situation.

text:
He pointed to Uriah, pale and glowering in a corner, evidently very much out in
his calculations, and taken by surprise.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Wickfield points to Uriah standing pale in the corner, taken by surprise; transitional description.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Wickfield points to Uriah, who stands pale and taken aback in the corner.

text:
‘Look at my torturer,’ he replied. ‘Before him I have step by
step abandoned name and reputation, peace and quiet, house and home.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Wickfield's anguished account of his progressive degradation and loss of everything to Uriah; a powerful confession of moral and psychological collapse.
enrichment.best_quote: Before him I have step by step abandoned name and reputation, peace and quiet, house and home.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Wickfield cries out that he has gradually surrendered everything—name, reputation, peace, house, and home—to Uriah.

text:
‘I have kept your name and reputation for you, and your peace and quiet,

a little beyond what you were prepared for, I can go back, I suppose?
There’s no harm done.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uriah's attempt to backtrack and soothe Mr. Wickfield, claiming he has protected him and suggesting no real harm is done; characterizes his sudden shift to defensive humility.
enrichment.best_quote: I have kept your name and reputation for you, and your peace and quiet, and your house and home too. Don't be foolish, Mr. Wickfield. If I have gone a little beyond what you were prepared for, I can go back, I suppose?
enrichment.summary: Uriah attempts to pacify Mr. Wickfield by claiming he has protected him and suggesting he can retreat if he has overstepped.

text:
‘I looked for single motives in everyone,’ said Mr. Wickfield,

see what he is—oh, see what he is!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Wickfield's reflection on his mistaken belief that he had bound Uriah through mutual interest; sees Uriah's true nature now.
enrichment.best_quote: I looked for single motives in everyone, and I was satisfied I had bound him to me by motives of interest. But see what he is—oh, see what he is!
enrichment.summary: Mr. Wickfield laments that he expected Uriah to be bound by self-interest alone, but now sees his true malicious nature.

text:
‘You had better stop him, Copperfield, if you can,’ cried Uriah,
with his long forefinger pointing towards me. ‘He’ll say something
presently—mind you!—he’ll be sorry to have said afterwards,
and you’ll be sorry to have heard!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uriah warns David that Mr. Wickfield might say something he regrets; threatens to expose secrets if Mr. Wickfield continues.
enrichment.best_quote: You had better stop him, Copperfield, if you can. He'll say something presently—mind you!—he'll be sorry to have said afterwards, and you'll be sorry to have heard!
enrichment.summary: Uriah threatens that Mr. Wickfield will say things he will regret and that David will regret hearing.

text:
‘I’ll say anything!’ cried Mr. Wickfield, with a desperate
air. ‘Why should I not be in all the world’s power if I am in
yours?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Wickfield's defiant response, asking why he should not be in Uriah's power if he is already in everyone else's; despair and resignation.
enrichment.best_quote: Why should I not be in all the world's power if I am in yours?
enrichment.summary: Mr. Wickfield despairingly asks why he should not be in everyone's power if he is already in Uriah's.

text:
‘Mind! I tell you!’ said Uriah, continuing to warn me. ‘If
you don’t stop his mouth, you’re not his friend! Why
shouldn’t you be in all the world’s power, Mr. Wickfield? Because
you have got a daughter. You and me know what we know, don’t we? Let
sleeping dogs lie—who wants to rouse ‘em? I don’t.
Can’t you see I am as umble as I can be? I tell you, if I’ve gone
too far, I’m sorry. What would you have, sir?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Uriah's escalating pressure and threats about secrets, particularly regarding Mr. Wickfield's daughter, and his continued false humility as a weapon.
enrichment.best_quote: You and me know what we know, don't we? Let sleeping dogs lie—who wants to rouse 'em?
enrichment.summary: Uriah threatens to reveal secrets about Mr. Wickfield and his daughter, using his knowledge as leverage while maintaining false humility.

text:
‘Oh, Trotwood, Trotwood!’ exclaimed Mr. Wickfield, wringing his
hands. ‘What I have come down to be, since I first saw you in this house!
I was on my downward way then, but the dreary, dreary road I have traversed
since! Weak indulgence has ruined me. Indulgence in remembrance, and indulgence
in forgetfulness. My natural grief for my child’s mother turned to
disease; my natural love for my child turned to disease. I have infected
everything I touched. I have brought misery on what I dearly love, I
know—you know! I thought it possible that I could truly love one creature
in the world, and not love the rest; I thought it possible that I could truly
mourn for one creature gone out of the world, and not have some part in the
grief of all who mourned. Thus the lessons of my life have been perverted! I
have preyed on my own morbid coward heart, and it has preyed on me. Sordid in
my grief, sordid in my love, sordid in my miserable escape from the darker side
of both, oh see the ruin I am, and hate me, shun me!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Wickfield's extended and extraordinarily moving confession of his moral and psychological ruin, his grief-turned-disease, and his sordid cowardice; one of the chapter's most profound passages.
enrichment.best_quote: Weak indulgence has ruined me. Indulgence in remembrance, and indulgence in forgetfulness. My natural grief for my child's mother turned to disease; my natural love for my child turned to disease. I have infected everything I touched. I have brought misery on what I dearly love, I know—you know!
enrichment.summary: Mr. Wickfield confesses that his grief and love have turned into disease, that he has infected everything, and that he is utterly ruined by his own sordid indulgence and cowardice.

text:

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Wickfield's physical and emotional collapse after his outburst; brief description of exhaustion.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Wickfield drops into a chair and sobs weakly as his emotional intensity exhausts itself.

excellent man, most exemplary in every way; and he pointed out to her that she
ought, as a Christian, to reconcile herself to the sacrifice (especially as it
was so uncertain), and to bear no uncharitable feeling towards me. As to
myself, Copperfield, I give you my word, I felt a perfect bird of prey towards
the family.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reverend Horace's Christian appeal for acceptance provides social critique while revealing Traddles' self-abnegating feelings, deepening sympathy.
enrichment.best_quote: he pointed out to her that she ought, as a Christian, to reconcile herself to the sacrifice
enrichment.summary: Reverend Horace persuaded Mrs Crewler to accept the engagement by appealing to her Christian duty to sacrifice for others, while Traddles felt like a predator toward the family.

text: ‘The sisters took your part, I hope, Traddles?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Minimal question inviting further elaboration on family support.

‘Why, I can’t say they did,’ he returned. ‘When we had
comparatively reconciled Mrs. Crewler to it, we had to break it to Sarah. You
recollect my mentioning Sarah, as the one that has something the matter with
her spine?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transitional line introducing the next family obstacle (Sarah) while acknowledging David's prior acquaintance with her.
enrichment.summary: Traddles explains that he had to tell Sarah Crewler (the sister with spinal troubles) separately about his engagement.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Single-word affirmation from David.

‘She clenched both her hands,’ said Traddles, looking at me in
dismay; ‘shut her eyes; turned lead-colour; became perfectly stiff; and
took nothing for two days but toast-and-water, administered with a
tea-spoon.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vividly comic and psychosomatic account of Sarah's extreme hysteria, exemplifying Victorian female fragility and emotional blackmail as domestic control.
enrichment.best_quote: She clenched both her hands, shut her eyes; turned lead-colour; became perfectly stiff; and took nothing for two days but toast-and-water, administered with a tea-spoon.
enrichment.summary: Traddles describes Sarah's extreme physical response to the news: she clenched her fists, turned pale, stiffened entirely, and consumed only toast-and-water for two days.

text: ‘What a very unpleasant girl, Traddles!’ I remarked.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's brief unsympathetic comment revealing his immaturity and lack of compassion.
enrichment.summary: David dismisses Sarah as unpleasant.

text:
‘Oh, I beg your pardon, Copperfield!’ said Traddles. ‘She is
a very charming girl, but she has a great deal of feeling. In fact, they all
have. Sophy told me afterwards, that the self-reproach she underwent while she
was in attendance upon Sarah, no words could describe. I know it must have been
severe, by my own feelings, Copperfield; which were like a criminal’s.
After Sarah was restored, we still had to break it to the other eight; and it
produced various effects upon them of a most pathetic nature. The two little
ones, whom Sophy educates, have only just left off de-testing me.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Traddles' magnanimous defense of Sarah and elaborate account of cascading family trauma reveals both his compassion and the Crewler family's emotional entanglement.
enrichment.best_quote: they all have. Sophy told me afterwards, that the self-reproach she underwent while she was in attendance upon Sarah, no words could describe.
enrichment.summary: Traddles generously defends Sarah as deeply feeling, recounting how Sophy's guilt during Sarah's crisis was immense, and how the news had to be broken to eight more sisters, with the youngest two only recently ceasing to detest him.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine reassurance-seeking question about family reconciliation.
enrichment.summary: David hopefully asks if the family is now reconciled to the engagement.

‘Ye-yes, I should say they were, on the whole, resigned to it,’
said Traddles, doubtfully. ‘The fact is, we avoid mentioning the subject;
and my unsettled prospects and indifferent circumstances are a great
consolation to them. There will be a deplorable scene, whenever we are married.
It will be much more like a funeral, than a wedding. And they’ll all hate
me for taking her away!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Traddles' poignant and darkly humorous account of the family's resigned rather than joyful acceptance and his awareness of future tragedy, revealing the cost of duty and sacrifice.

enrichment.summary: Traddles admits the family is resigned rather than reconciled, noting that his poor prospects actually comfort them, and predicting his wedding will resemble a funeral when he takes Sophy away.

His honest face, as he looked at me with a serio-comic shake of his head,
impresses me more in the remembrance than it did in the reality, for I was by
this time in a state of such excessive trepidation and wandering of mind, as to
be quite unable to fix my attention on anything. On our approaching the house
where the Misses Spenlow lived, I was at such a discount in respect of my
personal looks and presence of mind, that Traddles proposed a gentle stimulant
in the form of a glass of ale. This having been administered at a neighbouring
public-house, he conducted me, with tottering steps, to the Misses
Spenlow’s door.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reflective passage contrasting Traddles' emotional sincerity with David's nervous distraction, moving toward the crucial meeting with the aunts.
enrichment.summary: David, overwhelmed by trepidation, can barely absorb Traddles' story; as they approach the Misses Spenlow's house, Traddles suggests a glass of ale to steady David's nerves.

text:
I had a vague sensation of being, as it were, on view, when the maid opened it;
and of wavering, somehow, across a hall with a weather-glass in it, into a
quiet little drawing-room on the ground-floor, commanding a neat garden. Also
of sitting down here, on a sofa, and seeing Traddles’s hair start up, now
his hat was removed, like one of those obtrusive little figures made of
springs, that fly out of fictitious snuff-boxes when the lid is taken off. Also
of hearing an old-fashioned clock ticking away on the chimney-piece, and trying
to make it keep time to the jerking of my heart,—which it wouldn’t.
Also of looking round the room for any sign of Dora, and seeing none. Also of
thinking that Jip once barked in the distance, and was instantly choked by
somebody. Ultimately I found myself backing Traddles into the fireplace, and
bowing in great confusion to two dry little elderly ladies, dressed in black,
and each looking wonderfully like a preparation in chip or tan of the late Mr.
Spenlow.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brilliantly comic stream-of-consciousness sequence capturing David's acute anxiety through fragmented, disorienting imagery; Dickens' mastery of interior comic psychology and vivid domestic detail.
enrichment.best_quote: Also of sitting down here, on a sofa, and seeing Traddles's hair start up, now his hat was removed, like one of those obtrusive little figures made of springs, that fly out of fictitious snuff-boxes when the lid is taken off.
enrichment.summary: David's nervous disorientation at the Misses Spenlow's house is rendered through a series of disconnected sensations: a weather-glass, an old-fashioned clock, failed attempts to see Dora, Jip's distant barking, Traddles' hair springing up, and finally the two elderly aunts resembling pickled preparations of their late brother.

text: ‘Pray,’ said one of the two little ladies, ‘be seated.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Minimal directive from one of the aunts.
enrichment.summary: One of the Misses Spenlow invites David and Traddles to sit.

When I had done tumbling over Traddles, and had sat upon something which was
not a cat—my first seat was—I so far recovered my sight, as to
perceive that Mr. Spenlow had evidently been the youngest of the family; that
there was a disparity of six or eight years between the two sisters; and that
the younger appeared to be the manager of the conference, inasmuch as she had
my letter in her hand—so familiar as it looked to me, and yet so
odd!—and was referring to it through an eye-glass. They were dressed
alike, but this sister wore her dress with a more youthful air than the other;
and perhaps had a trifle more frill, or tucker, or brooch, or bracelet, or some
little thing of that kind, which made her look more lively. They were both
upright in their carriage, formal, precise, composed, and quiet. The sister who
had not my letter, had her arms crossed on her breast, and resting on each
other, like an Idol.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Detailed characterization of the two aunts through physical observation and behavioral minutiae, revealing their formality, family hierarchy, and physical peculiarities.
enrichment.best_quote: They were dressed alike, but this sister wore her dress with a more youthful air than the other; and perhaps had a trifle more frill, or tucker, or brooch, or bracelet, or some little thing of that kind, which made her look more lively.
enrichment.summary: David observes that Mr Spenlow was youngest of the family; the younger sister appears to be the managing conference leader with David's letter; both are formal and composed, with the elder sister posed idol-like.
