‘Mr. Copperfield, I believe,’ said the sister who had got my
letter, addressing herself to Traddles.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Comic confusion-of-identity scene establishing the Misses Spenlow's confusion and adding humorous tension to the interview.
enrichment.summary: Miss Lavinia mistakenly addresses Traddles as Mr Copperfield, creating an awkward clarification scene.

This was a frightful beginning. Traddles had to indicate that I was Mr.
Copperfield, and I had to lay claim to myself, and they had to divest
themselves of a preconceived opinion that Traddles was Mr. Copperfield, and
altogether we were in a nice condition. To improve it, we all distinctly heard
Jip give two short barks, and receive another choke.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Comic elaboration of the confusion, with Jip's interruption adding farcical element and relieving tension.
enrichment.summary: Everyone must clarify the identity mix-up; Jip barks twice and is choked again, heightening the comic chaos.

text: ‘Mr. Copperfield!’ said the sister with the letter.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Confirmation line from the aunt.
enrichment.summary: Miss Lavinia confirms she is addressing Mr Copperfield.

text:
I did something—bowed, I suppose—and was all attention, when the
other sister struck in.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Minimal action tag describing David's response.
enrichment.summary: David makes some gestural response and readies himself to listen.

text:
‘My sister Lavinia,’ said she ‘being conversant with matters
of this nature, will state what we consider most calculated to promote the
happiness of both parties.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Formal introduction establishing Miss Lavinia as the spokesperson on matters of the heart.
enrichment.summary: Miss Clarissa introduces Miss Lavinia as the authority who will present their views on the engagement.

text:
I discovered afterwards that Miss Lavinia was an authority in affairs of the
heart, by reason of there having anciently existed a certain Mr. Pidger, who
played short whist, and was supposed to have been enamoured of her. My private
opinion is, that this was entirely a gratuitous assumption, and that Pidger was
altogether innocent of any such sentiments—to which he had never given
any sort of expression that I could ever hear of. Both Miss Lavinia and Miss
Clarissa had a superstition, however, that he would have declared his passion,
if he had not been cut short in his youth (at about sixty) by over-drinking his
constitution, and over-doing an attempt to set it right again by swilling Bath
water. They had a lurking suspicion even, that he died of secret love; though I
must say there was a picture of him in the house with a damask nose, which
concealment did not appear to have ever preyed upon.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Magnificent satirical digression on Miss Lavinia's supposed expertise derived from the dubious Mr Pidger, revealing Dickens' penetrating social comedy about spinster mythology and self-deception.
enrichment.best_quote: My private opinion is, that this was entirely a gratuitous assumption, and that Pidger was altogether innocent of any such sentiments
enrichment.summary: David reveals that Lavinia's expertise stems from a supposed suitor, Mr Pidger, who played whist and allegedly harbored secret passion for her before dying from over-drinking at sixty, though David suspects Pidger was entirely innocent of romantic feeling toward her.

‘We will not,’ said Miss Lavinia, ‘enter on the past history
of this matter. Our poor brother Francis’s death has cancelled
that.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Lavinia's formal opening statement setting aside the past and transitioning to the engagement discussion.
enrichment.summary: Miss Lavinia announces they will not revisit past family history since Francis Spenlow's death has settled that matter.

‘We had not,’ said Miss Clarissa, ‘been in the habit of
frequent association with our brother Francis; but there was no decided
division or disunion between us. Francis took his road; we took ours. We
considered it conducive to the happiness of all parties that it should be so.
And it was so.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Clarissa's defensive explanation of past family estrangement, revealing tension and her controlling impulse toward family narrative.
enrichment.best_quote: We considered it conducive to the happiness of all parties that it should be so.
enrichment.summary: Miss Clarissa explains that the family maintained cordial separation from Francis, considering it advantageous for everyone's happiness.

Each of the sisters leaned a little forward to speak, shook her head after
speaking, and became upright again when silent. Miss Clarissa never moved her
arms. She sometimes played tunes upon them with her fingers—minuets and
marches I should think—but never moved them.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Physical characterization revealing the aunts' formulaic, ritualistic mannerism and Miss Clarissa's immobility and restraint.
enrichment.summary: David observes that each sister leans slightly forward to speak, shakes her head after speaking, and straightens again; Miss Clarissa never moves her arms except to play silent tunes on them.

brother Francis’s death,’ said Miss Lavinia; ‘and therefore
we consider our brother’s opinions as regarded her position as being
changed too. We have no reason to doubt, Mr. Copperfield, that you are a young
gentleman possessed of good qualities and honourable character; or that you
have an affection—or are fully persuaded that you have an
affection—for our niece.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Lavinia's measured acknowledgment of Dora's changed position and careful, qualified assessment of David's character and affection.

I replied, as I usually did whenever I had a chance, that nobody had ever loved
anybody else as I loved Dora. Traddles came to my assistance with a
confirmatory murmur.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's passionate assertion of love and Traddles' supporting murmur.
enrichment.summary: David passionately declares that no one has ever loved anyone as he loves Dora, with Traddles offering confirmatory support.

Miss Lavinia was going on to make some rejoinder, when Miss Clarissa, who
appeared to be incessantly beset by a desire to refer to her brother Francis,
struck in again:

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transition line noting Miss Clarissa's interruption with her obsessive reference to Francis.
enrichment.summary: Miss Clarissa interrupts Miss Lavinia, returning compulsively to the subject of their brother Francis.

parties.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Clarissa's resentful, controlling observation about Dora's mother's exclusionary behavior, revealing family bitterness and social grievance.

‘Sister Clarissa,’ said Miss Lavinia. ‘Perhaps we
needn’t mind that now.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Lavinia's attempt to move past Miss Clarissa's grievance.
enrichment.summary: Miss Lavinia suggests they need not dwell on the past now.

text:
‘Sister Lavinia,’ said Miss Clarissa, ‘it belongs to the
subject. With your branch of the subject, on which alone you are competent to
speak, I should not think of interfering. On this branch of the subject I have
a voice and an opinion. It would have been better for the happiness of all
parties, if Dora’s mama, when she married our brother Francis, had
mentioned plainly what her intentions were. We should then have known what we
had to expect. We should have said “Pray do not invite us, at any
time”; and all possibility of misunderstanding would have been
avoided.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Clarissa's elaborate, controlling assertion of her right to speak on family matters, revealing her resentful need for recognition and authority.

When Miss Clarissa had shaken her head, Miss Lavinia resumed: again referring

eyes, by the way, which were like birds’ eyes. They were not unlike
birds, altogether; having a sharp, brisk, sudden manner, and a little short,
spruce way of adjusting themselves, like canaries.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Physical description comparing the aunts to birds, reinforcing their fussy, formulaic, and somewhat absurd character.

‘You ask permission of my sister Clarissa and myself, Mr. Copperfield, to

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Lavinia's formal statement of the aunts' condition: they are willing to allow David's visits as Dora's accepted suitor.
enrichment.summary: Miss Lavinia formally requests David's permission to visit as Dora's accepted suitor.

‘If our brother Francis,’ said Miss Clarissa, breaking out again,
if I may call anything so calm a breaking out, ‘wished to surround
himself with an atmosphere of Doctors’ Commons, and of Doctors’
Commons only, what right or desire had we to object? None, I am sure. We have
ever been far from wishing to obtrude ourselves on anyone. But why not say so?
Let our brother Francis and his wife have their society. Let my sister Lavinia
and myself have our society. We can find it for ourselves, I hope.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Miss Clarissa's defensive assertion of social autonomy and resentment toward Francis's monopoly of society, revealing class consciousness and wounded pride.
enrichment.best_quote: We can find it for ourselves, I hope.
enrichment.summary: Miss Clarissa questions why they should object if Francis wished to surround himself with Doctors' Commons society exclusively, and asserts the sisters' right to their own separate social sphere.

‘Affection,’ said Miss Lavinia, glancing at her sister for
corroboration, which she gave in the form of a little nod to every clause,
‘mature affection, homage, devotion, does not easily express itself. Its

ripening in the shade.’

Now, although I had not received any express encouragement as yet, I fancied
that I saw in the two little sisters, and particularly in Miss Lavinia, an
intensified enjoyment of this new and fruitful subject of domestic interest, a
settling down to make the most of it, a disposition to pet it, in which there
was a good bright ray of hope. I thought I perceived that Miss Lavinia would
have uncommon satisfaction in superintending two young lovers, like Dora and
me; and that Miss Clarissa would have hardly less satisfaction in seeing her
superintend us, and in chiming in with her own particular department of the
subject whenever that impulse was strong upon her. This gave me courage to
protest most vehemently that I loved Dora better than I could tell, or anyone
believe; that all my friends knew how I loved her; that my aunt, Agnes,
Traddles, everyone who knew me, knew how I loved her, and how earnest my love
had made me. For the truth of this, I appealed to Traddles. And Traddles,
firing up as if he were plunging into a Parliamentary Debate, really did come
out nobly: confirming me in good round terms, and in a plain sensible practical
manner, that evidently made a favourable impression.

I feel as if it were not for me to record, even though this manuscript is
intended for no eyes but mine, how hard I worked at that tremendous short-hand,
and all improvement appertaining to it, in my sense of responsibility to Dora
and her aunts. I will only add, to what I have already written of my
perseverance at this time of my life, and of a patient and continuous energy
which then began to be matured within me, and which I know to be the strong
part of my character, if it have any strength at all, that there, on looking
back, I find the source of my success. I have been very fortunate in worldly
matters; many men have worked much harder, and not succeeded half so well; but
I never could have done what I have done, without the habits of punctuality,
order, and diligence, without the determination to concentrate myself on one
object at a time, no matter how quickly its successor should come upon its
heels, which I then formed. Heaven knows I write this, in no spirit of
self-laudation. The man who reviews his own life, as I do mine, in going on
here, from page to page, had need to have been a good man indeed, if he would
be spared the sharp consciousness of many talents neglected, many opportunities
wasted, many erratic and perverted feelings constantly at war within his
breast, and defeating him. I do not hold one natural gift, I dare say, that I
have not abused. My meaning simply is, that whatever I have tried to do in
life, I have tried with all my heart to do well; that whatever I have devoted
myself to, I have devoted myself to completely; that in great aims and in
small, I have always been thoroughly in earnest. I have never believed it
possible that any natural or improved ability can claim immunity from the
companionship of the steady, plain, hard-working qualities, and hope to gain
its end. There is no such thing as such fulfilment on this earth. Some happy
talent, and some fortunate opportunity, may form the two sides of the ladder on
which some men mount, but the rounds of that ladder must be made of stuff to
stand wear and tear; and there is no substitute for thorough-going, ardent, and
sincere earnestness. Never to put one hand to anything, on which I could throw
my whole self; and never to affect depreciation of my work, whatever it was; I
find, now, to have been my golden rules.

retorted or openly exasperated me, it would have been a relief and a
justification; but he had put me on a slow fire, on which I lay tormented half

In the morning, when I came out, the early church-bell was ringing, and he was
walking up and down with his mother. He addressed me as if nothing had
happened, and I could do no less than reply. I had struck him hard enough to
give him the toothache, I suppose. At all events his face was tied up in a

The Doctor gave out that he was not quite well; and remained alone, for a
considerable part of every day, during the remainder of the visit. Agnes and
her father had been gone a week, before we resumed our usual work. On the day
preceding its resumption, the Doctor gave me with his own hands a folded note
not sealed. It was addressed to myself; and laid an injunction on me, in a few
affectionate words, never to refer to the subject of that evening. I had
confided it to my aunt, but to no one else. It was not a subject I could
discuss with Agnes, and Agnes certainly had not the least suspicion of what had
passed.

Neither, I felt convinced, had Mrs. Strong then. Several weeks elapsed before I
saw the least change in her. It came on slowly, like a cloud when there is no
wind. At first, she seemed to wonder at the gentle compassion with which the
Doctor spoke to her, and at his wish that she should have her mother with her,
to relieve the dull monotony of her life. Often, when we were at work, and she
was sitting by, I would see her pausing and looking at him with that memorable
face. Afterwards, I sometimes observed her rise, with her eyes full of tears,
and go out of the room. Gradually, an unhappy shadow fell upon her beauty, and
deepened every day. Mrs. Markleham was a regular inmate of the cottage then;
but she talked and talked, and saw nothing.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The slow change in Mrs. Strong—from wonder at the Doctor's compassion to tears and shadow—shows the gradual realization of her situation and the burden of knowledge she must bear.
enrichment.best_quote: Gradually, an unhappy shadow fell upon her beauty, and deepened every day.
enrichment.summary: Over weeks, Mrs. Strong shows increasing signs of sorrow and awareness, her beauty shadowed by unhappiness.

text:
As this change stole on Annie, once like sunshine in the Doctor’s house,
the Doctor became older in appearance, and more grave; but the sweetness of his
temper, the placid kindness of his manner, and his benevolent solicitude for
her, if they were capable of any increase, were increased. I saw him once,
early on the morning of her birthday, when she came to sit in the window while
we were at work (which she had always done, but now began to do with a timid
and uncertain air that I thought very touching), take her forehead between his
hands, kiss it, and go hurriedly away, too much moved to remain. I saw her
stand where he had left her, like a statue; and then bend down her head, and
clasp her hands, and weep, I cannot say how sorrowfully.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The Doctor's tender gesture on Annie's birthday—kissing her forehead and leaving moved—is the emotional and physical expression of his love despite the sorrow, and Annie's response shows her recognition of his devotion.
enrichment.best_quote: I saw him once, early on the morning of her birthday, when she came to sit in the window while we were at work (which she had always done, but now began to do with a timid and uncertain air that I thought very touching), take her forehead between his hands, kiss it, and go hurriedly away, too much moved to remain.
enrichment.summary: David witnesses the Doctor kissing Annie's forehead on her birthday with deep emotion, showing his unchanging devotion despite the sorrow.

text:
Sometimes, after that, I fancied that she tried to speak even to me, in
intervals when we were left alone. But she never uttered a word. The Doctor
always had some new project for her participating in amusements away from home,
with her mother; and Mrs. Markleham, who was very fond of amusements, and very
easily dissatisfied with anything else, entered into them with great good-will,
and was loud in her commendations. But Annie, in a spiritless unhappy way, only
went whither she was led, and seemed to have no care for anything.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Annie's lack of engagement with life and her passive participation in amusements show her withdrawal and despair.
enrichment.summary: Annie shows no interest in amusements and seems uncareful about anything, going wherever she is led.

text:
I did not know what to think. Neither did my aunt; who must have walked, at
various times, a hundred miles in her uncertainty. What was strangest of all
was, that the only real relief which seemed to make its way into the secret
region of this domestic unhappiness, made its way there in the person of Mr.
Dick.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The introduction of Mr. Dick as the sole source of relief suggests that innocence and love can penetrate where judgment and suspicion have poisoned.
enrichment.best_quote: the only real relief which seemed to make its way into the secret region of this domestic unhappiness, made its way there in the person of Mr. Dick.
enrichment.summary: David notes that Mr. Dick's presence is the only source of relief from the household's unhappiness.

text:
What his thoughts were on the subject, or what his observation was, I am as
unable to explain, as I dare say he would have been to assist me in the task.
But, as I have recorded in the narrative of my school days, his veneration for
the Doctor was unbounded; and there is a subtlety of perception in real
attachment, even when it is borne towards man by one of the lower animals,
which leaves the highest intellect behind. To this mind of the heart, if I may
call it so, in Mr. Dick, some bright ray of the truth shot straight.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's tribute to Mr. Dick's 'mind of the heart' and his natural attachment shows profound respect for emotional and intuitive wisdom over intellectual capacity.
enrichment.best_quote: there is a subtlety of perception in real attachment, even when it is borne towards man by one of the lower animals, which leaves the highest intellect behind.
enrichment.summary: David reflects on Mr. Dick's intuitive perception and wisdom that comes from love rather than intellect.

text:
He had proudly resumed his privilege, in many of his spare hours, of walking up
and down the garden with the Doctor; as he had been accustomed to pace up and
down The Doctor’s Walk at Canterbury. But matters were no sooner in this
state, than he devoted all his spare time (and got up earlier to make it more)
to these perambulations. If he had never been so happy as when the Doctor read
that marvellous performance, the Dictionary, to him; he was now quite miserable
unless the Doctor pulled it out of his pocket, and began. When the Doctor and I
were engaged, he now fell into the custom of walking up and down with Mrs.
Strong, and helping her to trim her favourite flowers, or weed the beds. I dare
say he rarely spoke a dozen words in an hour: but his quiet interest, and his
wistful face, found immediate response in both their breasts; each knew that
the other liked him, and that he loved both; and he became what no one else
could be—a link between them.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Dick's role as a 'link' between the Doctor and Annie, his quiet companionship, and his natural goodness create a healing presence that no one else can provide.
enrichment.best_quote: he became what no one else could be—a link between them.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Dick spends time with both the Doctor and Annie, helping Annie with her flowers and becoming a healing presence and link between them.

text:
When I think of him, with his impenetrably wise face, walking up and down with
the Doctor, delighted to be battered by the hard words in the Dictionary; when
I think of him carrying huge watering-pots after Annie; kneeling down, in very
paws of gloves, at patient microscopic work among the little leaves; expressing
as no philosopher could have expressed, in everything he did, a delicate desire
to be her friend; showering sympathy, trustfulness, and affection, out of every
hole in the watering-pot; when I think of him never wandering in that better
mind of his to which unhappiness addressed itself, never bringing the
unfortunate King Charles into the garden, never wavering in his grateful
service, never diverted from his knowledge that there was something wrong, or
from his wish to set it right—I really feel almost ashamed of having
known that he was not quite in his wits, taking account of the utmost I have
done with mine.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's extended tribute to Mr. Dick is one of the most moving passages in the novel, celebrating his steadfast love, his refusal to be diverted by unhappiness, and his intuitive understanding of what is needed.
enrichment.best_quote: when I think of him never wandering in that better mind of his to which unhappiness addressed itself, never bringing the unfortunate King Charles into the garden, never wavering in his grateful service, never diverted from his knowledge that there was something wrong, or from his wish to set it right—I really feel almost ashamed of having known that he was not quite in his wits, taking account of the utmost I have done with mine.
enrichment.summary: David expresses profound admiration for Mr. Dick's steadfast devotion, his clarity of mind in what matters, and his natural goodness.

text:
‘Nobody but myself, Trot, knows what that man is!’ my aunt would
proudly remark, when we conversed about it. ‘Dick will distinguish
himself yet!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's proud remark about Mr. Dick affirms David's judgment and shows her recognition of Dick's true worth.
enrichment.summary: Betsey remarks proudly that no one but herself knows what Mr. Dick truly is, and that he will distinguish himself.

I must refer to one other topic before I close this chapter. While the visit at
the Doctor’s was still in progress, I observed that the postman brought
two or three letters every morning for Uriah Heep, who remained at Highgate
until the rest went back, it being a leisure time; and that these were always
directed in a business-like manner by Mr. Micawber, who now assumed a round
legal hand. I was glad to infer, from these slight premises, that Mr. Micawber
was doing well; and consequently was much surprised to receive, about this
time, the following letter from his amiable wife.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The observation of Uriah receiving letters from Mr. Micawber and the inference that Micawber is doing well sets up the next major plot development.
enrichment.summary: David notices that Uriah receives regular letters from Mr. Micawber and infers from this that Micawber is doing well.

text: ‘CANTERBURY, Monday Evening.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The salutation begins a letter, with minimal content.
enrichment.summary: The letter begins with a formal salutation from Mrs. Micawber to David.

text:
‘You will doubtless be surprised, my dear Mr. Copperfield, to receive
this communication. Still more so, by its contents. Still more so, by the
stipulation of implicit confidence which I beg to impose. But my feelings as a
wife and mother require relief; and as I do not wish to consult my family
(already obnoxious to the feelings of Mr. Micawber), I know no one of whom I
can better ask advice than my friend and former lodger.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Micawber's opening establishes her need for confidential advice and her reliance on David, showing her distress about her situation.
enrichment.best_quote: Still more so, by its contents. Still more so, by the stipulation of implicit confidence which I beg to impose.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Micawber expresses her surprise and asks for David's confidence and advice about a pressing matter.

text:
‘You may be aware, my dear Mr. Copperfield, that between myself and Mr.
Micawber (whom I will never desert), there has always been preserved a spirit
of mutual confidence. Mr. Micawber may have occasionally given a bill without
consulting me, or he may have misled me as to the period when that obligation
would become due. This has actually happened. But, in general, Mr. Micawber has
had no secrets from the bosom of affection—I allude to his wife—and
has invariably, on our retirement to rest, recalled the events of the day.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Micawber's account of her usual relationship with her husband and her acceptance of his occasional deceptions establishes the baseline of their marriage.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Micawber describes how she and her husband have maintained mutual confidence, though he has occasionally mislead her about financial matters.

text:
‘You will picture to yourself, my dear Mr. Copperfield, what the
poignancy of my feelings must be, when I inform you that Mr. Micawber is
entirely changed. He is reserved. He is secret. His life is a mystery to the
partner of his joys and sorrows—I again allude to his wife—and if I
should assure you that beyond knowing that it is passed from morning to night
at the office, I now know less of it than I do of the man in the south,
connected with whose mouth the thoughtless children repeat an idle tale
respecting cold plum porridge, I should adopt a popular fallacy to express an
actual fact.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mrs. Micawber's revelation that her husband is now secretive and reserved marks a dramatic change and suggests he may be involved in something serious.
enrichment.best_quote: Mr. Micawber is entirely changed. He is reserved. He is secret. His life is a mystery to the partner of his joys and sorrows.
enrichment.summary: Mrs. Micawber expresses alarm that her husband has become secretive and mysterious, no longer sharing his daily activities with her.

text:
‘But this is not all. Mr. Micawber is morose. He is severe. He is
estranged from our eldest son and daughter, he has no pride in his twins, he
looks with an eye of coldness even on the unoffending stranger who last became
a member of our circle. The pecuniary means of meeting our expenses, kept down

under fearful threats that he will Settle himself (the exact expression); and

enrichment.summary: Mrs. Micawber describes her husband's coldness to his children and his refusal to explain his behavior or provide adequate funds.

text:
‘This is hard to bear. This is heart-breaking. If you will advise me,
knowing my feeble powers such as they are, how you think it will be best to

smile from the happily-unconscious stranger, I remain, dear Mr. Copperfield,

‘Your afflicted,         
‘EMMA MICAWBER.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: The signature of the letter is minimal content.
enrichment.summary: The letter is signed by Mrs. Micawber as 'Your afflicted'.

text:
I did not feel justified in giving a wife of Mrs. Micawber’s experience
any other recommendation, than that she should try to reclaim Mr. Micawber by
patience and kindness (as I knew she would in any case); but the letter set me
thinking about him very much.

enrichment.summary: David advises Mrs. Micawber to be patient and kind, though he is uncertain what else to recommend and finds himself thinking about Micawber.

Once again, let me pause upon a memorable period of my life. Let me stand
aside, to see the phantoms of those days go by me, accompanying the shadow of
myself, in dim procession.

enrichment.summary: David pauses to reflect on a memorable period of his life, invoking the passage of time as a procession of shadows and phantoms.

text:
Weeks, months, seasons, pass along. They seem little more than a summer day and
a winter evening. Now, the Common where I walk with Dora is all in bloom, a
field of bright gold; and now the unseen heather lies in mounds and bunches
underneath a covering of snow. In a breath, the river that flows through our
Sunday walks is sparkling in the summer sun, is ruffled by the winter wind, or
thickened with drifting heaps of ice. Faster than ever river ran towards the
sea, it flashes, darkens, and rolls away.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Lyrical description of time's passage through the seasons, using natural imagery to convey the swift blur of courtship and the cycle of David's walks with Dora.
enrichment.best_quote: Faster than ever river ran towards the sea, it flashes, darkens, and rolls away.
enrichment.summary: Seasons and months blur together as David recalls his Sunday walks with Dora, where nature cycles rapidly from bloom to snow and back again.

text:
Not a thread changes, in the house of the two little bird-like ladies. The
clock ticks over the fireplace, the weather-glass hangs in the hall. Neither
clock nor weather-glass is ever right; but we believe in both, devoutly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine domestic detail establishing the unchanging nature of the boarding house where Dora's aunts live.
enrichment.summary: The house of Dora's aunts remains perpetually unchanged, with clock and weather-glass defying correction yet receiving devout faith.

text:
I have come legally to man’s estate. I have attained the dignity of
twenty-one. But this is a sort of dignity that may be thrust upon one. Let me
think what I have achieved.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David reflects on achieving legal manhood at twenty-one, a marker of adulthood that prompts self-assessment.
enrichment.summary: David notes he has come of age legally, though he questions what real achievement this honour represents.

text:
I have tamed that savage stenographic mystery. I make a respectable income by
it. I am in high repute for my accomplishment in all pertaining to the art, and
am joined with eleven others in reporting the debates in Parliament for a
Morning Newspaper. Night after night, I record predictions that never come to
pass, professions that are never fulfilled, explanations that are only meant to
mystify. I wallow in words. Britannia, that unfortunate female, is always
before me, like a trussed fowl: skewered through and through with office-pens,
and bound hand and foot with red tape. I am sufficiently behind the scenes to
know the worth of political life. I am quite an Infidel about it, and shall
never be converted.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's satirical account of his Parliamentary reporting career reveals both personal success and Dickens's sharp critique of political theatre and institutional corruption.
enrichment.best_quote: I wallow in words. Britannia, that unfortunate female, is always before me, like a trussed fowl: skewered through and through with office-pens, and bound hand and foot with red tape.
enrichment.summary: David has mastered stenography and earns respectably reporting parliamentary debates, but he expresses cynical disdain for the false promises and obfuscation of political life.

text:
My dear old Traddles has tried his hand at the same pursuit, but it is not in
Traddles’s way. He is perfectly good-humoured respecting his failure, and
reminds me that he always did consider himself slow. He has occasional
employment on the same newspaper, in getting up the facts of dry subjects, to
be written about and embellished by more fertile minds. He is called to the
bar; and with admirable industry and self-denial has scraped another hundred
pounds together, to fee a Conveyancer whose chambers he attends. A great deal
of very hot port wine was consumed at his call; and, considering the figure, I
should think the Inner Temple must have made a profit by it.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Character update on Traddles's career progress and romantic prospects, establishing his perseverance and good humour, with light comic detail about his call to the bar.
enrichment.summary: Traddles has pursued the same reporting work without success but has been called to the bar and is slowly saving money for his legal education.

text:
I have come out in another way. I have taken with fear and trembling to
authorship. I wrote a little something, in secret, and sent it to a magazine,
and it was published in the magazine. Since then, I have taken heart to write a
good many trifling pieces. Now, I am regularly paid for them. Altogether, I am
well off, when I tell my income on the fingers of my left hand, I pass the
third finger and take in the fourth to the middle joint.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David reveals his emergence as a writer, marking a significant achievement in his ambition for literary success and financial stability.
enrichment.summary: David has secretly taken up authorship, published pieces in magazines, and now earns a respectable regular income from his writing.

text:
We have removed, from Buckingham Street, to a pleasant little cottage very near
the one I looked at, when my enthusiasm first came on. My aunt, however (who
has sold the house at Dover, to good advantage), is not going to remain here,
but intends removing herself to a still more tiny cottage close at hand. What
does this portend? My marriage? Yes!

enrichment.best_quote: What does this portend? My marriage? Yes!

text:
Yes! I am going to be married to Dora! Miss Lavinia and Miss Clarissa have
given their consent; and if ever canary birds were in a flutter, they are. Miss
Lavinia, self-charged with the superintendence of my darling’s wardrobe,

a highly respectable young man, with a long bundle, and a yard measure under
his arm. A dressmaker, always stabbed in the breast with a needle and thread,
boards and lodges in the house; and seems to me, eating, drinking, or sleeping,
never to take her thimble off. They make a lay-figure of my dear. They are
always sending for her to come and try something on. We can’t be happy
together for five minutes in the evening, but some intrusive female knocks at
the door, and says, ‘Oh, if you please, Miss Dora, would you step
upstairs!’

Miss Clarissa and my aunt roam all over London, to find out articles of
furniture for Dora and me to look at. It would be better for them to buy the
goods at once, without this ceremony of inspection; for, when we go to see a
kitchen fender and meat-screen, Dora sees a Chinese house for Jip, with little
bells on the top, and prefers that. And it takes a long time to accustom Jip to
his new residence, after we have bought it; whenever he goes in or out, he
makes all the little bells ring, and is horribly frightened.

Peggotty comes up to make herself useful, and falls to work immediately. Her

with perpetual friction. And now it is, that I begin to see her solitary
brother passing through the dark streets at night, and looking, as he goes,
among the wandering faces. I never speak to him at such an hour. I know too
well, as his grave figure passes onward, what he seeks, and what he dreads.

text:

have time? The realization of my boyish day-dreams is at hand. I am going to
take out the licence.

upon my desk, half in admiration, half in awe. There are the names, in the
sweet old visionary connexion, David Copperfield and Dora Spenlow; and there,
in the corner, is that Parental Institution, the Stamp Office, which is so
benignantly interested in the various transactions of human life, looking down

on us in print, and doing it as cheap as could possibly be expected.

text:
Nevertheless, I am in a dream, a flustered, happy, hurried dream. I can’t
believe that it is going to be; and yet I can’t believe but that everyone
I pass in the street, must have some kind of perception, that I am to be
married the day after tomorrow. The Surrogate knows me, when I go down to be

between us. Traddles is not at all wanted, but is in attendance as my general
backer.

text:
‘I hope the next time you come here, my dear fellow,’ I say to
Traddles, ‘it will be on the same errand for yourself. And I hope it will
be soon.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Simple dialogue expressing David's hope that Traddles will soon marry, a routine conversational beat with little dramatic weight.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Reconciliation scene; David and Dora make up after their quarrel, both claiming fault and vowing no future differences; shows the cyclical nature of their marital dynamic—conflict, tears, reconciliation, renewal.
enrichment.best_quote: our first little difference was to be our last, and that we were never to have another if we lived a hundred years
enrichment.summary: Dora comes down in her slippers to meet David alone; they confess to being naughty and hard-hearted, and vow their first difference will be their last.

text:
The next domestic trial we went through, was the Ordeal of Servants. Mary
Anne’s cousin deserted into our coal-hole, and was brought out, to our
great amazement, by a piquet of his companions in arms, who took him away
handcuffed in a procession that covered our front-garden with ignominy. This
nerved me to get rid of Mary Anne, who went so mildly, on receipt of wages,
that I was surprised, until I found out about the tea-spoons, and also about
the little sums she had borrowed in my name of the tradespeople without
authority. After an interval of Mrs. Kidgerbury—the oldest inhabitant of
Kentish Town, I believe, who went out charing, but was too feeble to execute
her conceptions of that art—we found another treasure, who was one of the
most amiable of women, but who generally made a point of falling either up or
down the kitchen stairs with the tray, and almost plunged into the parlour, as
into a bath, with the tea-things. The ravages committed by this unfortunate,
rendering her dismissal necessary, she was succeeded (with intervals of Mrs.
Kidgerbury) by a long line of Incapables; terminating in a young person of
genteel appearance, who went to Greenwich Fair in Dora’s bonnet. After
whom I remember nothing but an average equality of failure.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Extended comic catalogue of domestic trials: Mary Anne's cousin deserts, servants are incompetent and dishonest (stealing tea-spoons), the parade of failed housekeepers is absurdist and satirical; Dickens mercilessly mocks David and Dora's hopelessness.
enrichment.best_quote: Mary Anne, who went so mildly, on receipt of wages, that I was surprised, until I found out about the tea-spoons, and also about the little sums she had borrowed in my name of the tradespeople without authority
enrichment.summary: David catalogs the succession of domestic disasters: Mary Anne's cousin deserts and is arrested, servants steal and disappear, and they go through a long line of incompetent help.

text:
Everybody we had anything to do with seemed to cheat us. Our appearance in a
shop was a signal for the damaged goods to be brought out immediately. If we
bought a lobster, it was full of water. All our meat turned out to be tough,
and there was hardly any crust to our loaves. In search of the principle on
which joints ought to be roasted, to be roasted enough, and not too much, I
myself referred to the Cookery Book, and found it there established as the
allowance of a quarter of an hour to every pound, and say a quarter over. But
the principle always failed us by some curious fatality, and we never could hit
any medium between redness and cinders.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Sardonic description of consumer failures: their inexperience makes them targets for fraud; every purchase is defective or unsuitable; the comic despair about meat roasting temperatures reflects their fundamental incapacity.
enrichment.best_quote: Our appearance in a shop was a signal for the damaged goods to be brought out immediately
enrichment.summary: David describes how merchants cheat them: lobsters full of water, tough meat, no crust on bread; they cannot master the principle of roasting meat.

text:
I had reason to believe that in accomplishing these failures we incurred a far
greater expense than if we had achieved a series of triumphs. It appeared to
me, on looking over the tradesmen’s books, as if we might have kept the
basement storey paved with butter, such was the extensive scale of our
consumption of that article. I don’t know whether the Excise returns of
the period may have exhibited any increase in the demand for pepper; but if our
performances did not affect the market, I should say several families must have
left off using it. And the most wonderful fact of all was, that we never had
anything in the house.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Darkly comic observation that their failures are financially ruinous; the accumulation of butter consumption, pepper, and general waste suggests they are spending far more for worse results.
enrichment.best_quote: we might have kept the basement storey paved with butter, such was the extensive scale of our consumption of that article
enrichment.summary: David observes that their household expenses are enormous despite their failures; they consume excessive amounts of butter and other provisions.

text:
As to the washerwoman pawning the clothes, and coming in a state of penitent
intoxication to apologize, I suppose that might have happened several times to
anybody. Also the chimney on fire, the parish engine, and perjury on the part
of the Beadle. But I apprehend that we were personally fortunate in engaging a
servant with a taste for cordials, who swelled our running account for porter
at the public-house by such inexplicable items as ‘quartern rum shrub
(Mrs. C.)’; ‘Half-quartern gin and cloves (Mrs. C.)’;
‘Glass rum and peppermint (Mrs. C.)’—the parentheses always
referring to Dora, who was supposed, it appeared on explanation, to have
imbibed the whole of these refreshments.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dark comic escalation: a servant pawns the clothes, there are chimney fires and parish engines, but the crowning absurdity is a servant's drinking bills charged to Dora's account, suggesting institutional corruption and the vulnerability of the household.
enrichment.best_quote: 'quartern rum shrub (Mrs. C.)'; 'Half-quartern gin and cloves (Mrs. C.)'; 'Glass rum and peppermint (Mrs. C.)'—the parentheses always referring to Dora, who was supposed, it appeared on explanation, to have imbibed the whole of these refreshments
enrichment.summary: David describes more household disasters: laundry stolen, chimney fires, and a servant with a taste for cordials whose drinking bill is falsely attributed to Dora.

text:
One of our first feats in the housekeeping way was a little dinner to Traddles.
I met him in town, and asked him to walk out with me that afternoon. He readily
consenting, I wrote to Dora, saying I would bring him home. It was pleasant
weather, and on the road we made my domestic happiness the theme of
conversation. Traddles was very full of it; and said, that, picturing himself
with such a home, and Sophy waiting and preparing for him, he could think of
nothing wanting to complete his bliss.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Introduction of Traddles dinner; David is proud of his domestic happiness and invites an old friend; this sets up a humorous test of his household's organization.
enrichment.summary: David invites Traddles to dinner; on the way they discuss David's happiness, and Traddles expresses his own longing for such domestic bliss with Sophy.

text:
I could not have wished for a prettier little wife at the opposite end of the
table, but I certainly could have wished, when we sat down, for a little more
room. I did not know how it was, but though there were only two of us, we were
at once always cramped for room, and yet had always room enough to lose
everything in. I suspect it may have been because nothing had a place of its
own, except Jip’s pagoda, which invariably blocked up the main
thoroughfare. On the present occasion, Traddles was so hemmed in by the pagoda
and the guitar-case, and Dora’s flower-painting, and my writing-table,
that I had serious doubts of the possibility of his using his knife and fork;
but he protested, with his own good-humour, ‘Oceans of room, Copperfield!
I assure you, Oceans!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brilliant satirical description of dining chaos: though only two guests, the room is cramped and cluttered; Jip's pagoda blocks the thoroughfare; guitar, flower-paintings, writing-table all prevent proper seating; Traddles gamely insists 'Oceans of room!' masking the absurdity.
enrichment.best_quote: Oceans of room, Copperfield! I assure you, Oceans!
enrichment.summary: Despite only having two guests, David and Dora's parlor is so cramped with furniture, Jip's pagoda, and various objects that Traddles can barely sit; he politely claims there is plenty of room.

text:
There was another thing I could have wished, namely, that Jip had never been
encouraged to walk about the tablecloth during dinner. I began to think there
was something disorderly in his being there at all, even if he had not been in
the habit of putting his foot in the salt or the melted butter. On this
occasion he seemed to think he was introduced expressly to keep Traddles at
bay; and he barked at my old friend, and made short runs at his plate, with
such undaunted pertinacity, that he may be said to have engrossed the
conversation.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Jip's misbehavior at dinner; he walks on the tablecloth, puts his feet in salt and butter, and barks at Traddles; his chaos is emblematic of the household's disorder and David's inability to impose discipline.
enrichment.best_quote: he seemed to think he was introduced expressly to keep Traddles at bay
enrichment.summary: Jip walks on the tablecloth during dinner, puts his feet in salt and butter, and barks at Traddles with such persistence that he dominates the conversation.

text:
However, as I knew how tender-hearted my dear Dora was, and how sensitive she
would be to any slight upon her favourite, I hinted no objection. For similar
reasons I made no allusion to the skirmishing plates upon the floor; or to the
disreputable appearance of the castors, which were all at sixes and sevens, and
looked drunk; or to the further blockade of Traddles by wandering vegetable
dishes and jugs. I could not help wondering in my own mind, as I contemplated
the boiled leg of mutton before me, previous to carving it, how it came to pass
that our joints of meat were of such extraordinary shapes—and whether our
butcher contracted for all the deformed sheep that came into the world; but I
kept my reflections to myself.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's reluctant acceptance of chaos; rather than object to Jip, the messy castors, or the disreputable appearance, he stays silent to avoid hurting Dora; he silently observes the misshapen mutton, knowing their butcher is defective.
enrichment.summary: David refrains from commenting on any of the household's disarray, knowing Dora would be upset; he silently puzzles over the odd shape of the mutton.

text:
‘My love,’ said I to Dora, ‘what have you got in that
dish?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's inquiry about the dish; marks the beginning of the oyster sequence where Dora's good intentions will be revealed as misguided.
enrichment.summary: David asks Dora what is in a particular dish.

text:
I could not imagine why Dora had been making tempting little faces at me, as if
she wanted to kiss me.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's observation of Dora's anticipation; she had been making enticing faces at him, suggesting she was pleased with her choice.
enrichment.summary: David notices Dora has been making tempting faces at him, as if hoping for a kiss.

text: ‘Oysters, dear,’ said Dora, timidly.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora timidly reveals oysters; her hesitation suggests she knows something might be wrong.
enrichment.summary: Dora timidly says the dish contains oysters.

text: ‘Was that YOUR thought?’ said I, delighted.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's delighted response; he learns these are oysters she chose herself, which pleases him.
enrichment.summary: David asks if the oysters were Dora's own thought and is delighted.

text: ‘Ye-yes, Doady,’ said Dora.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's hesitant confirmation; brief dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Dora hesitantly confirms the oysters were her idea.

text:
‘There never was a happier one!’ I exclaimed, laying down the
carving-knife and fork. ‘There is nothing Traddles likes so much!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's exclamation of joy; oysters are Traddles' favorite, making Dora's choice particularly well-intentioned.
enrichment.summary: David exclaims that there is nothing Traddles likes so much as oysters.

text:
‘Ye-yes, Doady,’ said Dora, ‘and so I bought a beautiful
little barrel of them, and the man said they were very good. But I—I am
afraid there’s something the matter with them. They don’t seem
right.’ Here Dora shook her head, and diamonds twinkled in her eyes.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The revelation: Dora bought a beautiful barrel of oysters, but they were never opened; her good intention and effort are undermined by her ignorance and carelessness; diamonds twinkle in her eyes showing her shame.
enrichment.best_quote: diamonds twinkled in her eyes
enrichment.summary: Dora confesses she bought a beautiful barrel of oysters, but fears something is wrong with them because they don't seem right.

text:
‘They are only opened in both shells,’ said I. ‘Take the top
one off, my love.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's gentle instruction; routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David gently instructs Dora to take the top shell off an oyster.

text:
‘But it won’t come off!’ said Dora, trying very hard, and
looking very much distressed.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's distress; the oyster won't open, symbolizing the barrier between her intentions and successful execution.
enrichment.summary: Dora tries to open the oyster but cannot; she looks very distressed.

text:
‘Do you know, Copperfield,’ said Traddles, cheerfully examining the
dish, ‘I think it is in consequence—they are capital oysters, but I
think it is in consequence—of their never having been opened.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Traddles' cheerful diagnosis: the oysters were never opened because they have no oyster-knives and wouldn't know how to use them anyway; his kindness in gently explaining masks the fundamental incompetence.
enrichment.best_quote: they are capital oysters, but I think it is in consequence—of their never having been opened
enrichment.summary: Traddles cheerfully observes that the oysters are fine but have never been opened, and they have no oyster-knives.

text:
They never had been opened; and we had no oyster-knives—and
couldn’t have used them if we had; so we looked at the oysters and ate
the mutton. At least we ate as much of it as was done, and made up with capers.
If I had permitted him, I am satisfied that Traddles would have made a perfect
savage of himself, and eaten a plateful of raw meat, to express enjoyment of
the repast; but I would hear of no such immolation on the altar of friendship,
and we had a course of bacon instead; there happening, by good fortune, to be
cold bacon in the larder.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The resolution: they cannot open the oysters so they eat mutton instead; Traddles would have eaten raw meat to be polite, but David prevents this; they make do with cold bacon, showing David's attempt at salvage and the basic inadequacy of the meal.
enrichment.best_quote: we looked at the oysters and ate the mutton
enrichment.summary: They cannot open the oysters and no oyster-knives are available; they eat the mutton instead, though it is tough, and are saved by cold bacon from the larder.

text:
My poor little wife was in such affliction when she thought I should be
annoyed, and in such a state of joy when she found I was not, that the
discomfiture I had subdued, very soon vanished, and we passed a happy evening;
Dora sitting with her arm on my chair while Traddles and I discussed a glass of
wine, and taking every opportunity of whispering in my ear that it was so good
of me not to be a cruel, cross old boy. By and by she made tea for us; which it
was so pretty to see her do, as if she was busying herself with a set of
doll’s tea-things, that I was not particular about the quality of the
beverage. Then Traddles and I played a game or two at cribbage; and Dora
singing to the guitar the while, it seemed to me as if our courtship and
marriage were a tender dream of mine, and the night when I first listened to
her voice were not yet over.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Touching denouement: despite the dinner's disasters, the evening becomes happy because David doesn't show annoyance; Dora is joyful, sits on his chair with her arm, and the memory of his courtship returns as dream-like; Dora singing to the guitar transforms failure into nostalgia.
enrichment.best_quote: it seemed to me as if our courtship and marriage were a tender dream of mine, and the night when I first listened to her voice were not yet over
enrichment.summary: Despite the dinner's failures, David's forbearance makes Dora happy; they pass a pleasant evening with her arm on his chair, playing cards, and Dora singing to the guitar.

text:
When Traddles went away, and I came back into the parlour from seeing him out,
my wife planted her chair close to mine, and sat down by my side. ‘I am
very sorry,’ she said. ‘Will you try to teach me, Doady?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's plea for David to teach her, following the failed dinner; she wants to improve but is apologetic and dependent; David must decide whether to invest in instruction or accept her as is.
enrichment.best_quote: Will you try to teach me, Doady?
enrichment.summary: After Traddles leaves, Dora sits close to David and asks if he will try to teach her to be better.

text:
‘I must teach myself first, Dora,’ said I. ‘I am as bad as
you, love.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's disclaimer: he too needs to learn; he defers to himself as a learner, tempering his ambitions for Dora's improvement.
enrichment.summary: David says he must teach himself first, admitting he is as bad as Dora.

text:
‘Ah! But you can learn,’ she returned; ‘and you are a clever,
clever man!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's flattery and confidence in David; she asserts he can learn and is clever, appealing to his ego rather than engaging with the deeper point about mutual improvement.
enrichment.summary: Dora insists David is clever and able to learn, unlike herself.

text: ‘Nonsense, mouse!’ said I.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's dismissive affection; he calls her 'mouse,' avoiding deeper discussion.
enrichment.summary: David calls Dora 'mouse,' dismissing the discussion affectionately.

text:
‘I wish,’ resumed my wife, after a long silence, ‘that I
could have gone down into the country for a whole year, and lived with
Agnes!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's significant wish: she wants to have spent a year in the country with Agnes, learning from her; this is the only time in the chapter she expresses a genuine desire for self-improvement and reveals her own insecurity about her inadequacy.
enrichment.best_quote: I wish that I could have gone down into the country for a whole year, and lived with Agnes
enrichment.summary: Dora expresses a wish that she could have lived with Agnes for a year and learned from her.

text:
Her hands were clasped upon my shoulder, and her chin rested on them, and her
blue eyes looked quietly into mine.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Physical intimacy; Dora's hands are on his shoulder, her chin rests on them, her blue eyes look quietly into his; this tender physical description echoes their emotional intimacy.
enrichment.summary: Dora rests her hands on David's shoulder with her chin on them, looking at him with her blue eyes.

text: ‘Why so?’ I asked.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's question; routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David asks why Dora wishes she had lived with Agnes.

text:
‘I think she might have improved me, and I think I might have learned
from her,’ said Dora.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's explanation: Agnes might have improved her and she might have learned from her; acknowledges Agnes' superior character and her own deficiency.
enrichment.summary: Dora says Agnes might have improved her and she might have learned from her.

text:
‘All in good time, my love. Agnes has had her father to take care of for
these many years, you should remember. Even when she was quite a child, she was
the Agnes whom we know,’ said I.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's deflection: he says Agnes has been occupied with her father, and even as a child she was as mature as now; this avoids engagement with Dora's genuine admission of deficiency.
enrichment.summary: David suggests Agnes has always been occupied with her father and has always been mature.

text:
‘Will you call me a name I want you to call me?’ inquired Dora,
without moving.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's request to be called 'child-wife' is the chapter's most significant revelation: she wants David to think of her as a child, not a woman; this codifies her identity and suggests acceptance of permanent dependence.
enrichment.best_quote: Will you call me a name I want you to call me?
enrichment.summary: Dora asks David to call her by a special name she wants him to use.

text: ‘What is it?’ I asked with a smile.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's inquiry; routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David asks what name Dora wants.

text:
‘It’s a stupid name,’ she said, shaking her curls for a
moment. ‘Child-wife.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora hesitantly reveals the name 'child-wife,' suggesting it is both ridiculous and serious for her.
enrichment.best_quote: It's a stupid name...Child-wife
enrichment.summary: Dora shyly says the name is 'child-wife.'

text:
I laughingly asked my child-wife what her fancy was in desiring to be so
called. She answered without moving, otherwise than as the arm I twined about
her may have brought her blue eyes nearer to me:

enrichment.interest_rationale: David laughs at first, not understanding the seriousness; Dora explains her meaning without moving, an intimate moment.
enrichment.summary: David laughs but then realizes Dora is serious; she begins to explain what she means.

text:
‘I don’t mean, you silly fellow, that you should use the name
instead of Dora. I only mean that you should think of me that way. When you are
going to be angry with me, say to yourself, “it’s only my
child-wife!” When I am very disappointing, say, “I knew, a long
time ago, that she would make but a child-wife!” When you miss what I
should like to be, and I think can never be, say, “still my foolish
child-wife loves me!” For indeed I do.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's definition of 'child-wife' is extraordinary: she doesn't want David to call her by the name instead of Dora, but to think of her as permanently childlike; when he is angry, weary, or disappointed, he should remember she is just a foolish child-wife who loves him. This is both touching and tragic—her self-aware acceptance of her permanent inadequacy and her claim on his eternal patience.
enrichment.best_quote: 'still my foolish child-wife loves me!'
enrichment.summary: Dora explains she wants David to think of her as a child-wife when he is angry, disappointed, or weary; she wants him to remember she is foolish but loving.

text:
I had not been serious with her; having no idea until now, that she was serious
herself. But her affectionate nature was so happy in what I now said to her
with my whole heart, that her face became a laughing one before her glittering
eyes were dry. She was soon my child-wife indeed; sitting down on the floor
outside the Chinese House, ringing all the little bells one after another, to
punish Jip for his recent bad behaviour; while Jip lay blinking in the doorway
with his head out, even too lazy to be teased.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's realization and emotional response: he had not been serious with Dora before this; her affectionate nature is so happy with his wholehearted commitment that she becomes literally the child-wife, ringing bells and punishing Jip. A moment of mutual understanding and love despite the tragedy of her permanent childishness.
enrichment.best_quote: She was soon my child-wife indeed; sitting down on the floor outside the Chinese House, ringing all the little bells one after another, to punish Jip for his recent bad behaviour
enrichment.summary: David suddenly realizes Dora is being serious; he commits fully to the idea; Dora's joy becomes childlike as she sits punishing Jip for his misbehavior.

text:
This appeal of Dora’s made a strong impression on me. I look back on the
time I write of; I invoke the innocent figure that I dearly loved, to come out
from the mists and shadows of the past, and turn its gentle head towards me
once again; and I can still declare that this one little speech was constantly
in my memory. I may not have used it to the best account; I was young and
inexperienced; but I never turned a deaf ear to its artless pleading.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Remarkable meta-textual passage: the adult narrator David reflects that Dora's speech constantly stayed with him, and he 'invokes' her innocent figure from the past to turn its gentle head toward him again. This is among the most touching passages in the novel—David's mature voice recognizing he may not have used the 'child-wife' concept to best account, but never forgot its artless pleading.
enrichment.best_quote: I invoke the innocent figure that I dearly loved, to come out from the mists and shadows of the past, and turn its gentle head towards me once again
enrichment.summary: The adult David reflects that Dora's child-wife speech was constantly in his memory; he invokes her innocent figure to turn toward him again from the past.

text:
Dora told me, shortly afterwards, that she was going to be a wonderful
housekeeper. Accordingly, she polished the tablets, pointed the pencil, bought
an immense account-book, carefully stitched up with a needle and thread all the
leaves of the Cookery Book which Jip had torn, and made quite a desperate
little attempt ‘to be good’, as she called it. But the figures had
the old obstinate propensity—they WOULD NOT add up. When she had entered
two or three laborious items in the account-book, Jip would walk over the page,
wagging his tail, and smear them all out. Her own little right-hand middle
finger got steeped to the very bone in ink; and I think that was the only
decided result obtained.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's attempt to become a housekeeper is tragicomic: she polishes tablets, points pencils, stitches Cookery Book pages; the figures 'WOULD NOT add up'; Jip walks over her entries and smears them out; her right-hand middle finger gets steeped in ink. She cannot overcome the union of her nature and external chaos.
enrichment.best_quote: But the figures had the old obstinate propensity—they WOULD NOT add up
enrichment.summary: Dora makes a desperate attempt to be a good housekeeper: she polishes tablets, buys an account-book, stitches the Cookery Book; but the figures won't add up and Jip smears her entries.

text:
Sometimes, of an evening, when I was at home and at work—for I wrote a
good deal now, and was beginning in a small way to be known as a writer—I
would lay down my pen, and watch my child-wife trying to be good. First of all,
she would bring out the immense account-book, and lay it down upon the table,
with a deep sigh. Then she would open it at the place where Jip had made it
illegible last night, and call Jip up, to look at his misdeeds. This would
occasion a diversion in Jip’s favour, and some inking of his nose,
perhaps, as a penalty. Then she would tell Jip to lie down on the table
instantly, ‘like a lion’—which was one of his tricks, though
I cannot say the likeness was striking—and, if he were in an obedient
humour, he would obey. Then she would take up a pen, and begin to write, and
find a hair in it. Then she would take up another pen, and begin to write, and
find that it spluttered. Then she would take up another pen, and begin to
write, and say in a low voice, ‘Oh, it’s a talking pen, and will
disturb Doady!’ And then she would give it up as a bad job, and put the
account-book away, after pretending to crush the lion with it.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Detailed comic scene of Dora's failed housekeeping attempts, observed by David in the evenings; she tries, finds distractions (pens with hairs, spluttering pens, 'talking pens'), pretends to crush Jip like a lion. The humor masks the sadness of her genuine effort against her nature.
enrichment.best_quote: 'Oh, it's a talking pen, and will disturb Doady!'
enrichment.summary: David watches Dora attempt to use her account-book in the evening; she repeatedly finds obstacles—hairs in pens, spluttering pens, talking pens—and eventually gives up.

text:
Or, if she were in a very sedate and serious state of mind, she would sit down
with the tablets, and a little basket of bills and other documents, which
looked more like curl-papers than anything else, and endeavour to get some
result out of them. After severely comparing one with another, and making

her left hand over and over again, backwards and forwards, she would be so
vexed and discouraged, and would look so unhappy, that it gave me pain to see
her bright face clouded—and for me!—and I would go softly to her,
and say:

enrichment.best_quote: it gave me pain to see her bright face clouded—and for me!
enrichment.summary: Dora tries another method with bills and documents, comparing them and counting on her fingers, but becomes vexed and discouraged.

text: ‘What’s the matter, Dora?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's inquiry; routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David asks Dora what is the matter.

text:
Dora would look up hopelessly, and reply, ‘They won’t come right.
They make my head ache so. And they won’t do anything I want!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's hopeless admission: the numbers won't come right, they make her head ache, and they won't do what she wants; her frustration is genuine and her inadequacy is not mere laziness.
enrichment.summary: Dora says the numbers won't come right and give her a headache.

text: Then I would say, ‘Now let us try together. Let me show you, Dora.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's offer to help; routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David suggests they try together and he will show her.

text:
Then I would commence a practical demonstration, to which Dora would pay
profound attention, perhaps for five minutes; when she would begin to be
dreadfully tired, and would lighten the subject by curling my hair, or trying
the effect of my face with my shirt-collar turned down. If I tacitly checked
this playfulness, and persisted, she would look so scared and disconsolate, as
she became more and more bewildered, that the remembrance of her natural gaiety
when I first strayed into her path, and of her being my child-wife, would come
reproachfully upon me; and I would lay the pencil down, and call for the
guitar.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Powerful passage showing David's dilemma: he demonstrates practical arithmetic, but Dora becomes tired after five minutes, diverts him with playfulness (curling his hair), and when he insists, she becomes scared and bewildered; the memory of her natural gaiety and their child-wife understanding makes him abandon instruction and call for the guitar. A key passage showing why he cannot improve her.
enrichment.best_quote: the remembrance of her natural gaiety when I first strayed into her path, and of her being my child-wife, would come reproachfully upon me
enrichment.summary: David attempts to demonstrate arithmetic to Dora, but she becomes tired and playful after five minutes; when he persists, she becomes frightened and bewildered, so he abandons the lesson and calls for the guitar.

text:
I had a great deal of work to do, and had many anxieties, but the same
considerations made me keep them to myself. I am far from sure, now, that it
was right to do this, but I did it for my child-wife’s sake. I search my
breast, and I commit its secrets, if I know them, without any reservation to
this paper. The old unhappy loss or want of something had, I am conscious, some
place in my heart; but not to the embitterment of my life. When I walked alone
in the fine weather, and thought of the summer days when all the air had been
filled with my boyish enchantment, I did miss something of the realization of
my dreams; but I thought it was a softened glory of the Past, which nothing
could have thrown upon the present time. I did feel, sometimes, for a little
while, that I could have wished my wife had been my counsellor; had had more
character and purpose, to sustain me and improve me by; had been endowed with
power to fill up the void which somewhere seemed to be about me; but I felt as
if this were an unearthly consummation of my happiness, that never had been
meant to be, and never could have been.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Profound self-examination: David acknowledges he has much work and anxiety but keeps them from Dora for her sake; he retrospectively questions whether this was right; he confesses an 'old unhappy loss or want of something' in his heart, wishing Dora could have been his counsellor and had more character to sustain him, but accepts this as an 'unearthly consummation' never meant to be. This is the chapter's most mature and honest moment.
enrichment.best_quote: but I felt as if this were an unearthly consummation of my happiness, that never had been meant to be, and never could have been
enrichment.summary: David reflects that he kept his cares from Dora and now questions whether this was right; he acknowledges missing having her as a counsellor but accepts this cannot be.

text:
I was a boyish husband as to years. I had known the softening influence of no
other sorrows or experiences than those recorded in these leaves. If I did any
wrong, as I may have done much, I did it in mistaken love, and in my want of
wisdom. I write the exact truth. It would avail me nothing to extenuate it now.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's defense and explanation: he was boyish as a husband, inexperienced, and if he did wrong it was in mistaken love and want of wisdom; he commits to writing the exact truth without extenuating it. A moment of narrative honesty that frames his entire relationship with Dora.
enrichment.best_quote: If I did any wrong, as I may have done much, I did it in mistaken love, and in my want of wisdom
enrichment.summary: David reflects that he was a boyish husband and any wrongs he committed were through mistaken love and inexperience.

text:
Thus it was that I took upon myself the toils and cares of our life, and had no
partner in them. We lived much as before, in reference to our scrambling
household arrangements; but I had got used to those, and Dora I was pleased to
see was seldom vexed now. She was bright and cheerful in the old childish way,
loved me dearly, and was happy with her old trifles.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Summary of their shared life: David took on the toils and cares alone, without partner; they continued in household chaos but David grew accustomed; Dora was bright, cheerful, loved him, and was happy with trifles. A resigned acceptance of their marriage's trajectory.
enrichment.summary: David took on all the toils of married life without partner; Dora remained bright and cheerful, loving him and content with trifles.

text:
When the debates were heavy—I mean as to length, not quality, for in the
last respect they were not often otherwise—and I went home late, Dora
would never rest when she heard my footsteps, but would always come downstairs
to meet me. When my evenings were unoccupied by the pursuit for which I had
qualified myself with so much pains, and I was engaged in writing at home, she
would sit quietly near me, however late the hour, and be so mute, that I would
often think she had dropped asleep. But generally, when I raised my head, I saw
her blue eyes looking at me with the quiet attention of which I have already
spoken.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Description of Dora's devotion: when debates are heavy she waits up; when he writes at home she sits quietly nearby, so mute he thinks she's asleep, but her blue eyes watch him with 'quiet attention.' Her wordless presence is both touching and somewhat melancholy.
enrichment.best_quote: her blue eyes looking at me with the quiet attention

‘Please let me hold the pens,’ said Dora. ‘I want to have
something to do with all those many hours when you are so industrious. May I
hold the pens?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Dora's request: to hold the pens so she has something to do with the many hours of his industriousness; she wants connection and purpose through his work.

text:
The remembrance of her pretty joy when I said yes, brings tears into my eyes.
The next time I sat down to write, and regularly afterwards, she sat in her old
place, with a spare bundle of pens at her side. Her triumph in this connexion
with my work, and her delight when I wanted a new pen—which I very often
feigned to do—suggested to me a new way of pleasing my child-wife. I
occasionally made a pretence of wanting a page or two of manuscript copied.
Then Dora was in her glory. The preparations she made for this great work, the
aprons she put on, the bibs she borrowed from the kitchen to keep off the ink,
the time she took, the innumerable stoppages she made to have a laugh with Jip
as if he understood it all, her conviction that her work was incomplete unless
she signed her name at the end, and the way in which she would bring it to me,
like a school-copy, and then, when I praised it, clasp me round the neck, are
touching recollections to me, simple as they might appear to other men.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Remarkably touching passage: the memory of Dora's joy when holding the pens brings tears to the adult David's eyes; he describes her triumph, her aprons and kitchen bibs, her laughter with Jip, her conviction she must sign her name, her schoolgirl delivery. This is the novel's most poignant moment—David cherishing these 'touching recollections' that 'might appear simple as they might appear to other men.' A perfect crystallization of love and tenderness despite limitation.
enrichment.best_quote: are touching recollections to me, simple as they might appear to other men
enrichment.summary: David describes the touching memory of Dora holding the pens and her joy at copying his manuscript, bringing him to tears with the recollection.
