And now, I tried to tell her of the struggle I had had, and the conclusion I
had come to. I tried to lay my mind before her, truly, and entirely. I tried to
show her how I had hoped I had come into the better knowledge of myself and of
her; how I had resigned myself to what that better knowledge brought; and how I
had come there, even that day, in my fidelity to this. If she did so love me (I
said) that she could take me for her husband, she could do so, on no deserving
of mine, except upon the truth of my love for her, and the trouble in which it
had ripened to be what it was; and hence it was that I revealed it. And O,
Agnes, even out of thy true eyes, in that same time, the spirit of my
child-wife looked upon me, saying it was well; and winning me, through thee, to
tenderest recollections of the Blossom that had withered in its bloom!

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's final explanation and emotional integration—connecting his struggle, his growth, Dora's memory, and his present love into a philosophical and deeply moving whole.
enrichment.best_quote: If she did so love me (I said) that she could take me for her husband, she could do so, on no deserving of mine, except upon the truth of my love for her, and the trouble in which it had ripened to be what it was; and hence it was that I revealed it. And O, Agnes, even out of thy true eyes, in that same time, the spirit of my child-wife looked upon me, saying it was well; and winning me, through thee, to tenderest recollections of the Blossom that had withered in its bloom!
enrichment.summary: David tells Agnes that his love is offered without deserving, founded only on its truth and the trouble that ripened it; he perceives Dora's spirit blessing the union through Agnes's eyes.

text:
‘I am so blest, Trotwood—my heart is so overcharged—but there
is one thing I must say.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Agnes begins to speak something important; suspenseful transition before her revelation.
enrichment.summary: Agnes says she has something important to tell David, her heart overcharged.

text: ‘Dearest, what?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's simple prompt; connective dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David invites Agnes to speak.

text: She laid her gentle hands upon my shoulders, and looked calmly in my face.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Agnes touches David and looks calmly at him, a moment of composed intensity before her confession.
enrichment.summary: Agnes lays her hands on David's shoulders and looks calmly into his face.

text: ‘Do you know, yet, what it is?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Agnes's question; suspenseful but brief.
enrichment.summary: Agnes asks if David knows what her secret is.

text: ‘I am afraid to speculate on what it is. Tell me, my dear.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David admits his uncertainty and asks her to tell him; routine connective dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David says he is afraid to guess and asks Agnes to tell him directly.

text: ‘I have loved you all my life!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Agnes's simple, beautiful declaration—'I have loved you all my life!'—is the perfect culmination, expressing long, constant devotion in six words.
enrichment.best_quote: I have loved you all my life!
enrichment.summary: Agnes reveals that her secret is her lifelong love for David.

text:
O, we were happy, we were happy! Our tears were not for the trials (hers so
much the greater) through which we had come to be thus, but for the rapture of
being thus, never to be divided more!

enrichment.interest_rationale: A rapturous culmination where David and Agnes's union is sanctified through joy and grateful tears, expressing the transcendent happiness at the chapter's heart.
enrichment.best_quote: O, we were happy, we were happy! Our tears were not for the trials (hers so much the greater) through which we had come to be thus, but for the rapture of being thus, never to be divided more!
enrichment.summary: David and Agnes celebrate their union with joyful tears, no longer focused on past trials but on their transcendent happiness.

text:
We walked, that winter evening, in the fields together; and the blessed calm
within us seemed to be partaken by the frosty air. The early stars began to
shine while we were lingering on, and looking up to them, we thanked our GOD
for having guided us to this tranquillity.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A serene, almost spiritual passage where David and Agnes walk in the frosty fields, their inner calm reflected in nature, with gratitude to God—a moment of profound peace.
enrichment.best_quote: We walked, that winter evening, in the fields together; and the blessed calm within us seemed to be partaken by the frosty air. The early stars began to shine while we were lingering on, and looking up to them, we thanked our GOD for having guided us to this tranquillity.
enrichment.summary: David and Agnes walk together in the winter fields, their inner peace reflected in nature; they thank God for their tranquility.

text:
We stood together in the same old-fashioned window at night, when the moon was
shining; Agnes with her quiet eyes raised up to it; I following her glance.
Long miles of road then opened out before my mind; and, toiling on, I saw a
ragged way-worn boy, forsaken and neglected, who should come to call even the
heart now beating against mine, his own.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's reflection at the window, imagining his future with Agnes and remembering his past as a neglected boy, brings the novel full circle with hope and redemption.
enrichment.best_quote: Long miles of road then opened out before my mind; and, toiling on, I saw a ragged way-worn boy, forsaken and neglected, who should come to call even the heart now beating against mine, his own.
enrichment.summary: David reflects on his future with Agnes and remembers his past as a neglected boy, integrating his entire life's journey into a vision of redemption.

text:
It was nearly dinner-time next day when we appeared before my aunt. She was up
in my study, Peggotty said: which it was her pride to keep in readiness and
order for me. We found her, in her spectacles, sitting by the fire.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Routine setup for the domestic scene with Betsey; connective narrative.
enrichment.summary: David and Agnes arrive at Betsey's home, where she is found in her study by the fire.

text:
‘Goodness me!’ said my aunt, peering through the dusk,
‘who’s this you’re bringing home?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's playful greeting; light, routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: Betsey peering through the dusk, playfully asks who David is bringing home.

text: ‘Agnes,’ said I.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's simple answer; routine dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David simply answers 'Agnes.'

text:
As we had arranged to say nothing at first, my aunt was not a little
discomfited. She darted a hopeful glance at me, when I said
‘Agnes’; but seeing that I looked as usual, she took off her
spectacles in despair, and rubbed her nose with them.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's comical confusion—her hopeful glance, disappointed taking off of spectacles, and nose-rubbing—is Dickensian comic business revealing her emotional investment.
enrichment.summary: Betsey had expected David to announce an engagement but finds nothing obvious in his manner; she removes her spectacles in disappointed bewilderment.

text:
She greeted Agnes heartily, nevertheless; and we were soon in the lighted
parlour downstairs, at dinner. My aunt put on her spectacles twice or thrice,
to take another look at me, but as often took them off again, disappointed, and
rubbed her nose with them. Much to the discomfiture of Mr. Dick, who knew this
to be a bad symptom.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Comic scene of Betsey repeatedly looking through her spectacles and rubbing her nose, with Mr. Dick perplexed; light character comedy surrounding the central revelation.
enrichment.summary: Betsey keeps peering through her spectacles at David during dinner, disappointed each time, frustrating Mr. Dick who recognizes her bad mood.

text:
‘By the by, aunt,’ said I, after dinner; ‘I have been
speaking to Agnes about what you told me.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David casually references his conversation with Agnes about what Betsey told him; a light transition toward his revelation.
enrichment.summary: David mentions to Betsey that he has spoken to Agnes about what his aunt told him.

text:
‘Then, Trot,’ said my aunt, turning scarlet, ‘you did wrong,
and broke your promise.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey indignantly accuses David of breaking his promise; comic reproval that sets up the final revelation.
enrichment.summary: Betsey, turning scarlet, accuses David of wrong-doing and breaking his promise.

text:
‘You are not angry, aunt, I trust? I am sure you won’t be, when you
learn that Agnes is not unhappy in any attachment.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's reassurance to Betsey; routine connective dialogue leading to the revelation.
enrichment.summary: David assures his aunt she won't be angry once she learns Agnes is not unhappy.

text: ‘Stuff and nonsense!’ said my aunt.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's dismissive exclamation; light comic retort.
enrichment.summary: Betsey curtly dismisses David's assurance.

text:
As my aunt appeared to be annoyed, I thought the best way was to cut her
annoyance short. I took Agnes in my arm to the back of her chair, and we both
leaned over her. My aunt, with one clap of her hands, and one look through her
spectacles, immediately went into hysterics, for the first and only time in all
my knowledge of her.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David and Agnes's physical gesture—leaning over Betsey's chair together—prompts her first and only hysteric fit, a comic release of her emotional investment in their union.
enrichment.best_quote: I took Agnes in my arm to the back of her chair, and we both leaned over her. My aunt, with one clap of her hands, and one look through her spectacles, immediately went into hysterics, for the first and only time in all my knowledge of her.
enrichment.summary: David and Agnes lean over Betsey together, prompting her to have her one and only hysterical fit.

text:
The hysterics called up Peggotty. The moment my aunt was restored, she flew at
Peggotty, and calling her a silly old creature, hugged her with all her might.
After that, she hugged Mr. Dick (who was highly honoured, but a good deal
surprised); and after that, told them why. Then, we were all happy together.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Betsey's joyful aftermath—hugging everyone and telling them why—is comic and warm, showing her relief and affection.
enrichment.summary: After recovering, Betsey hugs Peggotty and Mr. Dick, tells them the news, and everyone is happy together.

text:
I could not discover whether my aunt, in her last short conversation with me,
had fallen on a pious fraud, or had really mistaken the state of my mind. It
was quite enough, she said, that she had told me Agnes was going to be married;
and that I now knew better than anyone how true it was.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David reflects on Betsey's earlier deception or mistake, with her playful response; a light, humorous conclusion to the subplot.
enrichment.summary: David notes the ambiguity of whether Betsey had deliberately deceived him or misread his mind, and her witty response.

text:
We were married within a fortnight. Traddles and Sophy, and Doctor and Mrs.
Strong, were the only guests at our quiet wedding. We left them full of joy;
and drove away together. Clasped in my embrace, I held the source of every
worthy aspiration I had ever had; the centre of myself, the circle of my life,
my own, my wife; my love of whom was founded on a rock!

enrichment.interest_rationale: The marriage within a fortnight, with selected guests and David's declaration of Agnes as his anchor, provides a triumphant and poignant conclusion to the love story.
enrichment.best_quote: Clasped in my embrace, I held the source of every worthy aspiration I had ever had; the centre of myself, the circle of my life, my own, my wife; my love of whom was founded on a rock!
enrichment.summary: David and Agnes are married within a fortnight in a quiet ceremony; David reflects on Agnes as the foundation of all his worthy aspirations.

text:
‘Dearest husband!’ said Agnes. ‘Now that I may call you by
that name, I have one thing more to tell you.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Agnes has one more revelation to share; a final mysterious turn suggesting there is still more emotional depth to uncover.
enrichment.summary: Agnes says she has one more thing to tell David now that she may call him husband.

text: ‘Let me hear it, love.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's simple prompt; routine connective dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David asks Agnes to tell him.

text: ‘It grows out of the night when Dora died. She sent you for me.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Agnes reveals the dying Dora asked for her—a touching connection between past and present, and an indication of what follows.
enrichment.summary: Agnes reveals that Dora sent for her before she died.

text: ‘She did.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's simple confirmation; routine connective dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David confirms that Dora did send for Agnes.

text:
‘She told me that she left me something. Can you think what it
was?’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Agnes's gentle question about Dora's parting gift; suspenseful setup for the revelation.
enrichment.summary: Agnes asks David if he can think what Dora left her.

text:
I believed I could. I drew the wife who had so long loved me, closer to my
side.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's understanding and his physical gesture of drawing Agnes closer suggest his comprehension of Dora's final wish.
enrichment.summary: David believes he understands and draws Agnes closer to his side.

text:
‘She told me that she made a last request to me, and left me a last
charge.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Agnes articulates Dora's request and charge; a formal, touching articulation of the dying wish.
enrichment.summary: Agnes speaks of Dora's final request and charge she left with her.

text: ‘And it was—’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's prompt; connective dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David waits for Agnes to continue.

text: ‘That only I would occupy this vacant place.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Agnes reveals Dora's final wish—that she alone fill the vacant place in David's heart—is profoundly moving, sanctifying the union and integrating Dora's memory.
enrichment.best_quote: That only I would occupy this vacant place.
enrichment.summary: Agnes reveals that Dora's last charge was that Agnes alone should occupy the vacant place in David's heart.

text:
And Agnes laid her head upon my breast, and wept; and I wept with her, though
we were so happy.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The novel's culmination: Agnes weeping on David's heart while he weeps with her, happiness and sorrow intermingled, perfect closure to the great love story.
enrichment.best_quote: And Agnes laid her head upon my breast, and wept; and I wept with her, though we were so happy.
enrichment.summary: Agnes rests her head on David's breast and they weep together, their tears mingling joy and tender sorrow.

text:
What I have purposed to record is nearly finished; but there is yet an incident
conspicuous in my memory, on which it often rests with delight, and without
which one thread in the web I have spun would have a ravelled end.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David frames the chapter's purpose as a final, meaningful incident that will complete his narrative, signaling something important about memory and closure.
enrichment.summary: David introduces a memorable incident that will complete his life story.

text:
I had advanced in fame and fortune, my domestic joy was perfect, I had been
married ten happy years. Agnes and I were sitting by the fire, in our house in
London, one night in spring, and three of our children were playing in the
room, when I was told that a stranger wished to see me.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Establishes the domestic contentment and stability David has achieved after ten years of marriage, creating the setting for the unexpected visitor.
enrichment.summary: David and his wife Agnes sit by the fire with their three children when a stranger asks to see him.

text:
He had been asked if he came on business, and had answered No; he had come for
the pleasure of seeing me, and had come a long way. He was an old man, my
servant said, and looked like a farmer.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Provides practical details about the mysterious visitor—an old man who has traveled far—but remains routine exposition.
enrichment.summary: The servant reports that an old farmer-like stranger has come a long distance to see David for pleasure, not business.

text:
As this sounded mysterious to the children, and moreover was like the beginning
of a favourite story Agnes used to tell them, introductory to the arrival of a
wicked old Fairy in a cloak who hated everybody, it produced some commotion.
One of our boys laid his head in his mother’s lap to be out of
harm’s way, and little Agnes (our eldest child) left her doll in a chair
to represent her, and thrust out her little heap of golden curls from between
the window-curtains, to see what happened next.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vivid domestic scene showing how the children's innocence and imagination respond to mystery, with charming detail about little Agnes and her doll.
enrichment.summary: The children are excited by the mysterious visitor, with little Agnes abandoning her doll to peek from the window curtains.

text: ‘Let him come in here!’ said I.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Single line of dialogue commanding the visitor's entry; purely functional transition.
enrichment.summary: David invites the visitor inside.

text:
There soon appeared, pausing in the dark doorway as he entered, a hale,
grey-haired old man. Little Agnes, attracted by his looks, had run to bring him
in, and I had not yet clearly seen his face, when my wife, starting up, cried
out to me, in a pleased and agitated voice, that it was Mr. Peggotty!

enrichment.interest_rationale: The dramatic revelation of Mr. Peggotty's identity—a beloved character's unexpected reappearance after years of separation—is deeply moving and narratively significant.
enrichment.summary: The mysterious visitor is revealed to be Mr. Peggotty, whom Agnes recognizes with joy and agitation.

text:
It WAS Mr. Peggotty. An old man now, but in a ruddy, hearty, strong old age.
When our first emotion was over, and he sat before the fire with the children
on his knees, and the blaze shining on his face, he looked, to me, as vigorous
and robust, withal as handsome, an old man, as ever I had seen.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Vivid description of how age has treated Mr. Peggotty—still vigorous and handsome despite being old—emphasizes resilience and the blessing of his Australian life.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Peggotty appears as a hale, grey-haired old man, still vigorous and handsome.

text:
‘Mas’r Davy,’ said he. And the old name in the old tone fell
so naturally on my ear! ‘Mas’r Davy, ‘tis a joyful hour as I
see you, once more, ‘long with your own trew wife!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Peggotty's distinctive speech and the affectionate use of 'Mas'r Davy' evoke nostalgia and emotional recognition of a beloved mentor figure.
enrichment.best_quote: 'Mas'r Davy,' said he. And the old name in the old tone fell so naturally on my ear! 'Mas'r Davy, 'tis a joyful hour as I see you, once more, 'long with your own trew wife!'
enrichment.summary: Mr. Peggotty greets David with the old familiar nickname, expressing joy at seeing him with his faithful wife.

text: ‘A joyful hour indeed, old friend!’ cried I.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Simple reciprocal greeting; functional exchange without additional depth.
enrichment.summary: David warmly returns Mr. Peggotty's greeting.

text:
‘And these heer pretty ones,’ said Mr. Peggotty. ‘To look at
these heer flowers! Why, Mas’r Davy, you was but the heighth of the
littlest of these, when I first see you! When Em’ly warn’t no
bigger, and our poor lad were BUT a lad!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Peggotty's nostalgic reflection on how much David has grown since childhood, anchoring their connection in memory and the passage of time.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Peggotty marvels at how David and his own daughter Emily have grown from tiny children.

text:
‘Time has changed me more than it has changed you since then,’ said
I. ‘But let these dear rogues go to bed; and as no house in England but
this must hold you, tell me where to send for your luggage (is the old black
bag among it, that went so far, I wonder!), and then, over a glass of Yarmouth
grog, we will have the tidings of ten years!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: David warmly insists Mr. Peggotty stay with them and references the symbolic old black bag, deepening the sense of reunion and continuity.
enrichment.summary: David insists Mr. Peggotty stay with them and asks for his luggage, enquiring about the old black bag.

text: ‘Are you alone?’ asked Agnes.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief question serving purely narrative function; no substantive content.
enrichment.summary: Agnes asks if Mr. Peggotty is alone.

text:
‘Yes, ma’am,’ he said, kissing her hand, ‘quite
alone.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Simple confirmation that carries the weight of solitude and the completeness of his journey.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Peggotty confirms he has traveled alone.

text:
We sat him between us, not knowing how to give him welcome enough; and as I
began to listen to his old familiar voice, I could have fancied he was still
pursuing his long journey in search of his darling niece.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's reflection on how Mr. Peggotty's voice evokes the sense of his long quest for Emily, connecting past trauma to present reunion.
enrichment.summary: David notes how Mr. Peggotty's voice triggers memories of his long journey searching for Emily.

text:
‘It’s a mort of water,’ said Mr. Peggotty, ‘fur to come
across, and on’y stay a matter of fower weeks. But water
(‘specially when ‘tis salt) comes nat’ral to me; and friends
is dear, and I am heer. —Which is verse,’ said Mr. Peggotty,
surprised to find it out, ‘though I hadn’t such intentions.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Peggotty's poetic reflection on his journey across salt water and his friendships demonstrates his growth and humanity in Australian exile.
enrichment.best_quote: Which is verse,' said Mr. Peggotty, surprised to find it out, 'though I hadn't such intentions.'
enrichment.summary: Mr. Peggotty reflects that despite the vast ocean journey, his friendship and love of friends brought him across the salt water.

text:
‘Are you going back those many thousand miles, so soon?’ asked
Agnes.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Agnes asks a practical question about Mr. Peggotty's departure plans, advancing the conversation but without deep narrative significance.
enrichment.summary: Agnes asks if Mr. Peggotty will return to Australia soon.

text:
‘Yes, ma’am,’ he returned. ‘I giv the promise to
Em’ly, afore I come away. You see, I doen’t grow younger as the
years comes round, and if I hadn’t sailed as ‘twas, most like I
shouldn’t never have done ‘t. And it’s allus been on my mind,
as I must come and see Mas’r Davy and your own sweet blooming self, in
your wedded happiness, afore I got to be too old.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Peggotty explains his promise to Emily and his awareness of mortality, adding poignancy to his long journey and reunion with David.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Peggotty explains he promised Emily he would return, and made this visit before he grows too old.

text:
He looked at us, as if he could never feast his eyes on us sufficiently. Agnes
laughingly put back some scattered locks of his grey hair, that he might see us
better.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tender moment of physical affection between Mr. Peggotty and Agnes, showing his contentment and her warmth toward him.
enrichment.summary: Agnes gently adjusts Mr. Peggotty's grey hair so he can see them better.

text:
‘And now tell us,’ said I, ‘everything relating to your
fortunes.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Simple prompt for Mr. Peggotty to share his news; functional transition to exposition.
enrichment.summary: David asks Mr. Peggotty to tell them about his fortunes.

text:
‘Our fortuns, Mas’r Davy,’ he rejoined, ‘is soon told.
We haven’t fared nohows, but fared to thrive. We’ve allus thrived.
We’ve worked as we ought to ‘t, and maybe we lived a leetle hard at
first or so, but we have allus thrived. What with sheep-farming, and what with
stock-farming, and what with one thing and what with t’other, we are as
well to do, as well could be. Theer’s been kiender a blessing fell upon
us,’ said Mr. Peggotty, reverentially inclining his head, ‘and
we’ve done nowt but prosper. That is, in the long run. If not yesterday,
why then today. If not today, why then tomorrow.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Peggotty's account of prosperity through hard work and divine blessing demonstrates the redemptive power of emigration and virtue, central to the novel's values.
enrichment.best_quote: We've worked as we ought to 't, and maybe we lived a leetle hard at first or so, but we have allus thrived.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Peggotty explains they have thrived through sheep and stock farming, and attribute their success to blessing and hard work.

text: ‘And Emily?’ said Agnes and I, both together.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David and Agnes both ask together about Emily, demonstrating her importance to both and building anticipation for her account.
enrichment.summary: David and Agnes ask together about Emily's fate.

text:
‘Em’ly,’ said he, ‘arter you left her,
ma’am—and I never heerd her saying of her prayers at night,
t’other side the canvas screen, when we was settled in the Bush, but what
I heerd your name—and arter she and me lost sight of Mas’r Davy,
that theer shining sundown—was that low, at first, that, if she had
know’d then what Mas’r Davy kep from us so kind and thowtful,
‘tis my opinion she’d have drooped away. But theer was some poor
folks aboard as had illness among ‘em, and she took care of them; and
theer was the children in our company, and she took care of them; and so she
got to be busy, and to be doing good, and that helped her.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Peggotty's account of Emily's emotional recovery through service to others reveals redemption through compassion and reveals the significance of David and Agnes to her Australian life.
enrichment.best_quote: and arter she and me lost sight of Mas'r Davy, that theer shining sundown—was that low, at first, that, if she had know'd then what Mas'r Davy kep from us so kind and thowtful, 'tis my opinion she'd have drooped away.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Peggotty recounts how Emily initially suffered deeply after leaving David, but found healing through caring for others on the voyage.

text: ‘When did she first hear of it?’ I asked.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief question asking when Emily learned of the storm; functional transition.
enrichment.summary: David asks when Emily learned about the shipwreck.

text:
‘I kep it from her arter I heerd on ‘t,’ said Mr. Peggotty,
‘going on nigh a year. We was living then in a solitary place, but among
the beautifullest trees, and with the roses a-covering our Beein to the roof.
Theer come along one day, when I was out a-working on the land, a traveller
from our own Norfolk or Suffolk in England (I doen’t rightly mind which),
and of course we took him in, and giv him to eat and drink, and made him
welcome. We all do that, all the colony over. He’d got an old newspaper
with him, and some other account in print of the storm. That’s how she
know’d it. When I came home at night, I found she know’d it.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Peggotty's account of learning the truth through a newspaper brought by a traveling Norfolk or Suffolk man evokes the small-world nature of colonial life and Victorian news transmission.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Peggotty kept Emily's knowledge of the shipwreck hidden for nearly a year until a traveling man brought an English newspaper with the story.

text:
He dropped his voice as he said these words, and the gravity I so well
remembered overspread his face.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief description of Mr. Peggotty's somber reaction, indicating the depth of emotional impact.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Peggotty's face grows grave as he speaks of Emily's discovery.

text: ‘Did it change her much?’ we asked.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Simple question about Emily's transformation; functional transition.
enrichment.summary: They ask if the news of the shipwreck changed Emily greatly.

text:
‘Aye, for a good long time,’ he said, shaking his head; ‘if
not to this present hour. But I think the solitoode done her good. And she had
a deal to mind in the way of poultry and the like, and minded of it, and come
through. I wonder,’ he said thoughtfully, ‘if you could see my
Em’ly now, Mas’r Davy, whether you’d know her!’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Mr. Peggotty's observation that solitude and work helped Emily recover, with his wonder if David would recognize her now, deepens the sense of her transformation through hardship and isolation.
enrichment.summary: Mr. Peggotty says the isolation did Emily good, and wonders if David would recognize her now.

text: ‘Is she so altered?’ I inquired.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Brief question confirming Emily's altered appearance; functional dialogue.
enrichment.summary: David asks if Emily has changed greatly.

text:
‘I doen’t know. I see her ev’ry day, and doen’t know;
But, odd-times, I have thowt so. A slight figure,’ said Mr. Peggotty,

‘The public dinner to our distinguished fellow-colonist and townsman,
WILKINS MICAWBER, ESQUIRE, Port Middlebay District Magistrate, came off
yesterday in the large room of the Hotel, which was crowded to suffocation. It
is estimated that not fewer than forty-seven persons must have been
accommodated with dinner at one time, exclusive of the company in the passage
and on the stairs. The beauty, fashion, and exclusiveness of Port Middlebay,
flocked to do honour to one so deservedly esteemed, so highly talented, and so
widely popular. Doctor Mell (of Colonial Salem-House Grammar School, Port
Middlebay) presided, and on his right sat the distinguished guest. After the
removal of the cloth, and the singing of Non Nobis (beautifully executed, and
in which we were at no loss to distinguish the bell-like notes of that gifted
amateur, WILKINS MICAWBER, ESQUIRE, JUNIOR), the usual loyal and patriotic
toasts were severally given and rapturously received. Doctor Mell, in a speech
replete with feeling, then proposed “Our distinguished Guest, the
ornament of our town. May he never leave us but to better himself, and may his
success among us be such as to render his bettering himself impossible!”
The cheering with which the toast was received defies description. Again and
again it rose and fell, like the waves of ocean. At length all was hushed, and
WILKINS MICAWBER, ESQUIRE, presented himself to return thanks. Far be it from
us, in the present comparatively imperfect state of the resources of our
establishment, to endeavour to follow our distinguished townsman through the
smoothly-flowing periods of his polished and highly-ornate address! Suffice it
to observe, that it was a masterpiece of eloquence; and that those passages in
which he more particularly traced his own successful career to its source, and
warned the younger portion of his auditory from the shoals of ever incurring
pecuniary liabilities which they were unable to liquidate, brought a tear into
the manliest eye present. The remaining toasts were DOCTOR MELL; Mrs. MICAWBER
(who gracefully bowed her acknowledgements from the side-door, where a galaxy
of beauty was elevated on chairs, at once to witness and adorn the gratifying
scene), Mrs. RIDGER BEGS (late Miss Micawber); Mrs. MELL; WILKINS MICAWBER,
ESQUIRE, JUNIOR (who convulsed the assembly by humorously remarking that he
found himself unable to return thanks in a speech, but would do so, with their
permission, in a song); Mrs. MICAWBER’S FAMILY (well known, it is
needless to remark, in the mother-country), &c. &c. &c. At the
conclusion of the proceedings the tables were cleared as if by art-magic for
dancing. Among the votaries of TERPSICHORE, who disported themselves until Sol
gave warning for departure, Wilkins Micawber, Esquire, Junior, and the lovely
and accomplished Miss Helena, fourth daughter of Doctor Mell, were particularly
remarkable.’

were happy at home. I had plenty to think of, therefore, besides my mind
running continually on the kind of place I was going to—which was an
awful speculation. Sometimes, I remember, I resigned myself to thoughts of home
and Peggotty; and to endeavouring, in a confused blind way, to recall how I had
felt, and what sort of boy I used to be, before I bit Mr. Murdstone: which I
couldn’t satisfy myself about by any means, I seemed to have bitten him

The Master, upon this, put his hand underneath the skirts of his coat, and

artificial. I don’t know what the tunes were—if there were such
things in the performance at all, which I doubt—but the influence of the
strain upon me was, first, to make me think of all my sorrows until I could
hardly keep my tears back; then to take away my appetite; and lastly, to make
me so sleepy that I couldn’t keep my eyes open. They begin to close
again, and I begin to nod, as the recollection rises fresh upon me. Once more

wondering when I first went in, what that peacock would have thought if he had

stupendous voice, ‘Hallo, you sir! You Copperfield! Show that badge
conspicuous, or I’ll report you!’ The playground was a bare
gravelled yard, open to all the back of the house and the offices; and I knew
that the servants read it, and the butcher read it, and the baker read it; that
everybody, in a word, who came backwards and forwards to the house, of a
morning when I was ordered to walk there, read that I was to be taken care of,
for I bit, I recollect that I positively began to have a dread of myself, as a
kind of wild boy who did bite.

There was an old door in this playground, on which the boys had a custom of
carving their names. It was completely covered with such inscriptions. In my
dread of the end of the vacation and their coming back, I could not read a
boy’s name, without inquiring in what tone and with what emphasis HE
would read, ‘Take care of him. He bites.’ There was one boy—a
certain J. Steerforth—who cut his name very deep and very often, who, I
conceived, would read it in a rather strong voice, and afterwards pull my hair.
There was another boy, one Tommy Traddles, who I dreaded would make game of it,
and pretend to be dreadfully frightened of me. There was a third, George
Demple, who I fancied would sing it. I have looked, a little shrinking
creature, at that door, until the owners of all the names—there were
five-and-forty of them in the school then, Mr. Mell said—seemed to send
me to Coventry by general acclamation, and to cry out, each in his own way,
‘Take care of him. He bites!’

It was the same with the places at the desks and forms. It was the same with

my own bed. I remember dreaming night after night, of being with my mother as

friend the waiter, and in all these circumstances making people scream and
stare, by the unhappy disclosure that I had nothing on but my little
night-shirt, and that placard.

In the monotony of my life, and in my constant apprehension of the re-opening
of the school, it was such an insupportable affliction! I had long tasks every
day to do with Mr. Mell; but I did them, there being no Mr. and Miss Murdstone
here, and got through them without disgrace. Before, and after them, I walked
about—supervised, as I have mentioned, by the man with the wooden leg.
How vividly I call to mind the damp about the house, the green cracked
flagstones in the court, an old leaky water-butt, and the discoloured trunks of
some of the grim trees, which seemed to have dripped more in the rain than
other trees, and to have blown less in the sun! At one we dined, Mr. Mell and
I, at the upper end of a long bare dining-room, full of deal tables, and
smelling of fat. Then, we had more tasks until tea, which Mr. Mell drank out of
a blue teacup, and I out of a tin pot. All day long, and until seven or eight
in the evening, Mr. Mell, at his own detached desk in the schoolroom, worked
hard with pen, ink, ruler, books, and writing-paper, making out the bills (as I
found) for last half-year. When he had put up his things for the night he took
out his flute, and blew at it, until I almost thought he would gradually blow
his whole being into the large hole at the top, and ooze away at the keys.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's detailed recollection of his daily life at Salem House—supervised by the gatekeeper, doing lessons with Mr. Mell, enduring the flute playing—conveys the monotonous misery and damp coldness of his imprisonment.

I picture my small self in the dimly-lighted rooms, sitting with my head upon
my hand, listening to the doleful performance of Mr. Mell, and conning
tomorrow’s lessons. I picture myself with my books shut up, still
listening to the doleful performance of Mr. Mell, and listening through it to
what used to be at home, and to the blowing of the wind on Yarmouth flats, and
feeling very sad and solitary. I picture myself going up to bed, among the
unused rooms, and sitting on my bed-side crying for a comfortable word from
Peggotty. I picture myself coming downstairs in the morning, and looking
through a long ghastly gash of a staircase window at the school-bell hanging on
the top of an out-house with a weathercock above it; and dreading the time when
it shall ring J. Steerforth and the rest to work: which is only second, in my
foreboding apprehensions, to the time when the man with the wooden leg shall
unlock the rusty gate to give admission to the awful Mr. Creakle. I cannot
think I was a very dangerous character in any of these aspects, but in all of
them I carried the same warning on my back.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's extended retrospective meditation on his suffering—sitting lonely in dim rooms, dreading Steerforth and Creakle, always carrying the placard—is a powerful evocation of childhood isolation and institutional dread.

Mr. Mell never said much to me, but he was never harsh to me. I suppose we were
company to each other, without talking. I forgot to mention that he would talk

pull his hair in an unaccountable manner. But he had these peculiarities: and
at first they frightened me, though I soon got used to them.

stump about with a mop and a bucket of water, from which I inferred that
preparations were making to receive Mr. Creakle and the boys. I was not

rarely shown themselves before, and were so continually in the midst of dust

consciousness of talking in that feeble way, made his angry face so much more

text:
‘Well!’ said Steerforth. ‘We must make it stretch as far as
we can; that’s all. I’ll do the best in my power for you. I can go
out when I like, and I’ll smuggle the prog in.’ With these words he
put the money in his pocket, and kindly told me not to make myself uneasy; he
would take care it should be all right. He was as good as his word, if that
were all right which I had a secret misgiving was nearly all wrong—for I
feared it was a waste of my mother’s two half-crowns—though I had
preserved the piece of paper they were wrapped in: which was a precious saving.
When we went upstairs to bed, he produced the whole seven shillings’
worth, and laid it out on my bed in the moonlight, saying:

enrichment.interest_rationale: Steerforth's reassurance and the feast contrast with David's nagging misgiving about squandering his mother's gift, revealing his conscience and awareness of propriety.
enrichment.best_quote: I feared it was a waste of my mother's two half-crowns
enrichment.summary: Steerforth comforts David about the spending and procures all the purchased items; David's worry about wasting his mother's money persists despite his relief.

text:
‘There you are, young Copperfield, and a royal spread you’ve
got.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Steerforth presents the lavish spread; establishes his generosity and prestige among the boys.
enrichment.best_quote: There you are, young Copperfield, and a royal spread you've got.
enrichment.summary: Steerforth displays the feast laid out on David's bed in the moonlight.

text:
I couldn’t think of doing the honours of the feast, at my time of life,
while he was by; my hand shook at the very thought of it. I begged him to do me
the favour of presiding; and my request being seconded by the other boys who
were in that room, he acceded to it, and sat upon my pillow, handing round the
viands—with perfect fairness, I must say—and dispensing the currant
wine in a little glass without a foot, which was his own property. As to me, I
sat on his left hand, and the rest were grouped about us, on the nearest beds
and on the floor.

enrichment.interest_rationale: David's awe and Steerforth's composed authority are captured; the nighttime feast becomes a moment of intimacy and hierarchy within the dormitory.
enrichment.best_quote: I couldn't think of doing the honours of the feast, at my time of life, while he was by; my hand shook at the very thought of it.
enrichment.summary: David is too awed by Steerforth to preside over the feast; Steerforth presides from David's pillow with studied fairness.

text:
How well I recollect our sitting there, talking in whispers; or their talking,
and my respectfully listening, I ought rather to say; the moonlight falling a
little way into the room, through the window, painting a pale window on the
floor, and the greater part of us in shadow, except when Steerforth dipped a
match into a phosphorus-box, when he wanted to look for anything on the board,
and shed a blue glare over us that was gone directly! A certain mysterious
feeling, consequent on the darkness, the secrecy of the revel, and the whisper
in which everything was said, steals over me again, and I listen to all they
tell me with a vague feeling of solemnity and awe, which makes me glad that
they are all so near, and frightens me (though I feign to laugh) when Traddles
pretends to see a ghost in the corner.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Exquisite atmospheric passage evoking the moonlit dormitory revel; David's retrospective meditation captures wonder and dread, with Steerforth as a mysterious, unknowable figure at the centre.
enrichment.best_quote: A certain mysterious feeling, consequent on the darkness, the secrecy of the revel, and the whisper in which everything was said, steals over me again, and I listen to all they tell me with a vague feeling of solemnity and awe
enrichment.summary: David evokes the magical atmosphere of the moonlit dormitory feast, the phosphorus-box glare, whispered talk, and his mixture of fascination and fear.

text:
I heard all kinds of things about the school and all belonging to it. I heard
that Mr. Creakle had not preferred his claim to being a Tartar without reason;
that he was the sternest and most severe of masters; that he laid about him,
right and left, every day of his life, charging in among the boys like a
trooper, and slashing away, unmercifully. That he knew nothing himself, but the
art of slashing, being more ignorant (J. Steerforth said) than the lowest boy
in the school; that he had been, a good many years ago, a small hop-dealer in
the Borough, and had taken to the schooling business after being bankrupt in
hops, and making away with Mrs. Creakle’s money. With a good deal more of
that sort, which I wondered how they knew.

enrichment.interest_rationale: The boys' gossip about Creakle's brutality, bankruptcy, and corruption exposes the master's hypocrisy and the institutional failures of the school; Steerforth's authority is confirmed.
enrichment.best_quote: he was the sternest and most severe of masters; that he laid about him, right and left, every day of his life, charging in among the boys like a trooper, and slashing away, unmercifully
enrichment.summary: The boys reveal Creakle's vicious character, his prior bankruptcy as a hop dealer, and his misappropriation of Mrs. Creakle's money.

text:
I heard that the man with the wooden leg, whose name was Tungay, was an
obstinate barbarian who had formerly assisted in the hop business, but had come
into the scholastic line with Mr. Creakle, in consequence, as was supposed
among the boys, of his having broken his leg in Mr. Creakle’s service,
and having done a deal of dishonest work for him, and knowing his secrets. I
heard that with the single exception of Mr. Creakle, Tungay considered the
whole establishment, masters and boys, as his natural enemies, and that the
only delight of his life was to be sour and malicious. I heard that Mr. Creakle
had a son, who had not been Tungay’s friend, and who, assisting in the
school, had once held some remonstrance with his father on an occasion when its
discipline was very cruelly exercised, and was supposed, besides, to have
protested against his father’s usage of his mother. I heard that Mr.
Creakle had turned him out of doors, in consequence; and that Mrs. and Miss
Creakle had been in a sad way, ever since.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Tungay's backstory—disability, loyalty born of past betrayal, malice—creates a complex character; the hint of Creakle's estrangement from his son adds emotional depth and foreshadows Mrs. and Miss Creakle's distress.
characters_present: the man with the wooden leg
enrichment.best_quote: the man with the wooden leg, whose name was Tungay, was an obstinate barbarian who had formerly assisted in the hop business, but had come into the scholastic line with Mr. Creakle, in consequence, as was supposed among the boys, of his having broken his leg in Mr. Creakle's service
enrichment.summary: The boys identify the wooden-legged man as Tungay, explain his origins and disability, and reveal that Creakle's son remonstrated against his father's cruelty and has been estranged.

text:
But the greatest wonder that I heard of Mr. Creakle was, there being one boy in
the school on whom he never ventured to lay a hand, and that boy being J.
Steerforth. Steerforth himself confirmed this when it was stated, and said that
he should like to begin to see him do it. On being asked by a mild boy (not me)
how he would proceed if he did begin to see him do it, he dipped a match into
his phosphorus-box on purpose to shed a glare over his reply, and said he would
commence by knocking him down with a blow on the forehead from the
seven-and-sixpenny ink-bottle that was always on the mantelpiece. We sat in the
dark for some time, breathless.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Steerforth's invulnerability and his bold threat reveal his courage and dominance; the phosphorus-box detail is atmospheric; the boys' breathless reaction emphasizes his power.
enrichment.best_quote: he dipped a match into his phosphorus-box on purpose to shed a glare over his reply, and said he would commence by knocking him down with a blow on the forehead from the seven-and-sixpenny ink-bottle that was always on the mantelpiece
enrichment.summary: The boys reveal that Creakle has never dared strike Steerforth; Steerforth boasts he would retaliate violently if Creakle tried.

text:
I heard that Mr. Sharp and Mr. Mell were both supposed to be wretchedly paid;
and that when there was hot and cold meat for dinner at Mr. Creakle’s
table, Mr. Sharp was always expected to say he preferred cold; which was again
corroborated by J. Steerforth, the only parlour-boarder. I heard that Mr.
Sharp’s wig didn’t fit him; and that he needn’t be so
‘bounceable’—somebody else said
‘bumptious’—about it, because his own red hair was very
plainly to be seen behind.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Gossip about Sharp's poverty, forced preference for cold meat, and ill-fitting wig satirizes the hypocrisy and humiliation of underpaid masters; Steerforth's role as parlour-boarder confirms his privilege.
enrichment.best_quote: when there was hot and cold meat for dinner at Mr. Creakle's table, Mr. Sharp was always expected to say he preferred cold
enrichment.summary: The boys reveal Sharp and Mell's penury and the false dignity Sharp must maintain about his wig.

text:
I heard that one boy, who was a coal-merchant’s son, came as a set-off
against the coal-bill, and was called, on that account, ‘Exchange or
Barter’—a name selected from the arithmetic book as expressing this
arrangement. I heard that the table beer was a robbery of parents, and the
pudding an imposition. I heard that Miss Creakle was regarded by the school in
general as being in love with Steerforth; and I am sure, as I sat in the dark,
thinking of his nice voice, and his fine face, and his easy manner, and his
curling hair, I thought it very likely. I heard that Mr. Mell was not a bad
sort of fellow, but hadn’t a sixpence to bless himself with; and that
there was no doubt that old Mrs. Mell, his mother, was as poor as job. I
thought of my breakfast then, and what had sounded like ‘My
Charley!’ but I was, I am glad to remember, as mute as a mouse about it.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A remarkable passage synthesizing social critique, character portrayal, and emotional resonance. The list of school gossip exposes class hierarchy, commercial degradation, poverty, and rumour; David's discretion about Mr. Mell is tender and morally mature.
enrichment.best_quote: I heard that one boy, who was a coal-merchant's son, came as a set-off against the coal-bill, and was called, on that account, 'Exchange or Barter'
enrichment.summary: The boys continue their gossip: a poor boy is traded against his father's bill; the food is overpriced; Miss Creakle admires Steerforth; Mell is poor and his mother is penniless. David notes Mr. Mell's connection to his breakfast and keeps silent.

text:
The hearing of all this, and a good deal more, outlasted the banquet some time.
The greater part of the guests had gone to bed as soon as the eating and
drinking were over; and we, who had remained whispering and listening
half-undressed, at last betook ourselves to bed, too.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Transitional paragraph concluding the feast and dormitory scene; functional but marks the winding down of the revel.
enrichment.summary: The guests depart and the remaining boys, who have been whispering and listening half-dressed, finally retire to bed.

text:
‘Good night, young Copperfield,’ said Steerforth. ‘I’ll
take care of you.’ ‘You’re very kind,’ I gratefully
returned. ‘I am very much obliged to you.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Steerforth's affectionate goodnight and David's grateful response establish their bond; Steerforth's promise to 'take care of' David is reassuring but hints at his control.
enrichment.best_quote: I'll take care of you.
enrichment.summary: Steerforth bids David goodnight with affectionate reassurance; David thanks him warmly.

‘You haven’t got a sister, have you?’ said Steerforth,
yawning.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Steerforth's question about David's sister is conversational but hints at his interest in David's intimate life and his idealized imaginings.
enrichment.summary: Steerforth asks if David has a sister.

text:
‘That’s a pity,’ said Steerforth. ‘If you had had one,
I should think she would have been a pretty, timid, little, bright-eyed sort of
girl. I should have liked to know her. Good night, young Copperfield.’

enrichment.interest_rationale: Steerforth's romantic idealization of a sister David doesn't have reveals his imaginative nature and his interest in David's intimate world; foreshadows his later destructive desires.

text:
I thought of him very much after I went to bed, and raised myself, I recollect,
to look at him where he lay in the moonlight, with his handsome face turned up,
and his head reclining easily on his arm. He was a person of great power in my
eyes; that was, of course, the reason of my mind running on him. No veiled
future dimly glanced upon him in the moonbeams. There was no shadowy picture of
his footsteps, in the garden that I dreamed of walking in all night.

enrichment.interest_rationale: A profound meditation on Steerforth's mystery and power; David's adult retrospection emphasizes how incomprehensible and unknowable Steerforth's future proves, lending tragic foreshadowing to their friendship.
enrichment.best_quote: No veiled future dimly glanced upon him in the moonbeams. There was no shadowy picture of his footsteps, in the garden that I dreamed of walking in all night.
enrichment.summary: David reflects on his contemplation of the sleeping Steerforth, marvelling at the mystery of him and the inability of premonition to foresee his fate.

text:
School began in earnest next day. A profound impression was made upon me, I
remember, by the roar of voices in the schoolroom suddenly becoming hushed as
death when Mr. Creakle entered after breakfast, and stood in the doorway
looking round upon us like a giant in a story-book surveying his captives.

enrichment.interest_rationale: Strong atmospheric opening establishing the terror of Mr. Creakle's entrance and control over the schoolroom.
enrichment.best_quote: stood in the doorway looking round upon us like a giant in a story-book surveying his captives
enrichment.summary: David describes the terrifying moment when the schoolroom falls silent at Mr. Creakle's entrance, comparing him to a giant surveying captives.
